metadata.title: The Polynomial Method Strikes Back: Tight Quantum Query Bounds via Dual Polynomials

extraction_notes.note: Five results are thmtools restatable environments, which latex_facts does not report; they were extracted by hand as environment bodies (confidence 1.0). The finishing step's 'prose node starts mid-sentence' warnings on them are spurious, and the \combinatorial* restatement in Section 2.7.1 gets no node.

Informal intro Theorems 1-6 are numbered environments, but they differ from the formal results (other parameters, one combines upper and lower bounds), so they were kept as nodes rather than dropped as restated copies. A uses edge links each formal result to the informal one.

Theorem 35's proof is prose spread over Section 3. It was split into a WLOG-reduction part (Section 3) and the final construction in 3.4.2, which ends 'This completes the proof'. The construction in between (definitions of P_R, p_R, Lemmas 36-41) consists of separate nodes.
Fact 46 states the cited alternating binomial-sum identity, so it was typed theorem (external) per Hard rule 4 rather than claim.
F^prop and F^{<=N} are introduced by one sentence and defined jointly in one align*, so they could not be split into two definition nodes.
In the parameter itemize lists the parser flags only some \item lines as author labels. Steps start at the flagged items, and each unflagged item is grouped with the preceding step.

Sections 3.2-3.3 develop the NOR warmup and the 'polynomials as algorithms' language informally. The warmup is one example node, and Algorithms 1-2 (informal pseudocode for polynomial constructions) are algorithm nodes.

Not extracted: the abstract, Tables 1-2 of prior bounds, the reduction diagram figure, the overview/outline paragraphs (Step 1/2/3 sketches), and cited prior bounds mentioned only as history in the introduction (Sherstov's O~(n^{3/4}) upper bound, Belovs' and Ambainis' k-distinctness algorithms, Aaronson-Shi).
Lemma 39 is called an immediate consequence of (imdoneguys) and Proposition 59 is stated without proof. Both kept their environment types and were given rigor semi_formal.

nodes.name: Approximate degree
nodes.statement: The approximate degree of a Boolean function $f \colon \{-1, 1\}^n \to \{-1, 1\}$, denoted $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}(f)$, is the least degree of a real polynomial $p$ such that $|p(x)-f(x)| \leq 1/3$ for all $x \in \{-1,1\}^n$.
nodes.genus: least degree of a real polynomial

nodes.name: Approximate degree lower-bounds quantum query complexity (Beals et al.)
nodes.statement: In 1998, Beals et al.~\cite{beals} observed that the bounded-error quantum query complexity of a function $f$ is lower bounded by (one half times) the approximate degree of $f$.
nodes.origin_citation: Beals, Buhrman, Cleve, Mosca, de Wolf 1998
nodes.statement_short: Bounded-error quantum query complexity is at least half the approximate degree (the polynomial method).
conclusions: the bounded-error quantum query complexity of a function $f$ is lower bounded by (one half times) the approximate degree of $f$

nodes.name: Input size n = N log R
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a power of two and $N \geq R$, and let $n=N \cdot \log_2 R$.

nodes.name: Frequency of a range item
nodes.statement: We let the \emph{frequency} $f_i$ of range item $i \in R$ denote the number of times $i$ appears in the input list.

nodes.name: k-junta testing
nodes.statement: $k$-junta testing: Given an input in $\{-1,1\}^n$ representing the truth table of a function $\{-1,1\}^{\log n} \to \{-1,1\}$, determine whether this function depends on at most $k$ of its input bits, or is at least $\varepsilon$-far from any such function.
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether a truth table of length n depends on at most k inputs or is eps-far from every such function.

nodes.name: Approximate degree of Surjectivity (informal)
nodes.statement: The approximate degree of $\mathsf{ SURJ}$ is $\tilde{\Theta}(n^{3/4})$.
nodes.statement_short: adeg(SURJ) = Theta~(n^{3/4}).
conclusions: The approximate degree of $\mathsf{ SURJ}$ is $\tilde{\Theta}(n^{3/4})$.
nodes.label: thm:introsurj

nodes.name: k-distinctness lower bound (informal)
nodes.statement: For any $k\geq 2$, the approximate degree and quantum query complexity of $k$-distinctness is $\tilde{\Omega}(n^{3/4-1/(2k)})$.
conclusions: the approximate degree and quantum query complexity of $k$-distinctness is $\tilde{\Omega}(n^{3/4-1/(2k)})$
nodes.label: thm:introkdist

nodes.name: Image Size Testing lower bound (informal)
nodes.statement: The approximate degree and quantum query complexity of Image Size Testing is $\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{n})$.
conclusions: The approximate degree and quantum query complexity of Image Size Testing is $\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{n})$.
nodes.label: thm:imagesize

nodes.name: k-junta testing lower bound (informal)
nodes.statement: The approximate degree and quantum query complexity of $k$-junta testing is $\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{k})$.
conclusions: The approximate degree and quantum query complexity of $k$-junta testing is $\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{k})$.
nodes.label: thm:juntatesting

nodes.name: Statistical distance from uniform lower bound (informal)
nodes.statement: There is a constant $c > 0$ such that the approximate degree and quantum query complexity of approximating the statistical distribution of a distribution over a range of size $n$ from the uniform distribution over the same range to additive error $c$ is is $\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{n})$.
nodes.statement_short: Approximating statistical distance from uniform to a small constant additive error needs degree/queries Omega~(sqrt n).
conclusions: There is a constant $c > 0$ such that the approximate degree and quantum query complexity of approximating the statistical distribution
nodes.label: thm:sdu

nodes.name: Shannon entropy approximation lower bound (informal)
nodes.statement: There is a constant $c > 0$ such that the approximate degree and quantum query complexity of approximating the Shannon entropy of a distribution over a range of size $n$ to additive error $c$ is is $\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{n})$.
nodes.statement_short: Approximating Shannon entropy to a small constant additive error needs degree/queries Omega~(sqrt n).
conclusions: There is a constant $c > 0$ such that the approximate degree and quantum query complexity of approximating the Shannon entropy
nodes.label: thm:introentropy

nodes.name: AC0 circuit with approximate degree n^{1-delta} (Bun and Thaler)
nodes.statement: For any constant $\delta \!>\! 0$, there is an AC$^0$ circuit with approximate degree $\Omega(n^{1-\delta})$.
nodes.section: 1.2 Prior Work on Lower Bounding Approximate Degree
conclusions: there is an AC$^0$ circuit with approximate degree $\Omega(n^{1-\delta})$
nodes.label: thm:mainthm

nodes.name: Sherstov's robust composition theorem
nodes.statement: For any Boolean functions $f$ and $h$, $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}(h \circ f) = O\left(\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}(h) \cdot \widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}(f)\right)$.
nodes.section: 1.2 Prior Work on Lower Bounding Approximate Degree
nodes.statement_short: Approximate degree is at most multiplicative under block composition.
conclusions: $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}(h \circ f) = O\left(\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}(h) \cdot \widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}(f)\right)$
nodes.label: thm:robust

nodes.name: Condition 1 (bounded frequency)
nodes.statement: Every range item has frequency at most $T$, for a specific threshold $T=O(N^{1/3}) \ll N$.
nodes.statement_short: Every range item has frequency at most T = O(N^{1/3}).
nodes.label: cond

nodes.name: Hamming weight decay condition for the OR dual witness
nodes.statement: |\gamma(x)| \cdot \binom{N}{|x|}\leq \frac{1}{\mathrm{poly}(|x|)},
nodes.label: decaykey

nodes.name: Notation [N] and [N]_0
nodes.statement: For a natural number $N$, let $[N] = \{1, 2, \dots, N\}$ and $[N]_0 = \{0, 1, 2, \dots, N\}$.

nodes.name: Soft-O notation
nodes.statement: As is standard, we say that a function $f(n)$ is in $\tilde{O}(h(n))$ if there exists a constant $k$ such that $f(n)$ is in $O(h(n) \cdot \log^k(h(n)))$.

nodes.name: Low Hamming weight inputs H^n_{<=T}
nodes.statement: For $1 \le T \le n$, let $H^n_{\leq T}$ denote the subset of $\{-1,1\}^n$ consisting of all inputs Hamming weight at most $T$. We use $|x|$ to denote the Hamming weight of an input $x \in \{-1,1\}^n$, so $H^n_{\leq T} = \{x \in \{-1,1\}^n \colon |x| \leq T\}$.
differentia: consisting of all inputs Hamming weight at most $T$
nodes.label: def:ht

nodes.name: Approximate Degree With Boundedness Outside of the Promise Required
nodes.statement: Let $\varepsilon > 0$ and $\mathcal{X} \subseteq \{-1,1\}^n$. The $\varepsilon$-\emph{approximate degree} of a Boolean function $f : \mathcal{X} \to \{-1,1\}$, denoted $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_\varepsilon(f)$, is the least degree of a real polynomial $p : \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $|p(x) - f(x)| \le \varepsilon$ for all $x \in \mathcal{X}$ and $|p(x)| \le 1 + \varepsilon$ for all $x \in \{-1,1\}^n \setminus \mathcal{X}$. We use the term \emph{approximate degree} without qualification to refer to $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}(f) = \widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_{1/3}(f)$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Two Variants of Approximate Degree and Their Dual Formulations
nodes.statement_short: eps-approximate degree of a partial function, with the approximant bounded by 1+eps off the promise.
nodes.genus: the least degree of a real polynomial $p : \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}$

nodes.name: Dual characterization of approximate degree
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{X} \subseteq \{-1,1\}^n$, and let $f : \mathcal{X} \to \{-1,1\}$. Then $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_{\varepsilon}(f) \geq d$ if and only if there exists a function $\psi \colon \{-1,1\}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying the following properties. \begin{align} &\sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}}\psi(x) \cdot f(x) - \sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^n \setminus \mathcal{X}} |\psi(x)| > \varepsilon, \\ &\sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^n} |\psi(x)| = 1, \text{ and } \\ &\text{ For every polynomial } p \colon \{-1,1\}^n \to \mathbb{R} \text{ of degree less than } d, \sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^n} p(x) \cdot \psi(x) = 0. \end{align}
nodes.section: 2.2 Two Variants of Approximate Degree and Their Dual Formulations
nodes.origin_citation: standard LP duality; e.g. Bun & Thaler (Theory of Computing)
nodes.statement_short: deg_eps(f) >= d iff some psi of l1-norm 1 has correlation > eps with f and pure high degree >= d.
conclusions: Then $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_{\varepsilon}(f) \geq d$ if and only if there exists a function
nodes.label: prop:duality

nodes.name: Dual witness conditions (correlation, unit norm, pure high degree)
nodes.statement: &\sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}}\psi(x) \cdot f(x) - \sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^n \setminus \mathcal{X}} |\psi(x)| > \varepsilon, \\ &\sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^n} |\psi(x)| = 1, \text{ and } \\ &\text{ For every polynomial } p \colon \{-1,1\}^n \to \mathbb{R} \text{ of degree less than } d, \sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^n} p(x) \cdot \psi(x) = 0.
nodes.section: 2.2 Two Variants of Approximate Degree and Their Dual Formulations
nodes.label: eq:corr

nodes.name: Dual polynomial
nodes.statement: We will refer to functions $\psi \colon \{-1,1\}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ as \emph{dual polynomials}.
nodes.section: 2.2 Two Variants of Approximate Degree and Their Dual Formulations

nodes.name: l1-norm of a dual polynomial
nodes.statement: We refer to $\sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^n} |\psi(x)|$ as the $\ell_1$-norm of $\psi$, and denote this quantity by $\|\psi\|_1$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Two Variants of Approximate Degree and Their Dual Formulations

nodes.name: Pure high degree
nodes.statement: If $\psi$ satisfies Equation \eqref{eq:phd}, it is said to have \emph{pure high degree} at least $d$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Two Variants of Approximate Degree and Their Dual Formulations

nodes.name: Correlation of f and psi
nodes.section: 2.2 Two Variants of Approximate Degree and Their Dual Formulations
nodes.statement_short: Correlation <f,psi> = sum over the promise of f psi minus the l1 mass of psi off the promise.

nodes.name: Approximate Degree With Unboundedness Permitted Outside of the Promise
nodes.statement: Let $\varepsilon > 0$ and $\mathcal{X}$ be a finite set. The $\varepsilon$-\emph{unbounded approximate degree} of a Boolean function $f : \mathcal{X} \to \{-1,1\}$, denoted $\widetilde{\operatorname{ubdeg}}_\varepsilon(f)$, is the least degree of a real polynomial $p : \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $|p(x) - f(x)| \le \varepsilon$ for all $x \in \mathcal{X}$ (if $\mathcal{X}$ is a strict subset of a larger domain, then no constraints are placed on $p(x)$ for $x \not\in \mathcal{X}$). We use the term \emph{unbounded approximate degree} without qualification to refer to $\widetilde{\operatorname{ubdeg}}(f) = \widetilde{\operatorname{ubdeg}}_{1/3}(f)$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Two Variants of Approximate Degree and Their Dual Formulations
nodes.statement_short: ubdeg_eps(f): least degree of a pointwise eps-approximant on the promise, unconstrained elsewhere.
nodes.genus: the least degree of a real polynomial $p : \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}$

nodes.name: Dual characterization of unbounded approximate degree
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{X} \subseteq \{-1,1\}^n$, and let $f : \mathcal{X} \to \{-1,1\}$. Then $\widetilde{\operatorname{ubdeg}}_{\varepsilon}(f) \geq d$ if and only if there exists a function $\psi \colon \{-1,1\}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying the following properties. \begin{align} &\psi(x) = 0 \text{ for all } x \not\in \mathcal{X}, \\ &\sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}}\psi(x) \cdot f(x) > \varepsilon, \\ &\sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^n} |\psi(x)| = 1, \text{ and } \\ &\text{ For every polynomial } p \colon \{-1,1\}^n \to \mathbb{R} \text{ of degree less than } d, \sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^n} p(x) \cdot \psi(x) = 0. \end{align}
nodes.section: 2.2 Two Variants of Approximate Degree and Their Dual Formulations
nodes.origin_citation: standard LP duality; e.g. Sherstov (pattern matrix method)
nodes.statement_short: ubdeg_eps(f) >= d iff a dual witness exists that vanishes off the promise.
conclusions: Then $\widetilde{\operatorname{ubdeg}}_{\varepsilon}(f) \geq d$ if and only if there exists a function
nodes.label: prop:ub-duality

nodes.name: Dual witness conditions for unbounded approximate degree
nodes.statement: &\psi(x) = 0 \text{ for all } x \not\in \mathcal{X}, \\ &\sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}}\psi(x) \cdot f(x) > \varepsilon, \\ &\sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^n} |\psi(x)| = 1, \text{ and } \\ &\text{ For every polynomial } p \colon \{-1,1\}^n \to \mathbb{R} \text{ of degree less than } d, \sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^n} p(x) \cdot \psi(x) = 0.
nodes.section: 2.2 Two Variants of Approximate Degree and Their Dual Formulations
nodes.label: eq:ub-zero

nodes.name: deg and ubdeg coincide for total functions
nodes.statement: Observe that $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}(f)$ and $\widetilde{\operatorname{ubdeg}}(f)$ coincide for total functions $f$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Two Variants of Approximate Degree and Their Dual Formulations
conclusions: $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}(f)$ and $\widetilde{\operatorname{ubdeg}}(f)$ coincide

nodes.name: Approximate degree of AND and OR (Nisan-Szegedy)
nodes.statement: For any constant $\varepsilon \in (0, 1)$, the functions $\mathsf{AND}$ and $\mathsf{ OR}$ on $n$ bits have $\varepsilon$-approximate degree $\Theta(n^{1/2})$, and the same holds for their negations.
conclusions: the functions $\mathsf{AND}$ and $\mathsf{ OR}$ on $n$ bits have $\varepsilon$-approximate degree $\Theta(n^{1/2})$
the same holds for their negations
nodes.label: andornor

nodes.name: Minsky-Papert symmetrization
nodes.statement: Let $p \colon \{-1,1\}^n \to \{-1,1\}$ be an arbitrary polynomial and let $[n]_0$ denote the set $\{0, 1, \dots, n\}$. Then there is a univariate polynomial $q \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ of degree at most $\deg(p)$ such that \[q(t) = \frac{1}{\binom{n}{ t}} \sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^n \colon |x|=t} p(x)\] for all $t \in [n]_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Averaging a polynomial over Hamming layers gives a univariate polynomial of no larger degree.
conclusions: there is a univariate polynomial $q \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ of degree at most $\deg(p)$
nodes.label: lem:mp

nodes.name: Surjectivity function SURJ
nodes.statement: For $N \ge R$, we define $\mathsf{ SURJ}_{N, R} : [R]^N \to \{-1,1\}$ by $\mathsf{ SURJ}_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = -1$ iff for every $j \in [R]$, there exists an $i$ such that $s_i = j$.
nodes.statement_short: SURJ_{N,R}(s) = -1 iff every range item in [R] appears in the list s.
nodes.label: def:surj

nodes.name: Dummy-augmented Surjectivity dSURJ
nodes.statement: For $N \ge R$, we define $\mathsf{dSURJ}_{N, R} : [R]_0^N \to \{-1,1\}$ by $\mathsf{dSURJ}_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = -1$ iff for every $j \in [R]$, there exists an $i$ such that $s_i = j$.
nodes.statement_short: Surjectivity on [R]_0^N where the dummy item 0 is ignored.
nodes.label: def:dumsurj

nodes.name: Reduction from dSURJ to SURJ
nodes.statement: Let $\varepsilon > 0$ and $N \ge R$. Then \[ \widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_\varepsilon(\mathsf{dSURJ}_{N, R}) \le \widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_\varepsilon(\mathsf{ SURJ}_{N + 1, R + 1}) \cdot \log(R+1).\]
conclusions: \widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_\varepsilon(\mathsf{dSURJ}_{N, R}) \le \widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_\varepsilon(\mathsf{ SURJ}_{N + 1, R + 1}) \cdot \log(R+1).
nodes.label: prop:dumsurj-reduction

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 18 (dSURJ to SURJ)
nodes.statement: Let $p : \{-1,1\}^{(N+1) \cdot \log(R+1)} \to \{-1,1\}$ be a polynomial of degree $d$ that $\varepsilon$-approximates $\mathsf{ SURJ}_{N + 1, R+1}$. We will use $p$ to construct a polynomial of degree $d$ that $\varepsilon$-approximates $\mathsf{dSURJ}_{N, R}$. Recall that an input to $\mathsf{dSURJ}_{N, R}$ takes the form $(s_1, \dots, s_N)$ where each $s_i$ is the binary representation of a number in $[R]_0$. Define the transformation $T : [R]_0 \to [R + 1]$ by \[T(s) = \begin{cases} R + 1 & \text{ if } s = 0 \\ s & \text{ otherwise}. \end{cases}\] Note that as a mapping between binary representations, the function $T$ is exactly computed by a vector of polynomials of degree at most $\log(R+1)$. For every $(s_1, \dots, s_N) \in [R]_0^N$, observe that \[\mathsf{dSURJ}_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = \mathsf{ SURJ}_{N + 1, R+1}(T(s_1), \dots, T(s_N), R+1).\] Hence, the polynomial \[p(T(s_1), \dots, T(s_N), R+1)\] is a polynomial of degree $d \cdot \log(R+1)$ that $\varepsilon$-approximates $\mathsf{dSURJ}_{N, R}$.
nodes.statement_short: Map the dummy item 0 to a fresh item R+1 and append one copy of R+1; compose the SURJ approximant with this low-degree map.

nodes.name: k-distinctness function DIST^k
nodes.statement: For integers $k, N, R$ with $k \le N$, define the function $\mathsf{DIST}^k_{N, R} : [R]^N \to \{-1,1\}$ by $\mathsf{DIST}^k_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = -1$ iff there exist $r \in [R]$ and distinct indices $i_1, \dots, i_k$ such that $s_{i_1} = \dots = s_{i_k} = r$.
nodes.statement_short: DIST^k(s) = -1 iff some range item appears at least k times.

nodes.name: Dummy-augmented k-distinctness dDIST^k
nodes.statement: For integers $k, N, R$ with $k \le N$, define the function $\mathsf{dDIST}^k_{N, R} : [R]_0^N \to \{-1,1\}$ by $\mathsf{dDIST}^k_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = -1$ iff there exist $r \in [R]$ and distinct indices $i_1, \dots, i_k$ such that $s_{i_1} = \dots = s_{i_k} = r$.

nodes.name: Why k >= 2 is needed for the dDIST reduction
nodes.statement: For $k \ge 2$, a lower bound on the approximate degree of $\mathsf{dDIST}^k$ implies a lower bound on the approximate degree of $\mathsf{DIST}^k$. The restriction that $k \ge 2$ is essential, because the function $\mathsf{DIST}^1$ is the constant function that evaluates to $\mathsf{TRUE}$ on \emph{any} input (since at least one range item must always have frequency at least one), whereas $\mathsf{dDIST}^1$ contains $\mathsf{ OR}_N$ as a subfunction, and hence has approximate degree at least $\Omega(\sqrt{N})$.
nodes.statement_short: For k=1 DIST is constant while dDIST contains OR_N, so the reduction needs k >= 2.

nodes.name: Reduction from dDIST^k to DIST^k
nodes.statement: Let $\varepsilon > 0$, $N, R \in \mathbb{N}$, and $k \ge 2$. Then \[ \deg_\varepsilon(\mathsf{dDIST}^k_{N, R}) \le \deg_\varepsilon(\mathsf{DIST}^k_{N, R+N}) \cdot \log(R+1).\]
conclusions: \deg_\varepsilon(\mathsf{dDIST}^k_{N, R}) \le \deg_\varepsilon(\mathsf{DIST}^k_{N, R+N}) \cdot \log(R+1).
nodes.label: prop:dumdist-reduction

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 21 (dDIST to DIST)
nodes.statement: The proof is similar to that of \Cref{prop:dumsurj-reduction}, but uses a slightly more involved reduction. Let $p : \{-1,1\}^{2N\cdot \log(R+N)} \to \{-1,1\}$ be a polynomial of degree $d$ that $\varepsilon$-approximates $\mathsf{DIST}^k_{N, R+N}$. We will use $p$ to construct a polynomial of degree $d$ that $\varepsilon$-approximates $\mathsf{dDIST}^k_{N, R}$. For each $i = 1, \dots, R$, define a transformation $T_i : [R]_0 \to [R+N]$ by \[T_i(s) = \begin{cases} R + i & \text{ if } s = 0 \\ s & \text{ otherwise}. \end{cases}\] As a mapping between binary representations, the function $T=(T_1, \dots, T_N)$ is exactly computed by a vector of polynomials of degree at most $\log(R+1)$. For every $(s_1, \dots, s_N) \in [R]_0^N$, observe that \[\mathsf{dDIST}^k_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = \mathsf{DIST}^k_{N, R+N}(T_1(s_1), \dots, T_N(s_N)).\] Hence, the polynomial \[p(T(s_1), \dots, T(s_N))\] is a polynomial of degree $d \cdot \log(R+1)$ that $\varepsilon$-approximates $\mathsf{dSURJ}_{N, R}$.
nodes.statement_short: As for Proposition 18: replace each dummy 0 in position i by a distinct fresh item R+i and compose.

nodes.name: Block composition
nodes.statement: For functions $f : Y^n \to Z$ and $g: X \to Y$, define the \emph{block composition} $f \circ g : X^n \to Z$ by $(f\circ g)(x_1, \dots, x_n) = f(g(x_1), \dots, g(x_n))$, for all $x_1, \dots, x_n \in X$.

nodes.name: Symmetric function
nodes.statement:
Suppose $g$ is a \emph{symmetric} function, in the sense that for any $x \in \{-1,1\}^N$ and any permutation $\sigma : [N] \to [N]$, we have
\[g(x_1, \dots, x_N) = g(x_{\sigma(1)}, \dots, x_{\sigma(N)}).\]
Equivalently, the value of $g$ on any input $x$ depends only on its Hamming weight $|x|$.

nodes.name: Symmetric property F^prop and promise composition F^{<=N}
nodes.section: 2.5 Connecting Symmetric Properties and Block Composed Functions
nodes.statement_short: F^prop applies f to the g-values of the R indicator vectors of a list; F^{<=N} is f o g restricted to total Hamming weight <= N.

nodes.name: Symmetric properties vs block compositions (Bun-Thaler reduction)
nodes.statement: Let $f : \{-1,1\}^R \to \{-1,1\}$ be any function and let $g : \{-1,1\}^N \to \{-1,1\}$ be a symmetric function. Then for $F^{\operatorname{prop}}$ and $F^{\le N}$ defined above, and for any $\varepsilon > 0$, we have \[\deg_\varepsilon(F^{\operatorname{prop}}) \ge \widetilde{\operatorname{ubdeg}}_\varepsilon(F^{\le N}).\]

conclusions: \deg_\varepsilon(F^{\operatorname{prop}}) \ge \widetilde{\operatorname{ubdeg}}_\varepsilon(F^{\le N}).

nodes.name: Justification of Corollary 24
nodes.statement: In the case where $f = \mathsf{AND}_R$ and $g = \mathsf{ OR}_N$, the function $F^{\operatorname{prop}}(s_1, \dots, s_N)$ is the Surjectivity function augmented with a dummy item, $\mathsf{dSURJ}_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N)$.

nodes.name: Dual block composition
nodes.statement: Let $\Psi : \{-1,1\}^M \to \mathbb{R}$ and $\psi : \{-1,1\}^m \to \mathbb{R}$ be functions that are not identically zero. Let $x=(x_1, \dots, x_M) \in \left(\{-1,1\}^{m}\right)^M$. Define the \emph{dual block composition} of $\Psi$ and $\psi$, denoted $\Psi \star \psi : (\{-1,1\}^m)^M \to \mathbb{R}$, by \[(\Psi \star \psi)(x_1, \dots, x_M) = 2^M \cdot \Psi(\dots, \operatorname{sgn}\left(\psi(x_i)\right), \dots) \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^M |\psi(x_i)|.\]
nodes.statement_short: (Psi*psi)(x) = 2^M Psi(sgn psi(x_1),...,sgn psi(x_M)) prod |psi(x_i)|.

nodes.name: Properties of dual block composition
nodes.statement: The dual block composition satisfies the following properties: \paragraph{\emph{Preservation of $\ell_1$-norm}:} If $\|\Psi\|_1 = 1$, $\|\psi\|_1 = 1$, and $\langle \psi, \mathbf{1}\rangle = 0$, then \begin{equation}\|\Psi \star \psi\|_1 = 1. \end{equation} \paragraph{\emph{Multiplicativity of pure high degree}:} If $\langle \Psi, P \rangle = 0$ for every polynomial $P \colon \{-1,1\}^M \to \{-1,1\}$ of degree less than $D$, and $\langle \psi, p \rangle = 0$ for every polynomial $p \colon \{-1,1\}^m \to \{-1,1\}$ of degree less than $d$, then for every polynomial $q \colon \{-1,1\}^{m \cdot M} \to \{-1,1\}$, \begin{equation}\deg q < D \cdot d \implies \langle \Psi \star \psi, q \rangle = 0. \end{equation} \paragraph{\emph{Associativity}:} For every $\zeta: \{-1,1\}^{m_\zeta} \to \mathbb{R}$, $\varphi: \{-1,1\}^{m_\varphi} \to \mathbb{R}$, and $\psi: \{-1,1\}^{m_\psi} \to \mathbb{R}$, we have \begin{equation} (\zeta \star \varphi) \star \psi = \zeta \star (\varphi \star \psi). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Dual block composition preserves l1-norm, multiplies pure high degree, and is associative.
conclusions: The dual block composition satisfies the following properties:
nodes.label: prop:ls

nodes.name: Associativity of dual block composition
nodes.statement: (\zeta \star \varphi) \star \psi = \zeta \star (\varphi \star \psi).

nodes.name: (alpha, beta)-decay condition

A function $\omega: [M]_0 \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfies the $(\alpha, \beta)$-decay condition if \begin{align} &\sum_{t = 0}^M \omega(t) = 0, \\ &\sum_{t = 0}^M |\omega(t)| = 1, \\ &|\omega(t)| \le \alpha \exp (-\beta t) / t^2 \quad \forall t = 1, 2, \dots, M. \end{align}

nodes.name: Primal view of Proposition 31
nodes.statement: \Cref{prop:correction} is framed exclusively in the language of dual polynomials: it states that if a dual polynomial $\xi$ places very little mass on inputs of Hamming weight more than $N$, then there exists another dual polynomial $\nu$ satisfying certain useful properties (we ultimately use $\nu$ to zero out the mass that $\xi$ places on inputs of Hamming weight more than $N$). \Cref{prop:correction} also has a clean \emph{primal} formulation. Roughly speaking, it is equivalent to a bound on the growth rate of any polynomial of degree at most $D$ that is bounded at all inputs of Hamming weight at most $D$. We direct the interested reader to \cite{violalecturenotes} for details of this primal formulation.

nodes.name: Binomial coefficient bound
nodes.statement: Let $k, n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $k \le n$. Then $\binom{n}{k} \le \left(\frac{en}{k}\right)^k$.

nodes.name: Geometric tail sum
nodes.statement: Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\eta > 0$. Then \[\sum_{r = m}^\infty e^{-\eta r} = \frac{1}{1 - e^{-\eta}} \cdot e^{-\eta m}.\]
conclusions: \sum_{r = m}^\infty e^{-\eta r} = \frac{1}{1 - e^{-\eta}} \cdot e^{-\eta m}.
nodes.label: lem:inv-exp-tail

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 33
nodes.statement: We calculate \[\sum_{r = m}^\infty e^{-\eta r} = e^{-\eta m} \cdot \sum_{r = 0}^\infty e^{-\eta r} = e^{-\eta m} \cdot \frac{1}{1 - e^{-\eta}}.\qedhere \]
nodes.statement_short: Factor out e^{-eta m} and sum the geometric series.

nodes.name: Sum of inverse square roots
nodes.statement: Let $m \in N$. Then \[\sum_{r = 1}^m \frac{1}{\sqrt{r}} \le 2 \sqrt{m}.\]
conclusions: \sum_{r = 1}^m \frac{1}{\sqrt{r}} \le 2 \sqrt{m}.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 34
nodes.statement: Using the fact that the function $1/\sqrt{t}$ is decreasing, we may estimate \[ \sum_{r = 1}^m \frac{1}{\sqrt{r}} \le \int_{0}^m \frac{1}{\sqrt{t}} \ dt = 2\sqrt{m}.\qedhere \]
nodes.statement_short: Compare the sum with the integral of 1/sqrt(t).

nodes.name: Proof of the combinatorial lemma (lem:combinatorial)
nodes.statement: Let $T = \lfloor \frac{N}{2M} \rfloor$. For each $s \in \{T, \dots, R\}$, let \[C(s) = \max \left\{ \frac{N}{6 s \ln R}, \frac{N}{6\sqrt{R \cdot s}} \right\}.\] We begin with a simple, but important, structural observation about the set $P$. Let $t = (t_1, \dots, t_R) \in [M]_0^R$ be a sequence such that $t_1 + \dots + t_R > N$. Then we claim that there exists an $s \in \{T \dots, R\}$ such that $t_i \ge C(s)$ for at least $s$ indices $i \in [R]$. To see this, assume without loss of generality that the entries of $\vec{t}$ are sorted so that $t_1 \ge t_2 \ge \dots \ge t_R$. Then there must exist an $s \geq T$ such that $t_s \ge C(s)$. Otherwise, because no $t_i$ can exceed $M$, we would have: \begin{align*} t_1 + \dots + t_R &< T \cdot M + \sum_{s = 1}^R C(s) \\ &\le \frac{N}{2} + \frac{N}{6 \ln R} \sum_{s = 1}^{\lfloor R / \ln^2 R \rfloor} \frac{1}{s} + \frac{N}{6\sqrt{R}} \sum_{s = \lceil R / \ln^2 R \rceil}^R \frac{1}{\sqrt{s}}\\ &\le \frac{N}{2}+ \frac{N}{6} + \frac{N}{3} \\ &= N. \end{align*} where the last inequality follows from \Cref{lem:inv-sqrt} and the fact that $\sum_{s = 1}^m s^{-1} \le \ln m + 1$ (and $R$ is sufficiently large). Since the entries of $\vec{t}$ are sorted, the preceding values $t_1, \dots, t_{s-1} \geq C(s)$ as well. For each subset $S \subseteq [R]$, define \[P_S = \{\vec{t} \in P : t_i \ge C(|S|)\text{ for all indices }i \in S\}.\] The observations above guarantee that for every $\vec{t}=(t_1, \dots, t_R) \in P$, there exists some set $S$ of size at least $s \in \{T, \dots, R\}$ such that $t_i \geq C(s)$ for all $i \in S$. Hence \begin{align*} \hspace{-10mm} \sum_{\vec{t} \in P} \prod_{i = 1}^R \eta_i(t_i) & \leq \sum_{s = T}^{R} \sum_{S \subseteq [R] : |S| = s} \sum_{\vec{t} \in P_S} \prod_{i = 1}^R \eta_i(t_i) \\ & \leq \sum_{s = T}^{R} \binom{R}{s} \left( \max_{i \in \{1, \dots, R\}} \left( \sum_{r=\lceil C(s) \rceil}^M \eta_i(r)\right) \right)^s \left( \max_{i \in \{1, \dots, R\}} \left( \sum_{r = 0}^M \eta_i(r) \right)\right)^{R-s} \hspace{-3.3em}&\hspace{-3em}\\ &\leq 2^{-R}\sum_{s = T}^{R} \binom{R}{s} \left( \sum_{r = \lceil C(s) \rceil}^M 2\alpha \exp(-\beta r ) r^{-2} \right)^s & \hspace{-28mm} \text{by Properties } \eqref{eqn:eta-bound} \text{ and } \eqref{eqn:eta-decay}\\ &\le 2^{-R} \sum_{s = T}^{R} \left( \frac{Re}{s} \right)^s \left(\frac{2\alpha}{(C(s))^2} \right)^{s} \cdot \sum_{r = \lceil C(s) \rceil}^\infty \exp\left(-\beta r s\right) & \hspace{-28mm} \text{by \Cref{lem:binomial}}\\ &\le 2^{-R} \sum_{s = T}^{R} \left( \frac{Re}{s} \right)^s \left(\frac{2\alpha}{(C(s))^2} \right)^{s} \cdot \frac{1}{1 - e^{-\beta s}} \cdot \exp\left(-\beta s C(s)\right) & \hspace{-28mm} \text{by \Cref{lem:inv-exp-tail}}\\ &\le 2^{-R} \sum_{s = T}^{R} \left( \frac{Re}{s} \right)^s \left(\frac{72\alpha R s}{N^2} \right)^{s} \cdot \frac{2}{\beta} \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{\beta N}{6\ln R}\right) & \text{by definition of $C(s)$}\\ &\qquad\qquad\text{ and since } \frac{1}{1 - e^{-\beta s}} \le \frac{1}{1 - (1-\beta/2)} = \frac{2}{\beta} \text{ for } s \ge 1, \beta \in (0, 1) \hspace{-10em}&\hspace{-10em} \\ &\le 2^{-R} \sum_{s = T}^{R} 2^{-s} \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{3 \beta \sqrt{\alpha} R }{ \ln R} + \ln(2/\beta)\right)&\hspace{-28mm}\text{setting } N = \lceil 20 \sqrt{\alpha}\rceil R \\ &\le 2^{-R} \cdot (2 N R)^{-2\Delta}, \end{align*} where \[\Delta = \frac{1}{2\ln(2NR)} \cdot \left(\frac{3\beta \sqrt{\alpha} R}{\ln R} - \ln(2/\beta) \right) \ge \frac{\beta \sqrt{\alpha} R}{4\ln^2 R}\] holds for sufficiently large $R$ by the restrictions placed on $\alpha$ and $\beta$ in the statement of the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Every profile with total weight > N has s coordinates at least C(s) for some s >= T; union bound over these sets using the decay and Lemmas 32-34.

nodes.name: Approximate degree upper bound for Surjectivity
nodes.statement: For any $R \in \mathbb{N}$, we have $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}(\mathsf{ SURJ}_{N,R}) = \tilde{O}(N^{3/4})$.
conclusions: $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}(\mathsf{ SURJ}_{N,R}) = \tilde{O}(N^{3/4})$
nodes.label: thm:surj_upper

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 35, part 1: reduction to R = Theta(N)
nodes.statement:
For the remainder of the section, we focus on proving \Cref{thm:upper} in the case that $R=\Theta(N)$. This is without loss of generality by the following argument. 
If $R > N$, then 
Surjectivity\ is identically false, and hence has (exact) degree 0. 
And if $R=o(N)$, then we can reduce to the case $R=\Theta(N)$ as follows. Let $N'=2N$ and $R' = R + N$;
clearly $R' = \Theta(N)$.
Given an input $x$ to $\mathsf{ SURJ}_{N, R}$, obtain an input $x'$ to $\mathsf{ SURJ}_{N', R'}$ by appending range elements $R+1, \dots, R+N$ to $x$. 
This construction guarantees that $\mathsf{ SURJ}_{N, R}(x) = \mathsf{ SURJ}_{N', R'}(x')$. It follows that an approximation of degree $\tilde{O}(N^{3/4})$ for $\mathsf{ SURJ}_{N', R'}$
implies an approximation of the same degree for $\mathsf{ SURJ}_{N, R}$.
nodes.statement_short: WLOG R = Theta(N): SURJ is constant if R > N, and padding with N new items reduces R = o(N) to R' = Theta(N').

Finally, we will also need to consider a generalized version of Surjectivity, $\mathcal{R}$-Surjectivity\ for some set $\mathcal{R} \subseteq [R]$, which we denote $\mathsf{ SURJ}_{\mathcal{R}}$. 
As with Surjectivity, 
\begin{equation}
    \mathsf{ SURJ}_{\mathcal{R}}:[R]^N \to \{0,1\},
\end{equation}
and $\mathsf{ SURJ}_{\mathcal{R}}(x_1, \ldots, x_N) = 1$ if and only if for all $r \in \mathcal{R}$ there exists an $i\in [N]$ such that $x_i = r$. 
In other words, $\mathsf{ SURJ}_\mathcal{R}(x)=1$ if and only if for all $r\in\mathcal{R}$ we have $\operatorname{\#}_r(x)\geq 1$.

nodes.name: Properties of Chebyshev Polynomials
nodes.statement: Let $d \in \mathbb{N}$. \begin{enumerate}[(1)] \item There exists a polynomial $T_d : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ (the Chebyshev polynomial of degree $d$) such that $T_d(x) \in [-1, 1]$ for all $x \in [-1, 1]$ and $T_d(1 + \mu) \ge \frac{1}{2} \exp(d\sqrt{\mu})$ for all $\mu \in (0, 1)$. \item For any polynomial $p : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ of degree $d$ with $|p(x)| \le 1$ for all $x \in [-1, 1]$, we have that for any $x$ with $|x| > 1$, \begin{equation} |p(x)| \leq |T_d(x)| \leq (2|x|)^d, \end{equation} where $T_d$ is the Chebyshev polynomial of degree $d$. \end{enumerate}

For any polynomial $p : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ of degree $d$ with $|p(x)| \le 1$ for all $x \in [-1, 1]$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 36
nodes.statement: To establish property (1), we use the fact that for $\mu > 0$, the value of the degree $d$ Chebyshev polynomial can be written~\cite[\S 3.2 Problem 8(f)]{cheney} as \begin{align*} T_d(1 + \mu) &= \cosh ( d \operatorname{arcosh} ( 1 + \mu) ) \\ & \ge \cosh ( d \sqrt{\mu} ) & \text{ for } \mu \le 1\\ & \ge \frac{1}{2} \cdot \exp(d \sqrt{\mu}). \end{align*} Property (2) appears as~\cite[3.2 Problem 19]{cheney}.

There is a polynomial $V_{T, \varepsilon}:\{0,1\}^N\to \mathbb{R}$ of degree $O(\sqrt{T}\log (1/\varepsilon))$ such that \begin{align} V_{T, \varepsilon}(x) \in \begin{cases} [0,\varepsilon] &\mathrm{if}~ |x| = 0 \\ [1-\varepsilon,1] & \mathrm{if}~ 1\leq |x| \leq T \\ [-a, a] \text{ for some } a \in {\exp\left(O\left(\sqrt{T} \cdot \log N \cdot \log\left(1/\varepsilon\right)\right)\right)} & \mathrm{if}~ |x| > T \end{cases}. \end{align}

nodes.statement: V_{T, \varepsilon}(x) \in \begin{cases} [0,\varepsilon] &\mathrm{if}~ |x| = 0 \\ [1-\varepsilon,1] & \mathrm{if}~ 1\leq |x| \leq T \\ [-a, a] \text{ for some } a \in {\exp\left(O\left(\sqrt{T} \cdot \log N \cdot \log\left(1/\varepsilon\right)\right)\right)} & \mathrm{if}~ |x| > T \end{cases}.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 37
nodes.statement: Choose $d = O(\sqrt{T} \log(1/\varepsilon))$ so that $M := T_d(1 + 1/T) + 1\ge 2/\varepsilon$ (as guaranteed by Property 1 of \Cref{lem:cheb}). Define $V_{T, \varepsilon}$ by the following affine transformation of $T_d$: \[V_{T, \varepsilon}(x) = \left(1 - \frac{1}{M}\right) - \frac{1}{M} \cdot T_d\left(1 + \frac{1}{T} - \frac{|x|}{T}\right).\] Then for $|x| = 0$, we have \[V_{T, \varepsilon}(x) = \left(1 - \frac{1}{M}\right) - \frac{1}{M} \cdot T_d\left(1 + \frac{1}{T}\right) = 0.\] If $1 \le |x| \le T$, then $1 + 1/T - |x| / T \in [-1, 1]$, so $V_{T, \varepsilon(x)} \in [1-\varepsilon, 1]$. Finally, if $T +1 \le |x| \le N$, then \[|V_{T, \varepsilon}(x)| \le 1 + \frac{1}{M} \cdot T_d(N / T) \le \exp(O(\sqrt{T} \cdot\log N \cdot\log(1/\varepsilon)),\] where the final inequality holds by Equation \eqref{eq:swell}.

nodes.statement: Let $f : \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$ and $g : X \to \{0,1\}$ be Boolean functions, where $X \subseteq \{0, 1\}^m$ for some $m$. Let $p : \{0,1\}^n \to [0, 1]$ be an $\varepsilon$-approximating polynomial for $f$, and let $q : X \to [0, 1]$ be a $\delta$-approximating polynomial for $g$. Then the block composition $p \circ q : X^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is an $(\varepsilon + \delta n)$-approximating polynomial for $f \circ g : X^n \to \{0,1\}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 38
nodes.statement: Fix any input $x = (x_1, \dots, x_n) \in X^n$, and let $y = (g(x_1), \dots, g(x_n)) \in \{0,1\}^n$. Let $z \in [0, 1]^n$ be defined by $z = (q(x_1), \dots, q(x_n))$. Since $p$ is an $\varepsilon$-approximating polynomial for $f$, by the triangle inequality, it suffices to show that $|p(y) - p(z)| \le \delta n$. Let $Z$ be a random variable on $\{0,1\}^n$ where each $Z_i = 1$ independently with probability $z_i$. Then due to the multilinearity of $p$, we have \[p(z) = \mathbb{E}[p(Z)] = \Pr[Z =y] \cdot p(y) + \Pr[Z \ne y] \cdot \mathbb{E}[p(Z) | Z \ne y].\] Since $q$ is a $\delta$-approximating polynomial for $g$, we have $|y_i - z_i| \le \delta$ for every $i \in [n]$. Hence, \[\Pr[Z = y] \ge \left(1 - \delta \right)^n \ge 1 - \delta n.\] Because $p$ is bounded in $[0, 1]$, this implies \[p(z) \ge (1 - \delta n) \cdot p(y) + 0 \ge p(y) - \delta n\] and \[p(z) \le 1 \cdot p(y) + \delta n \cdot 1 = p(y) + \delta n,\] completing the proof.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 40
nodes.statement: We prove the lemma by induction on the number of variables $n$. If $n = 0$, then $p$ is a constant in the interval $[0, 1]$ and the claim is true. Now suppose the claim is true for $n-1$ variables, and let $p : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ with $p(x) \in [0, 1]$ for $x \in \{0,1\}^n$. We begin by decomposing \[p(x) = (1-x_n) \cdot q_0(x_1, \dots, x_{n-1}) + x_n \cdot q_1(x_1, \dots, x_{n-1})\] where $q_0$ and $q_1$ are themselves multilinear polynomials. Since $p(x) \in [0, 1]$ for all $x \in \{0,1\}^n$, this is in particular true when $x_n = 0$. Hence $q_0(x') \in [0, 1]$ for all $x' \in \{0,1\}^{n-1}$. Similarly, setting $x_n = 1$ reveals that $q_1(x') \in [0, 1]$ for all $x' \in \{0,1\}^{n-1}$. Now for any $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with $x' = (x_1, \dots, x_{n-1})$ we have \begin{align*} |p(x)| &= \left| (1 - x_n) \cdot q_0(x') + x_n \cdot q_1(x')\right| \\ &\le |1 - x_n| \cdot |q_0(x')| + |x_n| \cdot |q_1(x')| \\ &\le (|1 - x_n| + |x_n|) \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^{n-1} (|1 - x_i| + |x_i|) \end{align*} where the final inequality uses the inductive hypothesis. This proves the claim.

To upper bound the value of $|p_\mathcal{R}(x)|$ for $x\notin \mathcal{P}_\mathcal{R}$, we exploit the structure of $p_\mathcal{R}$ as a multilinear polynomial $w$ of degree $O(\sqrt{N})$ over the variables $z_1,\ldots,z_{|\mathcal{R}|}$, where each $z_r$ is the output of the $r^\mathrm{th}$ polynomial from \Cref{lem:orT}. That is, $$z_r = V_{T, 1/(20n)}\left({\mathds{1}}[x_1 = r], \dots, {\mathds{1}}[x_N = r]\right).$$ If $b_\mathcal{R}(x)$ range items appear greater than $T$ times, this means that up to $b_\mathcal{R}(x)$ of the variables $z_r$ might take values outside $[0,1]$. By \Cref{lem:real-bound}, \[|w(z)| \le \prod_{r \in \mathcal{R}} \left(|1 - z_r| + |z_r|\right) \le \exp\left(b_\mathcal{R}(x) \cdot \tilde{O}\left(\sqrt{T}\right)\right),\] since each $z_r $ that is in $[0, 1]$ contributes a factor of exactly $1$ to the product, whereas each of the remaining $b_\mathcal{R}(x)$ variables contributes a factor of at most ${\exp(\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T}))}$ to the product.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 35, part 2: the approximating polynomial r(x)
nodes.statement:
Using the tools from \Cref{sec:surj-hard-inputs} and the above discussion, we can now construct a polynomial that corresponds to the informal description in \Cref{alg:SURJalmost}:
\begin{equation}
    r(x) = \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\mathcal{S} \in \binom{[N]}{S}} \sum_{y \in [R]^S} {\mathds{1}}_y(x_\mathcal{S}) p_{\mathcal{R}(y)}(x). 
\end{equation}
This is a polynomial of degree $S\log R + \max_{y}\{\deg(p_{\mathcal{R}(y)})\} = \tilde{O}(S + \sqrt{NT}) = \tilde{O}(N^{3/4})$, using $S=\tilde{\Theta}(N^{3/4})$ and $T=\tilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{N})$ (where the factors hidden by the $\tilde{\Theta}$ notation will be chosen later). The value of the polynomial on input $x$ is
\begin{equation} r(x) = \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\mathcal{S} \in \binom{[N]}{S}} p_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x). 
\end{equation}
where recall that $\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})$ is as defined in Equation \eqref{nomoreeqs}.
The right hand side of Equation \eqref{fleck} is precisely the expected value of the polynomial $p_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x)$ when $\mathcal{S}$ is a uniformly random set of size $S$. We will now show that $r(x)$ is an approximating polynomial for Surjectivity, i.e., that for all $x\in[R]^N$, $|\mathsf{ SURJ}(x)-r(x)|\leq 1/3$.




Recalling that $b_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}$ is the number of range items $r \in \mathcal{R}$ that appear in $x$ greater than $T$ times (cf. Equation \eqref{eq:b}),
we compute the value of the polynomial $r(x)$ on an input $x$:
\begin{align}
    r(x) &= \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\mathcal{S} \in \binom{[N]}{S}} p_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x) \\
    &= \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \left(\sum_{\mathcal{S} \in \binom{[N]}{S}} \sum_{b=0}^{N/T} {\mathds{1}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x)=b] \cdot p_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x) \right)\\
    &= \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\mathcal{S} \in \binom{[N]}{S}} {\mathds{1}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x)=0] \cdot p_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x) \\
    &\qquad\qquad\qquad + \sum_{b=1}^{N/T} \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\mathcal{S} \in \binom{[N]}{S}}  {\mathds{1}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x)=b]  \cdot p_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x), \end{align}
where we split up the sum into the $b=0$ \eqref{eq:t1} and $b\geq 1$ \eqref{eq:t2}  cases.
We first show that the $b\geq1$ term \eqref{eq:t2} has essentially no contribution to the final value. 

When $b_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x) \geq 1$, we know by \Cref{lem:boundonprcal} that the magnitude of the polynomial $|p_\mathcal{R}(x)|$ is at most $\exp\left(b_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x) \cdot \tilde{O}\left(\sqrt{T}\right)\right)$.
Thus the magnitude of the term in Expression \eqref{eq:t2} is at most
\begin{align}
    &\sum_{b=1}^{N/T} \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\mathcal{S} \in \binom{[N]}{S}}  {\mathds{1}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x)=b] \cdot \exp(b \cdot \tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})) \\
    =&\sum_{b=1}^{N/T} \Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x)=b] \cdot \exp\left(b \cdot \tilde{O}\left(\sqrt{T}\right)\right).
\end{align}


We now need to compute the value of $\Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x)=b]$ for each $b$. Intuitively, this roughly corresponds to the probability that we sample $S=\tilde{\Theta}(N^{3/4})$ elements from the input and miss all $bT$ elements that correspond to the $T = \tilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{N})$ copies of the $b$ range items that appear at least $T$ times. 
If we were to sample $N / (bT)$ elements, the probability of seeing none of the $b T$ elements would be $\Theta(1)$. 
Since we are sampling $S=\tilde{\Theta}(N^{3/4}) \gg N / (bT)$ elements, the probability of not seeing one of the $bT$ elements is ${\exp(-bST/N)} = {\exp(-b \cdot \tilde{\Omega}(N^{1/4}))}$. We make this heuristic calculation formal in the following lemma:

\begin{lemma} Let $S, T \le N$. Let $\mathcal{S} \subset [N]$ be a random subset of size $S$. Then for every $x \in [R]^N$ and every $b \ge 1$,
\[\Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x) \ge b] \leq {\exp(-b \cdot (ST/N - \log N))},\]
recalling that $b_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}$ is the number of range items $r \in \mathcal{R}$ that appear in $x$ more than $T$ times, but do not appear in $x_\mathcal{S}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
To calculate the probability of interest, we begin by analyzing a simplified experiment. Suppose there are $b$ range items $r_1, \dots, r_b$ each appearing greater than $T$ times in $x$. We compute the probability that \emph{none} of the items $r_1, \dots, r_b$ appear in the sample $x_\mathcal{S}$. If $T \ge N - S$, then this probability is zero. Otherwise, by direct calculation, we have for each $i = 1, \dots, b$:
\[\Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[r_i \notin x_\mathcal{S} | r_1 \notin x_\mathcal{S}, \dots, r_{i-1} \notin x_\mathcal{S}] \le \prod_{j = 0}^{S-1} \left(1 - \frac{T}{N-j} \right) \le \left( 1 - \frac{T}{N}\right)^S \le \exp \left(-\frac{ST}{N} \right).\]
Hence the probability that none of $r_1, \dots, r_b$ appear is
\[\Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[r_1 \notin x_\mathcal{S} \land \dots \land r_b \notin x_\mathcal{S}] = \prod_{i  = 1}^b \Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[r_i \notin x_\mathcal{S} | r_1 \notin x_\mathcal{S}, \dots, r_{i-1} \notin x_\mathcal{S}] \le \exp \left(-\frac{bST}{N} \right).\]

Now fix an arbitrary $x$, and let $r_1, \dots, r_{k}$ be the range items appearing greater than $T$ times in $x$. Observe that $k \le N/T$. We estimate the probability of interest by taking a union bound over all subsets of $r_1, \dots, r_k$ of size $b$:
\begin{align*}
\Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x) \ge b] &\le \sum_{Y \subseteq [k] : |Y| = b} \Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[r_{i_j} \notin x_\mathcal{S} \quad \forall j \in Y] \\
& \le \binom{k}{b} \exp \left(-\frac{bST}{N}\right) \\
&\le \exp \left( -\frac{bST}{N} + b \log N\right).
\end{align*}
\end{proof}


From \Cref{lem:prob-b} we know that $\Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x)=b] \leq {\exp(-b \cdot \tilde{\Omega}(ST/N))}$.
Hence the $b\geq1$ term \eqref{eq:t2} is at most
\begin{align}
    \sum_{b=1}^{N/T} {\exp(-b \cdot \tilde{\Omega}(ST/N))} \cdot {\exp(b \cdot \tilde{O}(\sqrt{T}))} = o(1),
\end{align}
by choosing $T = \tilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{N})$ and $S = \tilde{\Theta}(N^{3/4})$ appropriately. This shows that the term in \eqref{eq:t2} does not significantly influence the value of the polynomial for any input $x$.

Thus we have for any input $x$,
\begin{align}
    r(x) = \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\mathcal{S} \in \binom{[N]}{S}} {\mathds{1}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x)=0]  \cdot p_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x) + o(1).
\end{align}

By \Cref{lem:promiseSURJ}, we know that if $b_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x)=0$ (and hence $x \in \mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}$), then $p_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x) $ is a $(1/10)$-approximation to $\mathsf{ SURJ}(x)$. Applying \Cref{lem:prob-b} once again shows that $\Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x) \ge 1] \le \exp(- \tilde{\Omega}(N^{1/4}))$, so $\Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x) = 0] = 1 - o(1)$. 
Hence, for all $x \in [R]^N$, $|r(x) - \mathsf{ SURJ}(x)| \le 1/10 + o(1) \le 1/3$. 

This completes
the proof of \Cref{thm:upper}.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 48
nodes.statement: We start by fixing choices of several key parameters: \begin{itemize} \item $d= \Theta(\sqrt{R})$ is the pure high degree of the dual witness $\Phi$ for $\mathsf{AND}_R$ in \Cref{prop:and-or}, \item $T = \lfloor(R/d)^{1/2}\rfloor^2 = \Theta(\sqrt{R})$, \item $\hat{D} = c_1 \sqrt{T} \cdot d =\Theta(R^{3/4})$, where $c_1$ is the constant from \Cref{prop:or-sym-dual}, \item $\delta =1/20$ \item $\alpha = 170/\delta = 3400$, \item $\beta = c_2 \cdot \sqrt{\delta} / \sqrt{T} = \Theta(1/R^{1/4})$, where $c_2$ is the constant from \Cref{prop:or-sym-dual}, \item $N = \lceil 20 \sqrt{\alpha} \rceil R = 693 R$. \end{itemize} Let $\psi : \{-1,1\}^N \to \{-1,1\}$ be the function constructed in \Cref{prop:or-dual} with $\delta:=1/20$. Let $\Phi : \{-1,1\}^R \to \{-1,1\}$ be the function constructed in \Cref{prop:and-or}, and define $\xi = \Phi \star \psi$. Then by \Cref{prop:ls}, $\xi$ satisfies the following properties: \begin{align}& \langle \xi, \mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N \rangle > 2/3, \\ & \| \xi \|_1 = 1, \\ & \text{ For every polynomial } p \text{ of degree less than } D, \text{ we have }\langle \xi, p \rangle = 0. \end{align} Recall that $\psi$ was obtained by symmetrizing the function $\omega$ constructed in \Cref{prop:or-sym-dual}. \Cref{prop:btzeroing} guarantees that for some $\Delta \ge \beta \sqrt{\alpha} R / 4\ln^2 R = \tilde{\Omega}(R^{3/4})$, the function $\xi$ can be modified to produce a function $\zeta : (\{-1,1\}^N)^R \to \mathbb{R}$ such that \begin{align*} &\zeta(x) = 0 \text{ for all } x \not\in H_{\le N}^{N \cdot R}, \\ &\langle \zeta, \mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N \rangle \ge \langle \xi, \mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N \rangle - \|\zeta - \xi\|_1 \ge 2/3 - 2/9 > 1/3, \\ &\|\zeta\|_1 = 1, \\ & \text{ For every polynomial } p \text{ of degree less than } \min\{\hat{D}, \Delta\}, \text{ we have }\langle \zeta, p \rangle = 0. \end{align*} Observing that \[D = \min\{\hat{D}, \Delta\} = \tilde{\Omega}(R^{3/4})\] shows that the function $\zeta$ satisfies the conditions necessary to prove \Cref{prop:surj-dual}.

nodes.name: Error regions E_+ and E_-
nodes.statement:
For functions $f : \mathcal{X} \to \{-1,1\}$ and $\psi : \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}$, define the error regions
\begin{align*}
E_+(\psi, f) = \{x \in \mathcal{X} : \psi(x) > 0, f(x) = -1\} \\
E_-(\psi, f) = \{x \in \mathcal{X} : \psi(x) < 0, f(x) = +1\}.
\end{align*}

These are the regions where $\psi$ disagrees in sign with $f$. 
We refer to $E_+$ as the set of ``false positive'' errors made by $\psi$,
and $E_-$ as the set of ``false negative'' errors.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 51
nodes.statement: If $k = 1$, then the function defined by $\omega(0) = \frac{1}{2}$ and $\omega(1) = -\frac{1}{2}$ satisfies the conditions of the proposition for $c_1 = c_2 = 1$. In what follows, we treat the complementary case where $k \ge 2$. Let $E_+ := \{t \colon \omega(t) > 0, t \ge k\}$, and $E_{-} := \{t\colon \omega(t) < 0, t < k\}$. By normalizing, it suffices to construct a function $\omega : [T]_0 \to \mathbb{R}$ such that \begin{align} & \sum_{t \in E_+} |\omega(t)| \le \frac{1}{48 N} \cdot \|\omega\|_1 \\ & \sum_{t \in E_-} |\omega(t)| \le \left(\frac{1}{2} - \frac{2}{4^k}\right) \cdot \|\omega\|_1 \\ & \text{For all univariate polynomials } q \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\text{, } \nonumber \\ &\deg p < c_1\sqrt{k^{-1} \cdot T \cdot N^{-1/k}} \implies \sum_{t=0}^k \omega(t) \cdot q(t) = 0 \\ & |\omega(t)| \le \frac{(2k)^k \exp(-c_2 t / \sqrt{k \cdot T \cdot N^{1/k}})\|\omega\|_1}{t^2} \qquad \forall t = 1, 2, \dots, T. \end{align} Let $c = 2k\lceil N^{1/k}\rceil$, and let $m = \lfloor \sqrt{T/c} \rfloor$. Define the set \[S = \{1, 2, \dots, k\} \cup \{ci^2 : 0 \le i \le m\}.\] Note that $|S| = \Omega(k^{-1/2}T^{1/2}N^{-1/(2k)})$. Define the polynomial \[\omega(t) = \frac{(-1)^{t+(T-m)+1}}{T!} \binom{T}{t} \prod_{r \in [T]_0 \setminus S} (t - r).\] The signs are chosen so that $\omega(k) < 0$. It is immediate from \Cref{fact:combinatorial} that $\omega$ satisfies~\eqref{eqn:thr-sym-phd-ref} for $c_1 = 1/\sqrt{2}$. We now show that~\eqref{eqn:thr-sym-decay-ref} holds. For $t = 1, \dots, k$, we have \[\frac{(2k)^k \exp(-c_2 t / \sqrt{k \cdot T \cdot N^{1/k}})}{t^2} \ge \frac{(2k)^k \exp(-c_2 \sqrt{k})}{k^2} \ge 1\] as long as $c_2 \le 1/2$ and $k \ge 2$. Since $|\omega(t)| \le \|\omega\|_1$, the bound holds for $t = 1, \dots, k$. For $t = cj^2$ with $j \ge 1$, we expand out the binomial coefficient in the definition of $\omega$ to obtain \[|\omega(t)| = \begin{cases} \prod\limits_{r \in S\setminus \{t\}} \frac{1}{|t - r|} & \text{ for } t \in S, \\ 0 & \text{ otherwise.} \end{cases}\] For $t \in \{0, 1, \dots, k\}$, we observe that \begin{equation} \frac{|\omega(t)|}{|\omega(k)|} = \frac{k! \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^m (c i^2 - k)}{t! \cdot (k - t)! \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^m (c i^2 - t)} \le \binom{k}{t}. \end{equation} Meanwhile, for $t = cj^2$ with $j \ge 1$, we get \begin{align*} \frac{|\omega(t)|}{|\omega(k)|} &= \frac{k! \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^m (ci^2 - k)}{\prod_{i = 1}^k(cj^2 - i) \cdot \prod_{i \in [m]_0 \setminus \{j\}} |ci^2 - cj^2|} \\ &\le \frac{k! \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^m ci^2}{(cj^2 - k)^{k} \cdot \prod_{i \in [m]_0 \setminus \{j\}} c(i+j)|i-j|} \\ &= \frac{k!}{j(cj^2 - k)^{k}} \cdot \frac{(m!)^2}{(m+j)!(m-j)!}. \end{align*} The first factor is bounded above by \[\frac{k!}{(c - k)^k j^{2k+1}}.\] As long as $c \ge 2k$ and $k \ge 2$, this expression is at most \[\frac{k^k}{(c/2)^kj^4} = \frac{(2k)^k}{c^k \cdot j^4}.\] We control the second factor by \begin{align*} \frac{(m!)^2}{(m+j)!(m-j)!} &= \frac{m}{m+j} \cdot \frac{m-1}{m+j-1} \cdot \ldots \cdot \frac{m-j+1}{m+1} \\ &\le \left(\frac{m}{m+j} \right)^j \\ &\le \left(1 - \frac{j}{2m} \right)^j \\ &\le e^{-j^2/2m}, \end{align*} where the last inequality uses the fact that $1 - x \le e^{-x}$ for all $x$. Hence, \begin{equation} \frac{|\omega(cj^2)|}{|\omega(k)|} \le \frac{(2k)^k}{c^k \cdot j^4} \cdot e^{-j^2/2m}. \end{equation} This immediately yields \[\frac{|\omega(cj^2)|}{\|\omega\|_1} \le \frac{|\omega(cj^2)|}{|\omega(k)|} \le \frac{(2k)^k}{(cj^2)^2} \cdot e^{-cj^2/(2cm)},\] which establishes~\eqref{eqn:thr-sym-decay-ref} for all $t = cj^2 > k$. Moreover, by \eqref{eqn:tail-bound} \begin{equation} \sum_{t > k} |\omega(t)| \le |\omega(k)| \cdot \sum_{j = 1}^m \frac{(2k)^k}{c^k \cdot j^4} \cdot e^{-j^2/2m} \le \frac{(2k)^k}{c^k} \cdot |\omega(k)| \cdot \sum_{j=1}^m \frac{1}{j^4} \le \frac{|\omega(k)|}{48 N}. \end{equation} Hence, since $\omega(k) < 0$, \[\sum_{t \in E_+} |\omega(t)| \le \sum_{t > k} |\omega(t)| \le \frac{|\omega(k)|}{48 N} \le \frac{\|\omega\|_1}{48N},\] which gives~\eqref{eqn:thr-sym-pos-corr-ref}. Finally, to establish~\eqref{eqn:thr-sym-neg-corr-ref}, we combine ~\eqref{eqn:head-bound} and~\eqref{eqn:tail-sum} to obtain \begin{equation} \frac{\|\omega\|_1}{|\omega(k)|} \le \sum_{t = 0}^k \binom{k}{t} + \frac{1}{48 N} < 2^k + 1 < \frac{1}{2} \cdot 4^k. \end{equation} We calculate \begin{align*} \frac{\|\omega\|_1}{2} - \sum_{t \in E_-} |\omega(t)| &= \sum_{t : \omega(t) < 0} (-\omega(t)) - \sum_{t \in E_-} (-\omega(t)) & \text{since $\langle \omega, \mathbf{1} \rangle = 0$}\\ &= \sum_{t \colon \omega(t) < 0, t \geq k} (-\omega(t)) \\ &\ge -\omega(k). \end{align*} Rearranging and applying the bound~\eqref{eqn:mass-on-k}, \[\sum_{t \in E_{-}} |\omega(t)| \le \left(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{\omega(k)}{\|\omega\|_1}\right) \cdot \|\omega\|_1 \le \left(\frac{1}{2} - 2 \cdot 4^{-k}\right) \cdot \|\omega\|_1.\]
nodes.statement_short: Construct omega supported on {1..k} and {ci^2} with c = 2k ceil(N^{1/k}); bound the head by binomials and the tail by e^{-j^2/2m}.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition (prop:error-amp)
nodes.statement:
Let $\varphi: \{-1, 1\}^M ightarrow \{-1, 1\}$ be defined such that $\varphi(\mathbf{1})=1/2$, $\varphi(-\mathbf{1})=-1/2$, and $\varphi(x)=0$ for all other $x$. Notice that  egin{equation} \sum_{(x_1, \dots, x_{M}) \in \{-1, 1\}^M} \varphi(x_1, \dots, x_{M}) = 0 \end{equation} so $\Psi$ has pure high degree $1$, and that $\|\Psi\|_1 = 1$. We now prove that (\Cref{eqn:error-amp-pos}) holds. Let $\lambda$ be the distribution on $\{-1, 1\}^{m}$ given by $\lambda(x) = |\psi(x)|$, and let $\lambda^{\otimes M}$ be the product distribution on $(\{-1, 1\}^m)^M$ given by $\lambda^{\otimes M}(x_1, \dots, x_M) = \prod_{i=1}^M |\psi(x_i)|$. Since $\psi$ is orthogonal to the constant polynomial, it has expected value 0, and hence the string $(\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots)$ is distributed uniformly in $\{-1, 1\}^{M}$ when one samples $(x_1, \dots, x_{M})$ according to $\lambda^{\otimes M}$. This allows us to write  egin{align} &\hspace{-2em}\sum_{(x_1, \dots, x_{M}) \in E^+(\varphi \star \psi, \mathsf{ OR}_M \circ f)} |(\varphi \star \psi)(x_1, \dots, x_M)| 
onumber \ &\hspace{-2em}= 2^{M} \mathbf{E}_{\lambda^{\otimes M}} [\varphi( \dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) \cdot \mathbb{I} (\varphi( \dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) > 0 \land \mathsf{ OR}_M\left( \dots, f(x_i), \dotsight) = -1)] 
onumber\ &\hspace{-2em}= \sum_{z : \varphi(z) > 0} \varphi(z) \cdot \Pr_{\lambda^{\otimes M}} [\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, f(x_i), \dots) = -1 | (\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) = z]. \end{align} Observe that for any bit $b$, \[\Pr_{x \sim \lambda} [f(x) 
e \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x)) | \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x)) = b] = 2\sum_{x \in A_b} |\psi(x)|,\] where for brevity, we have written $A_{+1} = E_+(\psi, f)$ and $A_{-1} = E_-(\psi, f)$. Therefore, as noted in \cite{sherstovhalfspaces1}, for any given $z \in \{-1, 1\}^{M}$, the following two random variables are identically distributed:  egin{itemize} \item The string $(\dots, f(x_i), \dots)$, when one chooses $(\dots, x_i, \dots)$ from $\lambda^{\otimes M}$ conditioned on 
ewline $(\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) = z$ \item The string $(\dots, y_iz_i, \dots)$, where $y \in \{-1, 1\}^{M}$ is a random string whose $i$th bit independently takes on value $-1$ with probability $2 \sum_{x \in A_{z_i}} |\psi(x)|$. \end{itemize} Thus, Expression~\eqref{eqn:error-amp-middle} equals  egin{equation}\sum_{z : \varphi(z) > 0} \varphi(z) \cdot \Pr_y[\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, y_iz_i, \dots) = -1], \end{equation} where $y \in \{-1, 1\}^{M}$ is a random string whose $i$th bit independently takes on value $-1$ with probability $2 \sum_{x \in A_{z_i}} |\psi(x)|$. The only term in this sum corresponds to $z=\mathbf{1}$, which we now argue is at most $M \delta^+$. By \eqref{eqn:error-base-pos}, each $y_i = -1$ with probability $2 \sum_{x \in A_{1}} |\psi(x)| = 2\sum_{x \in E^+(\psi, f)} |\psi(x)| \le 2\delta^+$. Hence, for $z = \mathbf{1}$, we have \[\Pr_y[\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, y_i, \dots) = -1] \le 2 M \delta^+\] by a union bound. Thus Expression~\eqref{eqn:error-amp-middle2} is at most $M \delta^+$, proving \eqref{eqn:error-amp-pos}. It now remains to prove the bound~\eqref{eqn:error-amp-neg}. By an identical argument as above, we have  egin{equation}\sum_{(x_1, \dots, x_{M}) \in E^-(\varphi \star \psi, \mathsf{ OR}_M \circ f)} |(\varphi \star \psi)(x_1, \dots, x_M)| = \sum_{z : \varphi(z) < 0} \varphi(z) \cdot \Pr_y[\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, y_iz_i, \dots) = 1]. \end{equation} The only term in the sum corresponds to $z=-\mathbf{1}$, which we argue takes value $ rac{1}{2} \cdot (2\delta^-)^{M}$. Here, each $y_i=-1$ independently with probability $\sum_{x \in A_{-1}} |\psi(x)| = 2\sum_{x \in E^-(\psi, f)} |\psi(x)| \le 2\delta^-$, and $\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, -y_i, \dots)=1$ only if $y_i = -1$ for every $i$. Hence, we conclude that \[\Pr_y[\mathsf{ OR}_{M}\left(\dots, -y_i, \dotsight) = 1] \le (2\delta^-)^M. \] It follows that Expression~\eqref{eqn:error-amp-end} is at most $ rac{1}{2} \cdot (2\delta^-)^M$, establishing~\eqref{eqn:error-amp-pos}. This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Take phi(1) = 1/2, phi(-1) = -1/2; under |psi|^{otimes M} the inputs' f-values are sign flips with probability 2x the error mass, then union bound / independence.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition (prop:degree-amp)
nodes.statement:
\Cref{andornor} shows that the function $\mathsf{ OR}_M$ has $(9/10)$-approximate degree $\Omega(\sqrt{M})$. Hence, \Cref{prop:duality} guarantees the existence of a function $ho : \{-1,1\}^M 	o \mathbb{R}$ with $\|ho\|_1 = 1$ and pure high degree $\Omega(\sqrt{M})$ such that  egin{equation} \langle ho, \mathsf{ OR}_M angle \ge  rac{9}{10}. \end{equation} What remains is to establish the correlation bound~\eqref{eqn:deg-amp-corr}. Letting $\lambda$ denote the distribution $\lambda(x) = |\psi(x)|$ as in the proof of \Cref{prop:error-amp}, we may write  egin{align} & \sum_{(x_1, \dots, x_{M}) \in (\{-1,1\}^m)^M} (\varphi \star \psi) (x_1, \dots, x_M) \cdot \mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, f(x_i), \dots) 
onumber \ &\qquad= 2^{M} \mathbf{E}_{\lambda^{\otimes M}} [\varphi( \dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) \cdot \mathsf{ OR}_M\left( \dots, f(x_i), \dotsight)] 
onumber\ &\qquad= \sum_{z \in \{-1,1\}^M} \varphi(z) \cdot \mathbf{E}_{\lambda^{\otimes M}} [\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, f(x_i), \dots) | (\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) = z] 
onumber\ &\qquad = \sum_{z \in \{-1,1\}^M} \varphi(z) \cdot \mathbf{E}_{y} [\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, y_i z_i, \dots)], \end{align} where $y \in \{-1,1\}^M$ is a random string whose $i$th bit independently takes the value $-1$ with probability $2 \sum_{x \in A_{z_i}} |\psi(x)|$. (Here, we are using the abbreviated notation $A_{+1} = E_+(\psi, f)$ and $A_{-1} = E_-(\psi, f)$.) We first consider the contribution of the term corresponding to $z = \mathbf{1}$ to the sum. Here, by a union bound,  egin{align*} \mathbf{E}_{y} [\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, y_i z_i, \dots)] &= 1 - 2 \Pr_y[\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, y_i, \dots) = -1] \ &\ge 1 - 2 M \cdot \left(2 \sum_{x \in A_{+1}} |\psi(x)|ight) \ &\ge 1 - 4 M\delta^+. \end{align*} Hence, the term $z = \mathbf{1}$ contributes $\varphi(\mathbf{1}) \cdot (1 - 4 M \delta^+)$ to the sum. Now we consider the contribution of any term corresponding to $z 
e \mathbf{1}$. Given such a $z$, let $i^*$ be an index such that $z_{i^*} = -1$. Then we have  egin{align*} -\mathbf{E}_{y} [\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, y_i z_i, \dots)] &= 1 - 2 \Pr_y[\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, y_i z_i, \dots) = 1] \ &\ge 1 - 2 \cdot \Pr_{y_{i^*}}[y_{i^*} = -1] \ &= 1 - 2 \cdot \left(2 \sum_{x \in A_{-1}} |\psi(x)|ight) \ &\ge 1 - 4 \delta^-. \end{align*} We can now lower bound~\eqref{eqn:deg-amp-middle} by  egin{align*}\hspace{-1.1em} \varphi(\mathbf{1}) \cdot (1 - 4 M \delta^+) - \sum_{z 
e \mathbf{1}} \varphi(z) (1 - 4\delta^-) &\ge \sum_{z \in \{-1,1\}^M} \varphi(z) \mathsf{ OR}_M(z) - 4M\delta^+ |\varphi(\mathbf{1})| - 4\delta^- \sum_{z 
e 1} |\varphi(z)| \ &\ge  rac{9}{10} - 4M\delta^+ - 4\delta^-.\qedhere \end{align*}

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 53
nodes.statement: Using the construction of \Cref{prop:error-amp} with $m = N$, $M = 4^k$, and $f = \mathsf{THR}_N^k$, we first obtain a function $\varphi : \{-1,1\}^{4^k} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $\|\varphi\|_1 = 1$ and pure high degree $1$ such that \begin{align*} &\sum_{x \in E_+(\varphi \star \psi, \mathsf{ OR}_{4^k} \circ \mathsf{THR}^k_N)} |(\varphi \star \psi)(x)| \le \frac{4^k}{48 N} \\ &\sum_{x \in E_-(\varphi \star \psi, \mathsf{ OR}_{4^k} \circ \mathsf{THR}^k_N)} |(\varphi \star \psi)(x)| \le \frac{1}{2} \cdot \left(1 - 4 \cdot 4^{-k} \right)^{4^k} \le \frac{e^{-4}}{2}. \end{align*} Now by the construction of \Cref{prop:degree-amp} with $m = 4^k \cdot N$, $M = R/4^{k}$ and $f = \mathsf{ OR}_{4^k} \circ \mathsf{THR}_N^k$, there exists a function $\rho : \{-1,1\}^{R / 4^k} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $\|\rho\|_1 = 1$ and pure high degree $\Omega(2^{-k}\sqrt{R})$ such that \[ \langle \rho \star (\varphi \star \psi), \mathsf{ OR}_{R/4^k} \circ (\mathsf{ OR}_{4^k} \circ \mathsf{THR}^k_N) \rangle \ge \frac{9}{10} - \frac{4R}{48 N} - 2e^{-4} \ge \frac{2}{3}.\] Let $\Phi : \{-1,1\}^R \to \mathbb{R}$ be the dual block composition $\rho \star \varphi$. Since the dual block composition preserves $\ell_1$-norms (\Cref{prop:ls}, Condition~\eqref{eqn:ls-norm}) and multiplies pure high degrees (\Cref{prop:ls}, Condition~\eqref{eqn:ls-phd}), the function $\Phi$ itself has $\ell_1$-norm $1$ and pure high degree $\Omega(2^{-k} \sqrt{R})$. The claim now follows from the associativity of dual block composition (\Cref{prop:ls}, Condition~\eqref{eqn:ls-assoc}) and the fact that $\mathsf{ OR}_R = \mathsf{ OR}_{R/4^k} \circ \mathsf{ OR}_{4^k}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 54
nodes.statement: We start by fixing choices of several key parameters: \begin{itemize} \item $d= \Theta(2^{-k}\sqrt{R})$ is the pure high degree of the dual witness $\Phi$ for $\mathsf{ OR}_R$ in \Cref{prop:dist-prelim}, \item $T = \lfloor (8k)^{k/2} \sqrt{R}\rfloor$, \item $\alpha = (2k)^k$, \item $N = \lceil 20 \sqrt{\alpha} \rceil R = \Theta((2k)^{k/2} R)$, \item $\hat{D} = c_1 \sqrt{k^{-1} \cdot T \cdot N^{-1/k}} \cdot d =\Theta(2^{-k/4} k^{(k-3)/4} \cdot R^{3/4 - 1/(2k)})$, where $c_1$ is the constant from \Cref{prop:thr-sym-dual}, \item $\beta = c_2 / \sqrt{k \cdot T \cdot N^{1/k}} = \Theta(2^{-3k/4} k^{(-k-3)/4} \cdot R^{-1/4 - 1/(2k)})$, where $c_2$ is the constant from \Cref{prop:thr-sym-dual}. \end{itemize} Let $\psi : \{-1,1\}^N \to \{-1,1\}$ be the function constructed in \Cref{prop:thr-dual}. Let $\Phi : \{-1,1\}^R \to \{-1,1\}$ be the function constructed in \Cref{prop:dist-prelim}, and define $\xi = \Phi \star \psi$. Then by \Cref{prop:ls}, $\xi$ satisfies the following properties: \begin{align}& \langle \xi, \mathsf{ OR}_R \circ \mathsf{THR}_N^k \rangle > 2/3, \\ & \| \xi \|_1 = 1, \\ & \text{ For every polynomial } p \text{ of degree less than } \hat{D}, \text{ we have }\langle \xi, p \rangle = 0. \end{align} Recall that $\psi$ was obtained by symmetrizing the function $\omega$ constructed in \Cref{prop:thr-sym-dual}. \Cref{prop:btzeroing} guarantees that for some $\Delta \ge \beta \sqrt{\alpha} R / 4\ln^2 R = \tilde{\Omega}(2^{-k/4} k^{(k-3)/4} \cdot R^{3/4 - 1/(2k)})$, the function $\xi$ can be modified to produce a function $\zeta : (\{-1,1\}^N)^R \to \mathbb{R}$ such that \begin{align*} &\zeta(x) = 0 \text{ for all } x \not\in H_{\le N}^{N \cdot R}, \\ &\langle \zeta, \mathsf{ OR}_R \circ \mathsf{THR}_N^k \rangle \ge \langle \xi, \mathsf{ OR}_R \circ \mathsf{THR}_N^k \rangle - \|\zeta - \xi\|_1 \ge 2/3 - 2/9 > 1/3, \\ &\|\zeta\|_1 = 1, \\ & \text{ For every polynomial } p \text{ of degree less than } \min\{\hat{D}, \Delta\}, \text{ we have }\langle \zeta, p \rangle = 0. \end{align*} Observing that \[D = \min\{\hat{D}, \Delta\} = \tilde{\Omega}(2^{-k/4} k^{(k-3)/ 4} \cdot R^{3/4-1/(2k)})\] shows that the function $\zeta$ satisfies the conditions necessary to prove \Cref{prop:dist-dual}.

\Cref{thm:dist-promise} now follows by combining \Cref{prop:dist-dual} with the dual characterization of unbounded approximate degree \Cref{prop:ub-duality}. The approximate degree lower bound in \Cref{thm:dist} is then a consequence of \Cref{prop:dumdist-reduction} and \Cref{cor:dist-reduction}. The quantum query lower bound follows via the standard fact

nodes.name: Image Size Testing IST
nodes.statement: Given an input $s=(s_1, \dots, s_N) \in [R]_0^N$, and $i \in [R]$, let $f_i = |\{j \colon s_j=i\}|$. The \emph{image size} of $s$ is the number of $i \in [R]$ such that $f_i > 0$. For $0 < \gamma < 1$, define: $$\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = \begin{cases} -1 & \text{ if the image size is } R\\ 1 & \text{ if the image size is at most } \gamma \cdot R\\ \text{undefined} & \text{otherwise}.\end{cases}$$
nodes.statement_short: IST(s) = -1 if all R range items appear, +1 if at most gamma R appear, undefined otherwise.

nodes.name: Lower bound for Image Size Testing
nodes.statement: For some constant $c > 0$, and any constant $\gamma \in (0, 1)$, $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}\left(\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}\right) \ge \tilde{\Omega}(R^{1/2})$, where $N = c \cdot \gamma^{-1/2} \cdot R$. The same lower bound applies to the quantum query complexity of $\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}$.
assumptions: For some constant $c > 0$, and any constant $\gamma \in (0, 1)$
conclusions: $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}\left(\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}\right) \ge \tilde{\Omega}(R^{1/2})$
The same lower bound applies to the quantum query complexity of $\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}$.

nodes.name: Stronger unbounded / large-error bounds for IST
nodes.statement: It is possible to refine our analysis to show that even the \emph{unbounded} approximate degree of $\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}$ is $\tilde{\Omega}(R^{1/2})$, and that this holds even if the error parameter is $1-2^{-n^{\Omega(1)}}$. However, for brevity we do not explicitly establish this stronger result. We direct the interested reader to subsequent work \cite{btlargeerror}, which shows that the threshold degree of $\mathsf{ SURJ}_{N, R}$ is $\tilde{\Omega}(R^{1/2})$ for $R \leq N/2$. The proof of that result can be extended with little difficulty to show that the threshold degree of $\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}$ is $\tilde{\Omega}(R^{1/2})$.
nodes.statement_short: The analysis extends to unbounded approximate degree and error 1 - 2^{-n^{Omega(1)}}; cf. later threshold degree results.

nodes.name: Double-promise approximate degree
nodes.statement: Let $Y \subset \{-1,1\}^R$ and $f \colon Y \to \{-1,1\}$, and let $g \colon \{-1,1\}^N \to \{-1,1\}$ be a symmetric (total) function. Let $G = \{x_1, \dots, x_R \colon (g(x_1), \dots, g(x_R)) \in Y\}.$ Let $F^{\le N}$ be defined as above. Observe that $F^{\le N}$ is defined at all inputs in $H_{\leq N}^{N \cdot R} \cap G$. The double-promise $\varepsilon$-approximate degree of $F^{\le N}$, denoted $\widetilde{\operatorname{dpdeg}}(F^{\le N})$ is the least degree of a real polynomial $p$ such that: \begin{align} & |p(x) - F^{\le N}(x)| \leq \varepsilon \text{ for all } x \in H_{\leq N}^{N \cdot R} \cap G.\\ & |p(x)| \leq 1+\varepsilon \text{ for all } x \in H_{\leq N}^{N \cdot R} \setminus G. \end{align}

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 56 (Image Size Testing)
nodes.statement: We construct a dual polynomial to witness the lower bound in \Cref{sethm}. Define the parameters \begin{itemize} \item $\delta = \gamma/4$, \item $\alpha = 170/\delta$, \item $T=N=\lceil 20 \sqrt{\alpha} \rceil R \leq 310 \cdot \gamma^{-1/2} \cdot R$, \item $\beta = c_2 \cdot \sqrt{\delta} / \sqrt{T}$, where $c_2$ is the constant from \Cref{prop:or-sym-dual}. \end{itemize} Let $\psi$ be the dual witness for $\mathsf{ OR}_N$ from \Cref{prop:or-dual} with $T=N$. Define $\Phi \colon \{-1,1\}^R \to \mathbb{R}$ as follows: $$\Phi(x) = \begin{cases} -1/2 & \text{ if } x=(-1, -1, \dots, -1)\\ 1/2 & \text{ if } x = (1, 1, \dots, 1)\\ 0 & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases}$$ The dual block composition $\Phi \star \psi$ is the same dual witness for $\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N$ which Bun and Thaler \cite{bt14} used to show that $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_{\varepsilon}(\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N) = \Omega(N^{1/2})$ for $\varepsilon = 1-2^{-R}$. This dual witness was also used in subsequent works \cite{sherstov14, bchtv}. Curiously, we are interested in this dual witness for a completely different reason than these prior works. These prior works were interested in $\Phi \star \psi$ because its correlation with the target function $\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N$ is exponentially closer to 1 than is the correlation of $\psi$ with $\mathsf{ OR}_N$. For our purposes, it will not be essential to exploit such a strong correlation guarantee---rather, we are interested in $\Phi \star \psi$ because most its ``$\ell_1$-mass'' lies on inputs either with full image or tiny image (i.e., most of its mass lies in the domain of $\mathsf{GapAND}_{R}^{\gamma} \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N$). As in \Cref{cor:se-reduction}, let $G$ denote the set of all inputs on which $\mathsf{GapAND}_{R}^{\gamma} \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N$ is defined, i.e., $$G=\{x_1, \dots, x_R \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R} \colon (\mathsf{ OR}_N(x_1), \dots, \mathsf{ OR}_N(x_R)) \in H_{\leq \gamma \cdot R}^R \cup \{\mathbf{-1}\}\}.$$ The analysis in these prior works \cite{bt14,bchtv} implies that $\Phi \star \psi$ satisfies the following three properties. \begin{align} &\|\Phi \star \psi \|_1=1, \\ &\sum_{x \in G} ( \Phi \star \psi)(x) \cdot \left(\mathsf{GapAND}_{R}^{\gamma} \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N\right)(x) - \sum_{x \in\{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R} \setminus G} |(\Phi \star \psi)(x)| \geq 9/10, \\ &\text{For any polynomial } p \colon \{-1,1\}^{N\cdot R} \to \mathbb{R}\text{, } \deg p < c_1\sqrt{\delta T} \implies \langle \Phi \star \psi, p \rangle = 0, \end{align} where $c_1$ is the constant from \Cref{prop:or-dual}. Indeed, Properties~\eqref{ughnorm} and~\eqref{ughphd} are immediate from \Cref{prop:ls} on the properties of dual block composition. For completeness, we prove that Property~\eqref{ughcor} holds in \Cref{sec:gap-and-corr} below, making use of the fact that $\delta = \gamma/4$ and taking $R$ to be sufficiently large. \Cref{prop:btzeroing} (with $\alpha$ and $\beta$ set as above) guarantees that for some $\Delta \ge \beta \sqrt{\alpha} R / 4\ln^2 R = \tilde{\Omega}(R^{1/2})$, the function $\Phi \star \psi$ can be modified to produce a function $\zeta : (\{-1,1\}^N)^R \to \mathbb{R}$ such that \begin{align*} &\zeta(x) = 0 \text{ for all } x \not\in H_{\le N}^{N \cdot R}, \\ &\langle \zeta, \mathsf{GapAND}_{R}^{\gamma} \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N \rangle \ge \langle \Phi \star \psi, \mathsf{GapAND}_{R}^{\gamma} \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N \rangle - \|\zeta - \Phi \star \psi\|_1 \ge 9/10 - 2/9 > 1/3, \\ &\|\zeta\|_1 = 1, \\ & \text{ For every polynomial } p \text{ of degree less than } D:=\min\{\hat{D}, \Delta\}, \text{ we have }\langle \zeta, p \rangle = 0. \end{align*} Observing that \[D = \min\{c_1\sqrt{\delta T}, \Delta\} = \tilde{\Omega}(R^{1/2})\] shows that the function $\zeta$ satisfies the conditions necessary to prove \Cref{sethm} via \Cref{prop:dualitydiedie}.
nodes.statement_short: Compose the OR dual (T = N) with the two-point dual Phi for AND; most mass lies in the GapAND domain (Lemma 62); zero out high weight with Proposition (prop:btzeroing).

nodes.statement:
We begin by observing that the quantity of interest can be written as  egin{align} &\sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R}} ( \Phi \star \psi)(x) \cdot \left(\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_Night)(x) - 
onumber \ &\qquad\qquad \left( \sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R} \setminus G} ( \Phi \star \psi)(x) \cdot \left(\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_Night)(x) + \sum_{x \in\{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R} \setminus G} |(\Phi \star \psi)(x)| ight) 
onumber \ \ge &\sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R}} ( \Phi \star \psi)(x) \cdot \left(\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_Night)(x) - 2 \sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R} \setminus G} |(\Phi \star \psi)(x)|. \end{align} We estimate each term of Expression~\eqref{eqn:buttz} separately, beginning with the first term. Just as in the proofs of \Cref{prop:error-amp} and \Cref{prop:degree-amp}, we have  egin{align*} \sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R}} (\Phi \star \psi)(x) \cdot (\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N)(x) &= \sum_{z \in \{-1,1\}^R} \Phi(z) \cdot \mathbb{E}_y[\mathsf{AND}_R(\dots, y_i z_i, \dots)] \end{align*} where $y \in \{-1,1\}^R$ is a random string whose $i$th bit independently takes the value $-1$ with probability $2 \sum_{x \in A_{z_i}} |\psi(x)|$. For $z = -\mathbf{1}$, we have by~\eqref{eqn:mybullshitequation} that $2 \sum_{x \in A_{-1}} |\psi(x)| = 0$, so the contribution of the corresponding term to the sum is $1/2$. For $z = \mathbf{1}$, we use the fact that $2 \sum_{x \in A_{+1}} |\psi(x)| \le \delta$ to compute  egin{align*}  rac{1}{2} \cdot \mathbb{E}_{y}[\mathsf{AND}_R(\dots, y_i, \dots)] &=  rac{1}{2} \cdot \left(1 - 2\Pr_y[\mathsf{AND}_R(\dots, y_i, \dots) = -1 ] ight) \ &\ge  rac{1}{2} \cdot \left(1 - 2\delta^Right). \end{align*} Hence, the first summand of~\eqref{eqn:buttz} is at least $1-\delta^R$. We now estimate the second summand, $2 \sum_{x 
otin G} |(\Phi \star \psi)(x)|$. As in the proofs of \Cref{prop:error-amp} and \Cref{prop:degree-amp}, we let $\lambda$ denote the distribution with probability mass function $\lambda(x) = |\psi(x)|$. Then  egin{align*}\hspace{-2.2em} 2\sum_{x 
otin G} |(\Phi \star \psi)(x)| &= 2^{R+1} \mathbb{E}_{\lambda^{\otimes R}} [|\Phi(\dots, \operatorname{sgn} \psi(x_i), \dots)| \cdot \mathbb{I}(x 
otin G)] \ &= 2\sum_{z \in \{-1,1\}^R} |\Phi(z)| \cdot \Pr_{\lambda^{\otimes R}}[x 
otin G | (\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) = z] \ &= \Pr_{\lambda^{\otimes R}}[x 
otin G | (\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) = \mathbf{-1}] + \Pr_{\lambda^{\otimes R}}[x 
otin G | (\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) = \mathbf{1}]. \end{align*} We analyze each term of this sum separately. For the first term, observe that by one-sided error of $\psi$, it follows that if $x = (x_1, \dots, x_R)$ is any input $\operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)) = -1$ for all $i$ then $\mathsf{ OR}_N(x_i) = -1$ for all $i$. Thus we are guaranteed that $x \in G$, so the contribution of the first summand is zero. To analyze the second summand, let us denote by $r_i \in \{0, 1\}$ the indicator random variable for the event $\mathsf{ OR}_N(x_i) = -1$ when $x_i$ is drawn from the conditional distribution $(\lambda | \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)) = 1)$. Then  egin{align*} \Pr[r_i = 1] &= \Pr_{x_i \sim \lambda}[\mathsf{ OR}_N(x_i) = -1 | \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)) = 1] \ &= 2\sum_{x \in A_{+1}} |\psi(x_i)| \ &\le \delta \end{align*} by~\eqref{eqn:mybullshitequation}. Hence,  egin{align*} \Pr_{\lambda^{\otimes R}}[x 
otin G | (\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) = \mathbf{1}] &\le \Pr\left[ \sum_{i = 1}^R r_i > \gamma Right] \ &\le \exp\left(- rac{(\gamma - \delta)R}{3}ight) \end{align*} by the multiplicative Chernoff bound. ootnote{The formulation we use here is as follows. Let $r_1, \dots, r_R$ be independent $\{0, 1\}$-valued random variables, $S = \sum_{i=1}^R r_i$, and $\mu = \mathbb{E}[S]$. Then for $\eta > 1$, we have $\Pr[S > (1+\eta) \mu] \le \exp(-\eta \mu / 3)$. In this application, we are taking $\mu \le \delta R$ and $\eta = \gamma R / \mu - 1 > 1$.} Thus, we have \[2 \sum_{x 
otin G} |(\Phi \star \psi)(x)| \le \exp\left(- rac{(\gamma - \delta)R}{3}ight).\] Putting everything together, we see that Expression~\eqref{eqn:buttz} is at least $1 - \delta^R - \exp\left(-(\gamma - \delta) R / 3ight)$ as we wanted to show.

Given an input $(s_1, \dots, s_N) \in [R]^N$, and $i \in [R]$, let

nodes.name: Statistical Distance from Uniform SDU
nodes.statement: Define $$\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = \begin{cases} -1 & \text{ if } \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^R |p_i - 1/R| \leq \gamma_1\\ 1 & \text{ if } \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^R |p_i - 1/R| \geq \gamma_2\\ \text{undefined} & \text{otherwise}.\end{cases}$$ Above, $ \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^R |p_i - 1/R| $ is the statistical distance between $p$ and the uniform distribution.
nodes.statement_short: SDU = -1 if the statistical distance of p from uniform is <= gamma_1, +1 if >= gamma_2.

nodes.name: Intuition: SDU reduces to IST
nodes.statement: The $\mathsf{ SDU}$ problem reduces to $\mathsf{ IST}$ in the sense that any approximating polynomial for $\mathsf{ SDU}$ implies the existence of an approximation to $\mathsf{ IST}$ of the same degree. Hence, the approximate degree of $\mathsf{ SDU}$ is at least as large as that of $\mathsf{ IST}$. For intuition as to why this is true, let us relate $\mathsf{ IST}^{1/2}_{N, R}$ to $\mathsf{ SDU}^{1/2, 0}_{N, R}$ in the special case where $N = R$ and no dummy (i.e., 0) items appear in the input to $\mathsf{ IST}$. If $(s_1, \dots, s_N)$ is a true input to $\mathsf{ IST}^{1/2}_{N, R}$, i.e., $\mathsf{ IST}^{1/2}_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = -1$, then every index $i \in [R]$ must appear in the input list exactly once. Hence, the distribution represented by $(s_1, \dots, s_N)$ is exactly uniform, so $\mathsf{ SDU}^{1/2, 0}_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = -1$. On the other hand, if $\mathsf{ IST}^{1/2}_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = 1$, then at most $R/2$ indices $i \in [R]$ appear in the input list, so the list represents a distribution with statistical distance at least $1/2$ from uniform. Thus, an approximating polynomial for $\mathsf{ SDU}^{1/2, 0}_{N, R}$ is also an approximating polynomial for $\mathsf{ IST}^{1/2}_{N, R}$.
nodes.statement_short: When N = R, full image means uniform and image <= R/2 means distance >= 1/2, so an SDU approximant approximates IST.

The same lower bound applies to the quantum query complexity of $\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}$.
