nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 67 (SDU)
nodes.statement: Fix $R >0$, let $c$ be the constant from \Cref{sethm}, $\gamma<(2/3c)^2$ be a sufficiently small constant, and $N= c \cdot \gamma^{-1/2} \cdot R$. As inputs in $\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}$ are interpreted as elements of $[R]_0^N$, we can equivalently interpret them as elements of $[R+1]^N$, i.e., as inputs to $\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R+1}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}$, for any desired $0 < \gamma_1 < \gamma_2 < 1$. Set $\gamma_1 = 1-3\gamma/2$ and $\gamma_2=1-\gamma^{1/2}/c$. Observe that since $\gamma < (2/3c)^2$, $\gamma_1$ is strictly greater than $\gamma_2$. We claim that \begin{align*} &\left(\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}\right)^{-1}(-1) \subseteq \left(\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R+1}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}\right)^{-1}(-1), \text{ and} \\ &\left(\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}\right)^{-1}(+1) \subseteq \left(\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R+1}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}\right)^{-1}(+1). \end{align*} Indeed, since inputs in $\left(\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}\right)^{-1}(-1)$ define a probability distribution over $[R+1]$ with support size at least $R$, with all probabilities being integer multiples of $1/N=\gamma^{1/2}/(cR)$, the statistical distance between any such distribution and the uniform distribution is at most $1-R/N = 1-\gamma^{1/2}/c$. This follows from the following calculation. Amongst probability distributions $(p_1, \dots, p_{R+1})$ over $[R+1]$ with support size at least $R$ and all probabilities $p_i$ being integer multiples of $1/N$, it is not hard to see that one maximizes the statistical distance from the uniform distribution over $[R+1]$ by setting $p_1=1-\frac{R-1}{N}$, $p_2=p_3 = \dots = p_{R}=1/N$, and $p_{R+1}=0$. The statistical distance from uniform is: \begin{align*} \frac{1}{2} \left( \left(1-\frac{R-1}{N}-\frac{1}{R+1}\right) + \left(R-1\right)\left(\frac{1}{R+1} - \frac1N\right) + \frac{1}{R+1} \right)\\ = 1-\frac{R}{N} + \frac1N - \frac{1}{R+1} \leq 1-\frac{R}{N}, \end{align*} where we have assumed that $N \geq R+1$, which is true for sufficiently small choice of $\gamma$. Similarly, since inputs in $\left(\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}\right)^{-1}(1)$ define a probability distribution over $[R+1]$ with support size at most $\gamma \cdot R +1$, the statistical distance between any such distribution and the uniform distribution is at least $1-3\gamma/2$. To see this, let $p=(p_1, \dots, p_{R+1})$ be any distribution of support size at most $\gamma \cdot R$, and let $S = \{i \colon p_i=0\}$ and $\bar{S}$ be the complement of $S$. Then the statistical distance of $p$ from uniform is at least \begin{align*} \frac{1}{2} \left(\sum_{i \in S} \left(p_i - \frac{1}{R+1} \right) \right) + \frac{1}{2} \left(\sum_{i \in \bar{S}} \left( p_i - \frac{1}{R+1} \right) \right) = \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{|S|}{R+1} + \left(\sum_{i \in \bar{S}} p_i\right) - \frac{|\bar{S}|}{R+1}\right)\\ = \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{|S|}{R+1} + 1 - \frac{|\bar{S}|}{R+1}\right) \geq \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{(1-\gamma) R}{R+1} + 1 - \frac{\gamma R + 1}{R+1}\right) = \frac{1}{2} \left(1 + \frac{R-2\gamma R - 1}{R+1}\right)\\ = 1 - \frac{\gamma R + 1}{R+1} = 1 - \gamma - \frac{\gamma + 1}{R+1} \geq 1-3\gamma/2. \end{align*} It is an easy consequence of the above that any $\varepsilon$-approximating polynomial of degree $d$ for $\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R+1}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}$ implies an approximation to $\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}$ of the same degree (i.e., that $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_{\varepsilon}(\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}) \leq d$). \Cref{sduthm} then follows from \Cref{sethm}.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce IST to SDU: full-image inputs are within 1 - R/N of uniform and small-image inputs are at least 1 - 3gamma/2 away, so Theorem 56 applies.

nodes.name: Shannon entropy
nodes.statement:
Given a distribution $p$ over $[R]$, the Shannon entropy of $p$, denoted $H(p)$,
is defined to be $H(p):=\sum_{i \in [R]} p_i \log_2(1/p_i)$.
nodes.section: 6.4 Lower Bound for Entropy Comparison and Approximation

nodes.name: Entropy comparison GapCmprEnt
nodes.statement:
Following Goldreich and Vadhan \cite{goldreichvadhansurvey}, we define a partial function $\mathsf{GapCmprEnt}_{N, R}^{\alpha, \beta}$ capturing the problem of comparing the entropies of two distributions.

The function $\mathsf{GapCmprEnt}_{N, R}^{\alpha, \beta}$  takes as input two 
vectors in $[R]^N$ and interprets each vector $i \in \{1, 2\}$ as a probability
distribution $p_i$ over $[R]$, with $p_i(j)=f_{i,j}/N$ where $f_{i,j}$ is the frequency of $j$
in the $i$th vector. The function $\mathsf{GapCmprEnt}_{N, R}^{\alpha, \beta}$ evaluates to 
$$\begin{cases}
-1 & \text{ if } H(p_1)-H(p_2) \leq \beta\\
1 & \text{ if } H(p_1)-H(p_2) \geq \alpha \\
\text{undefined} & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$
nodes.section: 6.4 Lower Bound for Entropy Comparison and Approximation
nodes.statement_short: Given two lists viewed as distributions, decide whether H(p_1)-H(p_2) <= beta or >= alpha.

nodes.name: Lower bound for entropy comparison
nodes.statement: There exist constants $0 < \beta < \alpha < 1$ such that $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}(\mathsf{GapCmprEnt}^{\alpha, \beta}_{N, R}) = \tilde{\Omega}(R^{1/2}).$ The same lower bound applies to the quantum query complexity of $\mathsf{GapCmprEnt}^{\alpha, \beta}_{N, R}$.

conclusions: There exist constants $0 < \beta < \alpha < 1$ such that $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}(\mathsf{GapCmprEnt}^{\alpha, \beta}_{N, R}) = \tilde{\Omega}(R^{1/2}).$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 68
nodes.statement: Vadhan \cite[Claim 4.4.2 and Remark 4.4.3]{vadhan} showed that as long as $H( (1+\gamma_1)/2) < 1-\gamma_2 - \lambda$, then $\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}$ is reducible to $\mathsf{GapCmprEnt}^{\alpha, \beta}_{4N, 2R}$ for some constants $\alpha, \beta$ such that $\alpha-\beta=\lambda$. This reduction (described next for completeness) implies that $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_{\varepsilon}(\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}) \leq \widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_{\varepsilon}(\mathsf{GapCmprEnt}^{\alpha, \beta}_{4N, 2R})$. For completeness, we sketch this transformation, closely following the presentation of Goldreich and Vadhan \cite{goldreichvadhansurvey}. At a high level, the reduction transforms an input in $[R]^N$ to $\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}$ (interpreted as a distribution $p$ over $[R]$) into two distributions $p_1, p_2$ over $[R] \times \{0, 1\}$ as follows. Both $p_1$ and $p_2$ start by sampling an $s \in \{0, 1\}$ at random. If $s=0$, then a random sample $r$ is chosen from $p$, and if $s=1$, then $r$ is set to a uniform random sample from $[R]$. Distribution $p_2$ outputs $(r, s)$, while $p_1$ outputs $(r, b)$ for a random $b \in \{0, 1\}$. The entropy of $p_1$ is always $v + 1$, where $v=\frac{1}{2} H(p) + \frac{1}{2} \log_2(R)$. As for the entropy of $p_2$, if $p$ is far from the uniform distribution, then the selection bit $s$ will be essentially determined by the sample $r$. Hence, the entropy of $p_2$ will be approximately $v$, which is noticeably smaller than the entropy of $p_1$. On the other hand, if the two input distributions are close then (even conditioned on the sample selected) the selection bit $s$ will be almost random and so $H(p_2) \approx v+1$, which is approximately the same as $H(p_1)$. Quantitatively, Vadhan \cite{vadhan} shows that if the statistical distance between $p$ and the uniform distribution is $\delta$, then $1-\delta \leq H(p_1) - H(p_2) \leq H( (1+\delta)/2)$. Since we are considering distributions specified as vectors in $[R]^N$, this transformation can be equivalently described as follows. Assume for simplicity that $R$ divides $N$. If $p$ is specified by a vector $u$ in $[R]^N$, then $p_2$ is specified by a vector $w$ in $([R]\times\{0,1\})^{4N}$ defined as follows. For all $i \in [N]$ and $j \in \{0, 1\}$, $w_{i, j}=(u_i, 0)$, and for $j \in \{2, 3\}$, $w_{i, j}=(\lceil Ri/N\rceil, 1)$. Similarly, $p_1$ is specified by a vector $v$ in $([R]\times\{0,1\})^{4N}$. For $i \in [R]$ and $j \in \{0, 1\}$, $v_{i, j}=(u_i, j)$, and for $j \in \{2, 3\}$, $v_{i, j} = (\lceil Ri/N\rceil, j-2)$. Observe that when representing $u$, $v$, and $w$ as vectors in $\{-1,1\}^{N \log_2(R)}$ or $\{-1,1\}^{4N \cdot \log_2(R)}$, each bit of $v$ and $w$ depends on at most one bit of $u$. Recall that in the statement of \Cref{sduthm}, $\gamma_1 = 1-3\gamma/2$ and $\gamma_2=1-\gamma^{1/2}/c$, where $\gamma$ is an arbitrary constant less than $(2/3c)^2$, where $c>1$ is the constant from \Cref{sethm}. Clearly, $H( (1+\gamma_1)/2)) = H(1-3 \gamma/4) = H(3 \gamma/4)$. Using the fact that for any $p \in [0, 1/2]$, \begin{align*} H(p) &= -p \log_2(p) - (1-p) \log_2(1-p) \\ &\le -2p\log_2(p) \\ &\le 6p^{3/4}, \end{align*} it follows that for some constant $\gamma \le 1/648c^4$, we have $H(3 \gamma/4) < \gamma^{1/2}/c$. Hence, Vadhan's reduction from $\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}$ to $\mathsf{GapCmprEnt}^{\alpha, \beta}_{4N, 2R}$ applies to this setting of $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$, and this shows that any degree $d$ $\varepsilon$-approximating polynomial for $\mathsf{GapCmprEnt}^{\alpha, \beta}_{4N, 2R}$ implies a degree $d$ polynomial $\varepsilon$-approximating polynomial for $\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}$. Combined with \Cref{sduthm}, this implies that $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}(\mathsf{GapCmprEnt}^{\alpha, \beta}_{4N, 2R}) = \tilde{\Omega}(R^{1/2}).$
nodes.section: 6.4 Lower Bound for Entropy Comparison and Approximation
nodes.statement_short: Vadhan's reduction from SDU to GapCmprEnt preserves degree (each output bit depends on one input bit); parameters from Theorem 67 satisfy its hypothesis.

nodes.name: Vadhan's reduction from SDU to entropy comparison
nodes.statement:
Vadhan \cite[Claim 4.4.2 and Remark 4.4.3]{vadhan} showed that as long as $H( (1+\gamma_1)/2) < 1-\gamma_2 - \lambda$, 
then $\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}$ is reducible
to $\mathsf{GapCmprEnt}^{\alpha, \beta}_{4N, 2R}$ for some constants $\alpha, \beta$
such that $\alpha-\beta=\lambda$.

conclusions:
$\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}$ is reducible
to $\mathsf{GapCmprEnt}^{\alpha, \beta}_{4N, 2R}$

nodes.name: Justification of Corollary 69
nodes.statement:
Clearly, a quantum query algorithm
that approximates entropy
up to additive error $(\alpha-\beta)/4$ can be used to solve $\mathsf{GapCmprEnt}^{\alpha, \beta}_{4N, 2R}$, by (approximately) computing the entropies of each of the two input distributions, and determining whether the difference is at most $(\beta + \alpha)/2$. Hence, \Cref{entropysucks} implies the following
lower bound for approximating entropy to additive error $\alpha-\beta$.
nodes.section: 6.4 Lower Bound for Entropy Comparison and Approximation
nodes.statement_short: An additive (alpha-beta)/4 entropy estimator decides GapCmprEnt, so Theorem 68 transfers.

nodes.name: Quantum lower bound for entropy approximation
nodes.statement: Let $N=c \cdot R$ for a sufficiently large constant $c$. Interpret an input in $[R]^N$ as a distribution $p$ in the natural way (i.e., for each $j \in [R]$, $p_j=f_j/N$, where $f_j$ is the number of times $j$ appears in the input). There is a constant $\varepsilon > 0$ such that any quantum algorithm that approximates the entropy of $p$ up to additive error $\varepsilon$ with probability at least $2/3$ requires $\tilde{\Omega}(R^{1/2})$ queries.

nodes.name: Bun-Thaler AC0 depth-(2k-1) approximate degree bound
nodes.statement:
Similarly, for any constant $k\geq 1$, Bun and Thaler exhibited an AC$^0$ circuit of depth $2k-1$
with approximate degree $\tilde{\Omega}\left(n^{1-2^{k-2}/3^{k-1}}\right)$.
nodes.section: 7.1 Additional Consequences: Approximate Degree Lower Bounds for DNFs and \texorpdfstring{AC$^0$}{AC0}
conclusions: Bun and Thaler exhibited an AC$^0$ circuit of depth $2k-1$

nodes.name: Improved AC0 approximate degree bounds
nodes.statement:
Our techniques can be used to give a polynomial improvement for any fixed $k\geq 2$, to
$\tilde{\Omega}\left(n^{1-2^{-k}}\right)$ (\Cref{thm:introsurj} 
is the special case of $k=2$, as $\mathsf{ SURJ}$ is computed by an AC$^0$ 
circuit of depth three).
nodes.section: 7.1 Additional Consequences: Approximate Degree Lower Bounds for DNFs and \texorpdfstring{AC$^0$}{AC0}
conclusions: $\tilde{\Omega}\left(n^{1-2^{-k}}\right)$

nodes.name: Closing the k-distinctness gap
nodes.statement:
It would also be interesting to close the gap between our $\Omega(n^{3/4-1/(2k)})$
lower bound for $k$-distinctness and Belovs' 
$O\left(n^{3/4-1/(2^{k+2} - 4})\right)$ upper bound, especially for small values of $k$ (e.g., $k=3$).

nodes.name: SDU with constants 2/3, 1/3
nodes.statement:
Although we prove a lower bound of $\tilde{\Omega}(R^{1/2})$
for $\mathsf{ SDU}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}_{N, R}$ for some constants $0 < \gamma_2 < \gamma_1$, we leave open whether or not $\mathsf{ SDU}^{2/3, 1/3}_{N, R} = \tilde{\Omega}(R^{1/2})$.

nodes.name: Polarization Lemma (Sahai-Vadhan)
nodes.statement:
The Polarization Lemma 
reduces $\mathsf{ SDU}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}_{N, R}$ for any pair of constant $\gamma_1, \gamma_2$
with $\gamma_2 < \gamma_1^2$ to  $\mathsf{ SDU}^{2/3, 1/3}_{N', R'}$ for an appropriate choice of $N'$ and $R'$.
assumptions:
for any pair of constant $\gamma_1, \gamma_2$
with $\gamma_2 < \gamma_1^2$
conclusions: to  $\mathsf{ SDU}^{2/3, 1/3}_{N', R'}$ for an appropriate choice of $N'$ and $R'$

nodes.name: Sublinear approximate degree for polynomial-size DNFs
nodes.statement: For every constant $c>0$ and every DNF formula $f\colon \{-1,1\}^n \to \{-1,1\}$ of size at most $n^c$, is there a $\delta > 0$ (depending only on $c$) such that $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}(f) = O(n^{1-\delta})$?
nodes.statement_short: Does every n^c-size DNF have approximate degree O(n^{1-delta}) for some delta(c) > 0?
nodes.label: op4

nodes.name: Approximate majority function
nodes.statement:
An approximate majority
function is any total Boolean function that evaluates to $-1$ (respectively $+1$) whenever at least $2/3$ of its 
inputs are $-1$ (respectively $+1$).

nodes.name: Approximate majorities in depth-3 AC0 (Ajtai)
nodes.statement:
It is well-known (via the probabilistic method) that there are approximate majorities computable by depth 3 circuits 
of quadratic size and logarithmic bottom fan-in \cite{ajtai}.
conclusions:
there are approximate majorities computable by depth 3 circuits 
of quadratic size and logarithmic bottom fan-in

nodes.name: Approximate degree of every approximate majority
nodes.statement:
It is possible that \emph{every} approximate majority has approximate degree $\Omega(n)$;
proving this would resolve a question of Srinivasan \cite{filmus2014real}.

nodes.name: Take an approximant for SURJ
nodes.statement: Let $p : \{-1,1\}^{(N+1) \cdot \log(R+1)} \to \{-1,1\}$ be a polynomial of degree $d$ that $\varepsilon$-approximates $\mathsf{ SURJ}_{N + 1, R+1}$. We will use $p$ to construct a polynomial of degree $d$ that $\varepsilon$-approximates $\mathsf{dSURJ}_{N, R}$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix a degree-d approximant p for SURJ_{N+1,R+1}.

nodes.name: Define the transformation T
nodes.statement: Recall that an input to $\mathsf{dSURJ}_{N, R}$ takes the form $(s_1, \dots, s_N)$ where each $s_i$ is the binary representation of a number in $[R]_0$. Define the transformation $T : [R]_0 \to [R + 1]$ by \[T(s) = \begin{cases} R + 1 & \text{ if } s = 0 \\ s & \text{ otherwise}. \end{cases}\]
nodes.statement_short: Map the dummy 0 to R+1.

nodes.name: T is low degree and preserves the function
nodes.statement: Note that as a mapping between binary representations, the function $T$ is exactly computed by a vector of polynomials of degree at most $\log(R+1)$. For every $(s_1, \dots, s_N) \in [R]_0^N$, observe that \[\mathsf{dSURJ}_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = \mathsf{ SURJ}_{N + 1, R+1}(T(s_1), \dots, T(s_N), R+1).\]
nodes.statement_short: T has degree <= log(R+1) and dSURJ(s) = SURJ(T(s), R+1).

nodes.name: Compose
nodes.statement: Hence, the polynomial \[p(T(s_1), \dots, T(s_N), R+1)\] is a polynomial of degree $d \cdot \log(R+1)$ that $\varepsilon$-approximates $\mathsf{dSURJ}_{N, R}$.
nodes.statement_short: p o T approximates dSURJ with degree d log(R+1).

nodes.name: Analogy with Proposition 18
nodes.statement: The proof is similar to that of \Cref{prop:dumsurj-reduction}, but uses a slightly more involved reduction.
nodes.statement_short: Same strategy as Proposition 18.

nodes.name: Take an approximant and define T_i
nodes.statement: Let $p : \{-1,1\}^{2N\cdot \log(R+N)} \to \{-1,1\}$ be a polynomial of degree $d$ that $\varepsilon$-approximates $\mathsf{DIST}^k_{N, R+N}$. We will use $p$ to construct a polynomial of degree $d$ that $\varepsilon$-approximates $\mathsf{dDIST}^k_{N, R}$. For each $i = 1, \dots, R$, define a transformation $T_i : [R]_0 \to [R+N]$ by \[T_i(s) = \begin{cases} R + i & \text{ if } s = 0 \\ s & \text{ otherwise}. \end{cases}\]
nodes.statement_short: Fix p for DIST^k_{N,R+N} and maps T_i sending 0 to R+i.

nodes.name: T preserves the function
nodes.statement: As a mapping between binary representations, the function $T=(T_1, \dots, T_N)$ is exactly computed by a vector of polynomials of degree at most $\log(R+1)$. For every $(s_1, \dots, s_N) \in [R]_0^N$, observe that \[\mathsf{dDIST}^k_{N, R}(s_1, \dots, s_N) = \mathsf{DIST}^k_{N, R+N}(T_1(s_1), \dots, T_N(s_N)).\]
nodes.statement_short: Distinct fresh items keep k-collisions unchanged.

nodes.name: Compose
nodes.statement: Hence, the polynomial \[p(T(s_1), \dots, T(s_N))\] is a polynomial of degree $d \cdot \log(R+1)$ that $\varepsilon$-approximates $\mathsf{dSURJ}_{N, R}$.
nodes.statement_short: p o T approximates dDIST^k.

nodes.name: Split omega
nodes.statement: Recall that $\psi(x) = \omega(|x|) / \binom{N}{|x|}$ where $\omega \colon [M]_{0} \to \mathbb{R}$. By Equation~\eqref{eqn:omega-balanced} we may write $\omega = \omega_{+1} - \omega_{-1}$ where $\omega_{+1}$ and $\omega_{-1}$ are non-negative functions satisfying \begin{equation} \sum_{t=0}^k \omega_{+1}(t) = \sum_{t=0}^k \omega_{-1}(t) = 1/2.\end{equation}

nodes.name: Sum over weight profiles
nodes.statement: Observe that for any $(t_1, \dots, t_R) \in [M]_0^R$, the number of inputs $(x_1, \dots, x_R) \in \left(\{-1,1\}^N\right)^R$ such that $|x_i| = t_i$ for all $i \in [R]$ is exactly $\prod_{i=1}^{R} \binom{N}{ t_i}$. Hence, defining $$P = \{(t_1, \dots, t_R) \in [M]_0^R : t_1 + \dots + t_R > N\},$$ we may rewrite Expression \eqref{finallineman} as \[2^R \sum_{z \in \{-1,1\}^R} |\Phi(z)| \left( \sum_{(t_1, \dots, t_R) \in P} \prod_{i = 1}^R \omega_{z_i}(t_i) \right).\]

nodes.name: State the combinatorial lemma
nodes.statement: To control this quantity, we appeal to the following combinatorial lemma, whose proof we delay to \Cref{s:proofofcomb} (this lemma is a substantial refinement of \cite[Lemma 32]{adegsurj}). \begin{restatable}{lemma}{combinatorial} Let $\alpha \le R^2$, let $\beta \in (4\ln^2 R/ \sqrt{\alpha} R, 1)$, and let $R$ be sufficiently large. Let $N = \lceil 20 \sqrt{\alpha}\rceil R$. Let $\eta_i :[M]_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, for $i = 1, \dots R$, be a sequence of non-negative functions where for every $i$, \begin{align}&\sum_{r = 0}^M \eta_i(r) \le 1 / 2 \\ &\eta_i(r) \le \alpha \exp(-\beta r) / r^2 \qquad \forall r = 1, \dots, M. \end{align} Let $P = \{\vec{t} = (t_1, \dots, t_R) \in [M]_0^R : t_1 + \dots + t_R > N\}$. Then \[\sum_{\vec{t} \in P} \prod_{i = 1}^R \eta_i(t_i) \le 2^{-R} \cdot (2NR)^{-2\Delta}\] where $\Delta \ge \beta\sqrt{\alpha} R / 4\ln^2 R$. \end{restatable}
nodes.statement_short: Invoke Lemma (lem:combinatorial), proved later.

nodes.name: Apply the lemma

Property~\eqref{eqn:omega-decay}). We complete the proof by bounding \begin{align*} 2^R \sum_{z \in \{-1,1\}^R} |\Phi(z)| \left( \sum_{\vec{t} \in P} \prod_{i = 1}^R \omega_{z_i}(t_i) \right) &\le 2^R \sum_{z \in \{-1,1\}^R} |\Phi(z)| \cdot \left(2^{-R} \cdot (2NR)^{-2\Delta}\right)\\ &=(2NR)^{-2 \Delta} . \end{align*} Here, the equality appeals to the condition that $\|\Phi\|_1 = 1$.
