u(x)| \ &\le \left(  rac{1}{\|\xi\|_1 - \|
u\|_1} - 1 ight) \cdot \|\xi\|_1 +  rac{1}{\|\xi\|_1 - \|
u\|_1} \cdot \|
u\|_1 \ &\le \left( rac{1}{1 - 1/10} - 1 ight)+  rac{1 /10 }{1 - 1/10} \ &=  rac{2}{9}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: zeta is supported on H_{<=N} and within 2/9 of xi.
nodes.section: 2.7 A Refinement of a Technical Lemma from Prior Work

nodes.name: Norm and pure high degree
nodes.statement: Equation~\eqref{eqn:final-norm} is immediate from the definition of $\zeta$. Finally,~\eqref{eqn:final-phd} follows from~\eqref{eqn:prelim-phd}, \eqref{eqn:correction-phd}, and linearity.
nodes.statement_short: Unit norm by definition; pure high degree by linearity.
nodes.section: 2.7 A Refinement of a Technical Lemma from Prior Work

nodes.name: Define T and C(s)
nodes.statement: Let $T = \lfloor \frac{N}{2M} \rfloor$. For each $s \in \{T, \dots, R\}$, let \[C(s) = \max \left\{ \frac{N}{6 s \ln R}, \frac{N}{6\sqrt{R \cdot s}} \right\}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Set T = floor(N/2M) and thresholds C(s).

nodes.name: Structural claim on heavy profiles
nodes.statement: We begin with a simple, but important, structural observation about the set $P$. Let $t = (t_1, \dots, t_R) \in [M]_0^R$ be a sequence such that $t_1 + \dots + t_R > N$. Then we claim that there exists an $s \in \{T \dots, R\}$ such that $t_i \ge C(s)$ for at least $s$ indices $i \in [R]$. To see this, assume without loss of generality that the entries of $\vec{t}$ are sorted so that $t_1 \ge t_2 \ge \dots \ge t_R$. Then there must exist an $s \geq T$ such that $t_s \ge C(s)$. Otherwise, because no $t_i$ can exceed $M$, we would have: \begin{align*} t_1 + \dots + t_R &< T \cdot M + \sum_{s = 1}^R C(s) \\ &\le \frac{N}{2} + \frac{N}{6 \ln R} \sum_{s = 1}^{\lfloor R / \ln^2 R \rfloor} \frac{1}{s} + \frac{N}{6\sqrt{R}} \sum_{s = \lceil R / \ln^2 R \rceil}^R \frac{1}{\sqrt{s}}\\ &\le \frac{N}{2}+ \frac{N}{6} + \frac{N}{3} \\ &= N. \end{align*} where the last inequality follows from \Cref{lem:inv-sqrt} and the fact that $\sum_{s = 1}^m s^{-1} \le \ln m + 1$ (and $R$ is sufficiently large). Since the entries of $\vec{t}$ are sorted, the preceding values $t_1, \dots, t_{s-1} \geq C(s)$ as well.
nodes.statement_short: Any profile with total > N has s >= T coordinates at least C(s).

nodes.name: Sorted profile argument
nodes.statement: To see this, assume without loss of generality that the entries of $\vec{t}$ are sorted so that $t_1 \ge t_2 \ge \dots \ge t_R$. Then there must exist an $s \geq T$ such that $t_s \ge C(s)$. Otherwise, because no $t_i$ can exceed $M$, we would have: \begin{align*} t_1 + \dots + t_R &< T \cdot M + \sum_{s = 1}^R C(s) \\ &\le \frac{N}{2} + \frac{N}{6 \ln R} \sum_{s = 1}^{\lfloor R / \ln^2 R \rfloor} \frac{1}{s} + \frac{N}{6\sqrt{R}} \sum_{s = \lceil R / \ln^2 R \rceil}^R \frac{1}{\sqrt{s}}\\ &\le \frac{N}{2}+ \frac{N}{6} + \frac{N}{3} \\ &= N. \end{align*} where the last inequality follows from \Cref{lem:inv-sqrt} and the fact that $\sum_{s = 1}^m s^{-1} \le \ln m + 1$ (and $R$ is sufficiently large).
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise the total would be at most N.

nodes.name: Monotonicity
nodes.statement: Since the entries of $\vec{t}$ are sorted, the preceding values $t_1, \dots, t_{s-1} \geq C(s)$ as well.
nodes.statement_short: The first s entries all exceed C(s).

nodes.name: Define P_S
nodes.statement: For each subset $S \subseteq [R]$, define \[P_S = \{\vec{t} \in P : t_i \ge C(|S|)\text{ for all indices }i \in S\}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Profiles heavy on the set S.

nodes.name: Union bound and decay
nodes.statement: The observations above guarantee that for every $\vec{t}=(t_1, \dots, t_R) \in P$, there exists some set $S$ of size at least $s \in \{T, \dots, R\}$ such that $t_i \geq C(s)$ for all $i \in S$. Hence \begin{align*} \hspace{-10mm} \sum_{\vec{t} \in P} \prod_{i = 1}^R \eta_i(t_i) & \leq \sum_{s = T}^{R} \sum_{S \subseteq [R] : |S| = s} \sum_{\vec{t} \in P_S} \prod_{i = 1}^R \eta_i(t_i) \\ & \leq \sum_{s = T}^{R} \binom{R}{s} \left( \max_{i \in \{1, \dots, R\}} \left( \sum_{r=\lceil C(s) \rceil}^M \eta_i(r)\right) \right)^s \left( \max_{i \in \{1, \dots, R\}} \left( \sum_{r = 0}^M \eta_i(r) \right)\right)^{R-s} \hspace{-3.3em}&\hspace{-3em}\\ &\leq 2^{-R}\sum_{s = T}^{R} \binom{R}{s} \left( \sum_{r = \lceil C(s) \rceil}^M 2\alpha \exp(-\beta r ) r^{-2} \right)^s & \hspace{-28mm} \text{by Properties } \eqref{eqn:eta-bound} \text{ and } \eqref{eqn:eta-decay}\\ &\le 2^{-R} \sum_{s = T}^{R} \left( \frac{Re}{s} \right)^s \left(\frac{2\alpha}{(C(s))^2} \right)^{s} \cdot \sum_{r = \lceil C(s) \rceil}^\infty \exp\left(-\beta r s\right) & \hspace{-28mm} \text{by \Cref{lem:binomial}}\\ &\le 2^{-R} \sum_{s = T}^{R} \left( \frac{Re}{s} \right)^s \left(\frac{2\alpha}{(C(s))^2} \right)^{s} \cdot \frac{1}{1 - e^{-\beta s}} \cdot \exp\left(-\beta s C(s)\right) & \hspace{-28mm} \text{by \Cref{lem:inv-exp-tail}}\\ &\le 2^{-R} \sum_{s = T}^{R} \left( \frac{Re}{s} \right)^s \left(\frac{72\alpha R s}{N^2} \right)^{s} \cdot \frac{2}{\beta} \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{\beta N}{6\ln R}\right) & \text{by definition of $C(s)$}\\ &\qquad\qquad\text{ and since } \frac{1}{1 - e^{-\beta s}} \le \frac{1}{1 - (1-\beta/2)} = \frac{2}{\beta} \text{ for } s \ge 1, \beta \in (0, 1) \hspace{-10em}&\hspace{-10em} \\ &\le 2^{-R} \sum_{s = T}^{R} 2^{-s} \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{3 \beta \sqrt{\alpha} R }{ \ln R} + \ln(2/\beta)\right)&\hspace{-28mm}\text{setting } N = \lceil 20 \sqrt{\alpha}\rceil R \\ &\le 2^{-R} \cdot (2 N R)^{-2\Delta}, \end{align*} where \[\Delta = \frac{1}{2\ln(2NR)} \cdot \left(\frac{3\beta \sqrt{\alpha} R}{\ln R} - \ln(2/\beta) \right) \ge \frac{\beta \sqrt{\alpha} R}{4\ln^2 R}\] holds for sufficiently large $R$ by the restrictions placed on $\alpha$ and $\beta$ in the statement of the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Union bound over S, then Lemmas 32-34 bound the sum by 2^{-R}(2NR)^{-2 Delta}.

nodes.name: WLOG R = Theta(N)
nodes.statement: For the remainder of the section, we focus on proving \Cref{thm:upper} in the case that $R=\Theta(N)$. This is without loss of generality by the following argument.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the case R = Theta(N).

nodes.name: Case R > N
nodes.statement:
If $R > N$, then 
Surjectivity\ is identically false, and hence has (exact) degree 0.
nodes.statement_short: SURJ is identically false.

nodes.name: Case R = o(N)
nodes.statement:
And if $R=o(N)$, then we can reduce to the case $R=\Theta(N)$ as follows. Let $N'=2N$ and $R' = R + N$;
clearly $R' = \Theta(N)$.
Given an input $x$ to $\mathsf{ SURJ}_{N, R}$, obtain an input $x'$ to $\mathsf{ SURJ}_{N', R'}$ by appending range elements $R+1, \dots, R+N$ to $x$. 
This construction guarantees that $\mathsf{ SURJ}_{N, R}(x) = \mathsf{ SURJ}_{N', R'}(x')$. It follows that an approximation of degree $\tilde{O}(N^{3/4})$ for $\mathsf{ SURJ}_{N', R'}$
implies an approximation of the same degree for $\mathsf{ SURJ}_{N, R}$.
nodes.statement_short: Pad the input with the new items R+1..R+N.

nodes.name: Define V from a Chebyshev polynomial
nodes.statement: Choose $d = O(\sqrt{T} \log(1/\varepsilon))$ so that $M := T_d(1 + 1/T) + 1\ge 2/\varepsilon$ (as guaranteed by Property 1 of \Cref{lem:cheb}). Define $V_{T, \varepsilon}$ by the following affine transformation of $T_d$: \[V_{T, \varepsilon}(x) = \left(1 - \frac{1}{M}\right) - \frac{1}{M} \cdot T_d\left(1 + \frac{1}{T} - \frac{|x|}{T}\right).\]
nodes.statement_short: Affine transform of T_d with M >= 2/eps.
nodes.section: 3.4.1 Approximating Surjectivity\ on the Hard Inputs

nodes.name: Weight zero
nodes.statement: Then for $|x| = 0$, we have \[V_{T, \varepsilon}(x) = \left(1 - \frac{1}{M}\right) - \frac{1}{M} \cdot T_d\left(1 + \frac{1}{T}\right) = 0.\]
nodes.section: 3.4.1 Approximating Surjectivity\ on the Hard Inputs

nodes.name: Low weight
nodes.statement: If $1 \le |x| \le T$, then $1 + 1/T - |x| / T \in [-1, 1]$, so $V_{T, \varepsilon(x)} \in [1-\varepsilon, 1]$.
nodes.statement_short: V in [1-eps, 1] on 1 <= |x| <= T.
nodes.section: 3.4.1 Approximating Surjectivity\ on the Hard Inputs

nodes.name: High weight growth
nodes.statement: Finally, if $T +1 \le |x| \le N$, then \[|V_{T, \varepsilon}(x)| \le 1 + \frac{1}{M} \cdot T_d(N / T) \le \exp(O(\sqrt{T} \cdot\log N \cdot\log(1/\varepsilon)),\] where the final inequality holds by Equation \eqref{eq:swell}.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 36 bounds |V| by exp(O(sqrt T log N log 1/eps)).
nodes.section: 3.4.1 Approximating Surjectivity\ on the Hard Inputs

nodes.name: Reduce to |p(y) - p(z)| <= delta n
nodes.statement: Fix any input $x = (x_1, \dots, x_n) \in X^n$, and let $y = (g(x_1), \dots, g(x_n)) \in \{0,1\}^n$. Let $z \in [0, 1]^n$ be defined by $z = (q(x_1), \dots, q(x_n))$. Since $p$ is an $\varepsilon$-approximating polynomial for $f$, by the triangle inequality, it suffices to show that $|p(y) - p(z)| \le \delta n$.
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to compare p at y = g(x) and z = q(x).
nodes.section: 3.4.1 Approximating Surjectivity\ on the Hard Inputs

nodes.name: Randomized rounding
nodes.statement: Let $Z$ be a random variable on $\{0,1\}^n$ where each $Z_i = 1$ independently with probability $z_i$. Then due to the multilinearity of $p$, we have \[p(z) = \mathbb{E}[p(Z)] = \Pr[Z =y] \cdot p(y) + \Pr[Z \ne y] \cdot \mathbb{E}[p(Z) | Z \ne y].\]
nodes.statement_short: By multilinearity p(z) = E[p(Z)].
nodes.section: 3.4.1 Approximating Surjectivity\ on the Hard Inputs

nodes.name: Z = y with high probability
nodes.statement: Since $q$ is a $\delta$-approximating polynomial for $g$, we have $|y_i - z_i| \le \delta$ for every $i \in [n]$. Hence, \[\Pr[Z = y] \ge \left(1 - \delta \right)^n \ge 1 - \delta n.\]
nodes.statement_short: Pr[Z = y] >= 1 - delta n.
nodes.section: 3.4.1 Approximating Surjectivity\ on the Hard Inputs

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Because $p$ is bounded in $[0, 1]$, this implies \[p(z) \ge (1 - \delta n) \cdot p(y) + 0 \ge p(y) - \delta n\] and \[p(z) \le 1 \cdot p(y) + \delta n \cdot 1 = p(y) + \delta n,\] completing the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Boundedness of p gives |p(z) - p(y)| <= delta n.
nodes.section: 3.4.1 Approximating Surjectivity\ on the Hard Inputs

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: We prove the lemma by induction on the number of variables $n$. If $n = 0$, then $p$ is a constant in the interval $[0, 1]$ and the claim is true.
nodes.statement_short: n = 0: p is a constant in [0,1].
nodes.section: 3.4.1 Approximating Surjectivity\ on the Hard Inputs

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: Now suppose the claim is true for $n-1$ variables, and let $p : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ with $p(x) \in [0, 1]$ for $x \in \{0,1\}^n$. We begin by decomposing \[p(x) = (1-x_n) \cdot q_0(x_1, \dots, x_{n-1}) + x_n \cdot q_1(x_1, \dots, x_{n-1})\] where $q_0$ and $q_1$ are themselves multilinear polynomials. Since $p(x) \in [0, 1]$ for all $x \in \{0,1\}^n$, this is in particular true when $x_n = 0$. Hence $q_0(x') \in [0, 1]$ for all $x' \in \{0,1\}^{n-1}$. Similarly, setting $x_n = 1$ reveals that $q_1(x') \in [0, 1]$ for all $x' \in \{0,1\}^{n-1}$. Now for any $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with $x' = (x_1, \dots, x_{n-1})$ we have \begin{align*} |p(x)| &= \left| (1 - x_n) \cdot q_0(x') + x_n \cdot q_1(x')\right| \\ &\le |1 - x_n| \cdot |q_0(x')| + |x_n| \cdot |q_1(x')| \\ &\le (|1 - x_n| + |x_n|) \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^{n-1} (|1 - x_i| + |x_i|) \end{align*} where the final inequality uses the inductive hypothesis. This proves the claim.
nodes.statement_short: Decompose along x_n and apply the hypothesis to q_0, q_1.
nodes.section: 3.4.1 Approximating Surjectivity\ on the Hard Inputs

nodes.name: Hard inputs; view p_R as w(z)
nodes.statement: The first two cases are an immediate consequence of \Cref{approxlemma}. To upper bound the value of $|p_\mathcal{R}(x)|$ for $x\notin \mathcal{P}_\mathcal{R}$, we exploit the structure of $p_\mathcal{R}$ as a multilinear polynomial $w$ of degree $O(\sqrt{N})$ over the variables $z_1,\ldots,z_{|\mathcal{R}|}$, where each $z_r$ is the output of the $r^\mathrm{th}$ polynomial from \Cref{lem:orT}. That is, $$z_r = V_{T, 1/(20n)}\left({\mathds{1}}[x_1 = r], \dots, {\mathds{1}}[x_N = r]\right).$$
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 39 handles x in P_R; elsewhere write p_R = w(z) with z_r the V-outputs.
nodes.section: 3.4.1 Approximating Surjectivity\ on the Hard Inputs

nodes.name: Few unbounded inputs
nodes.statement: If $b_\mathcal{R}(x)$ range items appear greater than $T$ times, this means that up to $b_\mathcal{R}(x)$ of the variables $z_r$ might take values outside $[0,1]$. However, by \Cref{lem:orT}, each of these $b_\mathcal{R}(x)$ variables is still at most ${\exp(\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T}))}$.
nodes.statement_short: At most b_R(x) of the z_r leave [0,1], each at most exp(O~(sqrt T)).
nodes.section: 3.4.1 Approximating Surjectivity\ on the Hard Inputs

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 40
nodes.statement: By \Cref{lem:real-bound}, \[|w(z)| \le \prod_{r \in \mathcal{R}} \left(|1 - z_r| + |z_r|\right) \le \exp\left(b_\mathcal{R}(x) \cdot \tilde{O}\left(\sqrt{T}\right)\right),\] since each $z_r $ that is in $[0, 1]$ contributes a factor of exactly $1$ to the product, whereas each of the remaining $b_\mathcal{R}(x)$ variables contributes a factor of at most ${\exp(\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T}))}$ to the product.
nodes.statement_short: The product bound gives |w(z)| <= exp(b_R(x) O~(sqrt T)).
nodes.section: 3.4.1 Approximating Surjectivity\ on the Hard Inputs

nodes.name: Define r(x)
nodes.statement_short: Average p_{R(y)} over samples; degree O~(S + sqrt(NT)) = O~(N^{3/4}).

nodes.name: r(x) as an expectation
nodes.statement:
The value of the polynomial on input $x$ is
\begin{equation} r(x) = \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\mathcal{S} \in \binom{[N]}{S}} p_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x). 
\end{equation}
where recall that $\mathcal{R}(x_{\mathcal{S}})$ is as defined in Equation \eqref{nomoreeqs}.
The right hand side of Equation \eqref{fleck} is precisely the expected value of the polynomial $p_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x)$ when $\mathcal{S}$ is a uniformly random set of size $S$. We will now show that $r(x)$ is an approximating polynomial for Surjectivity, i.e., that for all $x\in[R]^N$, $|\mathsf{ SURJ}(x)-r(x)|\leq 1/3$.
nodes.statement_short: r(x) = E_S[p_{R(x_S)}(x)]; goal |SURJ - r| <= 1/3.

nodes.name: Split by b
nodes.statement:
Recalling that $b_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}$ is the number of range items $r \in \mathcal{R}$ that appear in $x$ greater than $T$ times (cf. Equation \eqref{eq:b}),
we compute the value of the polynomial $r(x)$ on an input $x$:
\begin{align}
    r(x) &= \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\mathcal{S} \in \binom{[N]}{S}} p_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x) \\
    &= \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \left(\sum_{\mathcal{S} \in \binom{[N]}{S}} \sum_{b=0}^{N/T} {\mathds{1}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x)=b] \cdot p_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x) \right)\\
    &= \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\mathcal{S} \in \binom{[N]}{S}} {\mathds{1}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x)=0] \cdot p_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x) \\
    &\qquad\qquad\qquad + \sum_{b=1}^{N/T} \frac{1}{\binom{N}{S}} \sum_{\mathcal{S} \in \binom{[N]}{S}}  {\mathds{1}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x)=b]  \cdot p_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x), \end{align}
where we split up the sum into the $b=0$ \eqref{eq:t1} and $b\geq 1$ \eqref{eq:t2}  cases.
We first show that the $b\geq1$ term \eqref{eq:t2} has essentially no contribution to the final value.
nodes.statement_short: Separate the b = 0 and b >= 1 terms.

nodes.name: Bound the b >= 1 terms
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 41 bounds each term by exp(b O~(sqrt T)).

nodes.name: State Lemma 42
nodes.statement:
We now need to compute the value of $\Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x)=b]$ for each $b$. Intuitively, this roughly corresponds to the probability that we sample $S=\tilde{\Theta}(N^{3/4})$ elements from the input and miss all $bT$ elements that correspond to the $T = \tilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{N})$ copies of the $b$ range items that appear at least $T$ times. 
If we were to sample $N / (bT)$ elements, the probability of seeing none of the $b T$ elements would be $\Theta(1)$. 
Since we are sampling $S=\tilde{\Theta}(N^{3/4}) \gg N / (bT)$ elements, the probability of not seeing one of the $bT$ elements is ${\exp(-bST/N)} = {\exp(-b \cdot \tilde{\Omega}(N^{1/4}))}$. We make this heuristic calculation formal in the following lemma:

\begin{lemma} Let $S, T \le N$. Let $\mathcal{S} \subset [N]$ be a random subset of size $S$. Then for every $x \in [R]^N$ and every $b \ge 1$,
\[\Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x) \ge b] \leq {\exp(-b \cdot (ST/N - \log N))},\]
recalling that $b_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}$ is the number of range items $r \in \mathcal{R}$ that appear in $x$ more than $T$ times, but do not appear in $x_\mathcal{S}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
To calculate the probability of interest, we begin by analyzing a simplified experiment. Suppose there are $b$ range items $r_1, \dots, r_b$ each appearing greater than $T$ times in $x$. We compute the probability that \emph{none} of the items $r_1, \dots, r_b$ appear in the sample $x_\mathcal{S}$. If $T \ge N - S$, then this probability is zero. Otherwise, by direct calculation, we have for each $i = 1, \dots, b$:
\[\Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[r_i \notin x_\mathcal{S} | r_1 \notin x_\mathcal{S}, \dots, r_{i-1} \notin x_\mathcal{S}] \le \prod_{j = 0}^{S-1} \left(1 - \frac{T}{N-j} \right) \le \left( 1 - \frac{T}{N}\right)^S \le \exp \left(-\frac{ST}{N} \right).\]
Hence the probability that none of $r_1, \dots, r_b$ appear is
\[\Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[r_1 \notin x_\mathcal{S} \land \dots \land r_b \notin x_\mathcal{S}] = \prod_{i  = 1}^b \Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[r_i \notin x_\mathcal{S} | r_1 \notin x_\mathcal{S}, \dots, r_{i-1} \notin x_\mathcal{S}] \le \exp \left(-\frac{bST}{N} \right).\]

Now fix an arbitrary $x$, and let $r_1, \dots, r_{k}$ be the range items appearing greater than $T$ times in $x$. Observe that $k \le N/T$. We estimate the probability of interest by taking a union bound over all subsets of $r_1, \dots, r_k$ of size $b$:
\begin{align*}
\Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x) \ge b] &\le \sum_{Y \subseteq [k] : |Y| = b} \Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[r_{i_j} \notin x_\mathcal{S} \quad \forall j \in Y] \\
& \le \binom{k}{b} \exp \left(-\frac{bST}{N}\right) \\
&\le \exp \left( -\frac{bST}{N} + b \log N\right).
\end{align*}
\end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: Probability of missing b frequent items, with its proof.

nodes.name: Simplified experiment
nodes.statement: To calculate the probability of interest, we begin by analyzing a simplified experiment. Suppose there are $b$ range items $r_1, \dots, r_b$ each appearing greater than $T$ times in $x$. We compute the probability that \emph{none} of the items $r_1, \dots, r_b$ appear in the sample $x_\mathcal{S}$.
nodes.statement_short: Consider b fixed items each appearing more than T times.

nodes.name: Trivial case
nodes.statement: If $T \ge N - S$, then this probability is zero.
nodes.statement_short: If T >= N - S some copy is always sampled.

nodes.name: Miss probability
nodes.statement:
Otherwise, by direct calculation, we have for each $i = 1, \dots, b$: \[\Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[r_i 
otin x_\mathcal{S} | r_1 
otin x_\mathcal{S}, \dots, r_{i-1} 
otin x_\mathcal{S}] \le \prod_{j = 0}^{S-1} \left(1 -  rac{T}{N-j} ight) \le \left( 1 -  rac{T}{N}ight)^S \le \exp \left(- rac{ST}{N} ight).\] Hence the probability that none of $r_1, \dots, r_b$ appear is \[\Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[r_1 
otin x_\mathcal{S} \land \dots \land r_b 
otin x_\mathcal{S}] = \prod_{i = 1}^b \Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[r_i 
otin x_\mathcal{S} | r_1 
otin x_\mathcal{S}, \dots, r_{i-1} 
otin x_\mathcal{S}] \le \exp \left(- rac{bST}{N} ight).\]
nodes.statement_short: Each item is missed with probability <= exp(-ST/N), so all b with exp(-bST/N).

nodes.name: Union bound
nodes.statement: Now fix an arbitrary $x$, and let $r_1, \dots, r_{k}$ be the range items appearing greater than $T$ times in $x$. Observe that $k \le N/T$. We estimate the probability of interest by taking a union bound over all subsets of $r_1, \dots, r_k$ of size $b$: \begin{align*} \Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x) \ge b] &\le \sum_{Y \subseteq [k] : |Y| = b} \Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[r_{i_j} \notin x_\mathcal{S} \quad \forall j \in Y] \\ & \le \binom{k}{b} \exp \left(-\frac{bST}{N}\right) \\ &\le \exp \left( -\frac{bST}{N} + b \log N\right). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Union bound over b-subsets of at most N/T frequent items.

nodes.name: b >= 1 terms are o(1)
nodes.statement_short: exp(-b ST/N) beats exp(b sqrt T) for S = N^{3/4}, T = sqrt N.

nodes.name: Reduce to b = 0
nodes.statement_short: r(x) equals the b = 0 term up to o(1).

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement:
By \Cref{lem:promiseSURJ}, we know that if $b_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x)=0$ (and hence $x \in \mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}$), then $p_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x) $ is a $(1/10)$-approximation to $\mathsf{ SURJ}(x)$. Applying \Cref{lem:prob-b} once again shows that $\Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x) \ge 1] \le \exp(- \tilde{\Omega}(N^{1/4}))$, so $\Pr_{\mathcal{S}}[b_{\mathcal{R}(x_\mathcal{S})}(x) = 0] = 1 - o(1)$. 
Hence, for all $x \in [R]^N$, $|r(x) - \mathsf{ SURJ}(x)| \le 1/10 + o(1) \le 1/3$. 

This completes
the proof of \Cref{thm:upper}.
nodes.statement_short: On b = 0 samples p_R is a 1/10-approximation, so |r - SURJ| <= 1/3.

nodes.name: Normalized goals
nodes.statement: By renormalizing, it suffices to construction a function $\omega : [T]_0 \to \mathbb{R}$ such that \begin{align} &\omega(0) - \sum_{t = 1}^T \omega(t) \ge (1 - \delta)\|\omega\|_1 \\ & \text{For all univariate polynomials } q \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\text{, } \deg q < c_1\sqrt{\delta T} \implies \sum_{t=0}^T \omega(t) \cdot q(t) = 0 \\ & |\omega(t)| \le \frac{170 \exp(-c_2 t \sqrt{\delta} /\sqrt{T})\|\omega\|_1}{\delta \cdot t^2} \qquad \forall t = 1, \dots, T.\end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Construct omega with the ratio versions of the properties.
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for \texorpdfstring{$\mathsf{ OR}_N$}{OR}

nodes.name: Define S and omega
nodes.statement: Let $c = \lceil 8 / \delta \rceil$ below. We will freely use the fact that since $\delta \le 1/2$, we have $c \le c^2 / (c-1) \le 10 /\delta$. Let $m = \lfloor \sqrt{T/2c} \rfloor$ and define the set \[S = \{1, c\} \cup \{2ci^2 : 0 \le i \le m\}.\] Note that $|S| \ge c_1 \sqrt{\delta T}$ for some absolute constant $c_1 > 0$. Define the function \[\omega(t) = \frac{(-1)^{t+(T-m)}}{T!} \binom{T}{t} \prod_{r \in [T]_0 \setminus S} (t - r).\]
nodes.statement_short: omega(t) proportional to (-1)^t binom(T,t) prod_{r not in S}(t - r).
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for \texorpdfstring{$\mathsf{ OR}_N$}{OR}

nodes.name: Binomial identity gives pure high degree
nodes.statement: Property~\eqref{eqn:or-sym-phd-ref} follows from the following well-known combinatorial identity. \begin{fact}[e.g., \cite{concrete} Equation (5.23) or \cite{osnewbounds}] Let $T \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $p$ be a polynomial of degree less than $T$. Then \[\sum_{t = 0}^T (-1)^t \binom{T}{t} p(t) = 0.\] \end{fact}
nodes.statement_short: Fact 46 implies the pure high degree property.
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for \texorpdfstring{$\mathsf{ OR}_N$}{OR}

nodes.name: Closed form for |omega(t)|
nodes.statement: Expanding out the binomial coefficient in the definition of $\omega$ reveals that \[|\omega(t)| = \begin{cases} \prod\limits_{r \in S \setminus \{t\}} \frac{1}{|t - r|} & \text{ for } t \in S, \\ 0 & \text{ otherwise.} \end{cases}\]
nodes.statement_short: |omega(t)| = prod_{r in S, r != t} 1/|t - r|.
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for \texorpdfstring{$\mathsf{ OR}_N$}{OR}

nodes.name: Decay at t = 1
nodes.statement: We now use this characterization to establish the improved tail decay property \eqref{eqn:or-sym-decay-ref}. This clearly holds for $t = 1$ with $c_2 = 1/10$, since $|\omega(1)| \le \|\omega\|_1$ and \[\frac{170}{\delta} \exp(-c_2\sqrt{\delta} / \sqrt{T}) \ge 340 \cdot e^{-\sqrt{2} / 10} > 1.\]
nodes.statement_short: Trivial at t = 1 with c_2 = 1/10.
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for \texorpdfstring{$\mathsf{ OR}_N$}{OR}

nodes.name: Decay at t = c
nodes.statement_short: |omega(c)|/omega(0) <= 6/(c-1).
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for \texorpdfstring{$\mathsf{ OR}_N$}{OR}

nodes.name: Decay at t = 2cj^2
nodes.statement: For $t = 2cj^2$ with $j \ge 1$, we get \begin{align*} \frac{|\omega(t)|}{\omega(0)} &= \frac{c\prod_{i = 1}^m (2ci^2)}{(2cj^2 - 1)(2cj^2-c)\prod_{i \in [m]_0 \setminus \{j\}} |2ci^2 - 2cj^2|} \\ &= \frac{c(m!)^2}{(4c^2j^4 - (2c^2 + 2c)j^2 + c)\prod_{i \in [m]_0 \setminus \{j\}} (i+j)|i-j|} \\ &= \frac{c}{4c^2j^4 - (2c^2 + 2c)j^2 + c} \cdot \frac{(m!)^2}{(m+j)!(m-j)!}. \end{align*} For $j \ge 1$, the first factor is bounded by \[\frac{c}{4c^2j^4 - (2c^2 + 2c)j^2 + c} \le \frac{3c}{(2cj^2)^2},\] using the fact that $c \ge 2$. We control the second factor by \begin{align*} \frac{(m!)^2}{(m+j)!(m-j)!} &= \frac{m}{m+j} \cdot \frac{m-1}{m+j-1} \cdot \ldots \cdot \frac{m-j+1}{m+1} \\ &\le \left(\frac{m}{m+j} \right)^j \\ &\le \left(1 - \frac{j}{2m} \right)^j \\ &\le e^{-j^2/2m}, \end{align*} where the last inequality uses the fact that $1 - x \le e^{-x}$ for all $x$. Since \[\frac{|\omega(t)|}{\|\omega\|_1} \le \frac{|\omega(2cj^2)|}{\omega(0)} \le \frac{3c}{(2cj^2)^2} \cdot e^{-2cj^2/(4cm)} \le \frac{170}{\delta \cdot t^2} \cdot e^{-t \sqrt{\delta} / 10 \sqrt{T}},\] this establishes~\eqref{eqn:or-sym-decay-ref}.
nodes.statement_short: Ratio bounded by 3c/(2cj^2)^2 times e^{-j^2/2m}.
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for \texorpdfstring{$\mathsf{ OR}_N$}{OR}

nodes.name: omega(1) dominates
nodes.statement: What remains is to perform the correlation calculation to establish~\eqref{eqn:or-sym-corr-ref}. For $t = 1$, we observe \[\frac{|\omega(1)|}{\omega(0)} = \frac{c\prod_{i = 1}^m (2ci^2)}{(c-1)\prod_{i = 1}^m (2ci^2 - 1)} \ge \prod_{i=1}^m \frac{i^2}{i^2 - 1/(2c)} \ge 1.\]
nodes.statement_short: |omega(1)| >= omega(0).
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for \texorpdfstring{$\mathsf{ OR}_N$}{OR}

nodes.name: Tail mass
nodes.statement: Next, we observe that the total contribution of $t > c$ to $\|\omega\|_1/\omega(0)$ is at most \begin{equation} \sum_{t > c} \frac{|\omega(t)|}{\omega(0)} \le \sum_{j=1}^{m} \frac{3c}{(2cj^2)^2} < \sum_{j=1}^\infty \frac{3}{4cj^4} = \frac{\pi^4}{120 c}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Mass beyond c is at most pi^4/(120c) omega(0).
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for \texorpdfstring{$\mathsf{ OR}_N$}{OR}

nodes.name: Bound numerator and norm
nodes.statement_short: Correlation numerator >= -omega(1) + (1-delta) omega(0); norm <= -omega(1) + (1+delta) omega(0).
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for \texorpdfstring{$\mathsf{ OR}_N$}{OR}

nodes.name: Correlation
nodes.statement: Combining~\eqref{eqn:fudgethis} and~\eqref{eqn:fudgethat}, and using the fact that $-\omega(1) \ge \omega(0)$ shows that \[\frac{\omega(0) - \sum_{t = 1}^k \omega(t)}{\|\omega\|_1} \ge \frac{-\omega(1) + (1-\delta) \omega(0)}{-\omega(1) + (1+\delta) \omega(0)} \ge \frac{2-\delta}{2 + \delta} \ge 1 - \delta.\] This establishes~\eqref{eqn:or-sym-corr-ref}, completing the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Ratio is at least (2-delta)/(2+delta) >= 1 - delta.
nodes.section: 4.1 Step 1: A Dual Witness for \texorpdfstring{$\mathsf{ OR}_N$}{OR}

nodes.name: Parameter choices
nodes.statement: We start by fixing choices of several key parameters:
nodes.statement_short: Fix the parameters.
nodes.section: 4.3 Step 3: Constructing the Final Dual Witness

nodes.name: d and T
nodes.statement: $d= \Theta(\sqrt{R})$ is the pure high degree of the dual witness $\Phi$ for $\mathsf{AND}_R$ in \Cref{prop:and-or}, \item $T = \lfloor(R/d)^{1/2}\rfloor^2 = \Theta(\sqrt{R})$,
nodes.statement_short: d = Theta(sqrt R) from the AND dual; T = Theta(sqrt R).
nodes.section: 4.3 Step 3: Constructing the Final Dual Witness

nodes.name: D-hat, delta, alpha
nodes.statement: $\hat{D} = c_1 \sqrt{T} \cdot d =\Theta(R^{3/4})$, where $c_1$ is the constant from \Cref{prop:or-sym-dual}, \item $\delta =1/20$ \item $\alpha = 170/\delta = 3400$,
nodes.statement_short: Target degree Theta(R^{3/4}), delta = 1/20, alpha = 3400.
nodes.section: 4.3 Step 3: Constructing the Final Dual Witness

nodes.name: beta and N
nodes.statement: $\beta = c_2 \cdot \sqrt{\delta} / \sqrt{T} = \Theta(1/R^{1/4})$, where $c_2$ is the constant from \Cref{prop:or-sym-dual}, \item $N = \lceil 20 \sqrt{\alpha} \rceil R = 693 R$.
nodes.statement_short: beta = Theta(R^{-1/4}), N = 693R.
nodes.section: 4.3 Step 3: Constructing the Final Dual Witness

nodes.name: Compose the duals
nodes.statement: Let $\psi : \{-1,1\}^N \to \{-1,1\}$ be the function constructed in \Cref{prop:or-dual} with $\delta:=1/20$. Let $\Phi : \{-1,1\}^R \to \{-1,1\}$ be the function constructed in \Cref{prop:and-or}, and define $\xi = \Phi \star \psi$. Then by \Cref{prop:ls}, $\xi$ satisfies the following properties: \begin{align}& \langle \xi, \mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N \rangle > 2/3, \\ & \| \xi \|_1 = 1, \\ & \text{ For every polynomial } p \text{ of degree less than } D, \text{ we have }\langle \xi, p \rangle = 0. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: xi = Phi * psi has correlation > 2/3 and pure high degree D-hat by Proposition 28.
nodes.section: 4.3 Step 3: Constructing the Final Dual Witness

nodes.name: Zero out high-weight mass
nodes.statement: Recall that $\psi$ was obtained by symmetrizing the function $\omega$ constructed in \Cref{prop:or-sym-dual}. \Cref{prop:btzeroing} guarantees that for some $\Delta \ge \beta \sqrt{\alpha} R / 4\ln^2 R = \tilde{\Omega}(R^{3/4})$, the function $\xi$ can be modified to produce a function $\zeta : (\{-1,1\}^N)^R \to \mathbb{R}$ such that \begin{align*} &\zeta(x) = 0 \text{ for all } x \not\in H_{\le N}^{N \cdot R}, \\ &\langle \zeta, \mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N \rangle \ge \langle \xi, \mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N \rangle - \|\zeta - \xi\|_1 \ge 2/3 - 2/9 > 1/3, \\ &\|\zeta\|_1 = 1, \\ & \text{ For every polynomial } p \text{ of degree less than } \min\{\hat{D}, \Delta\}, \text{ we have }\langle \zeta, p \rangle = 0. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Proposition (prop:btzeroing) yields zeta supported on H_{<=N}.
nodes.section: 4.3 Step 3: Constructing the Final Dual Witness

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Observing that \[D = \min\{\hat{D}, \Delta\} = \tilde{\Omega}(R^{3/4})\] shows that the function $\zeta$ satisfies the conditions necessary to prove \Cref{prop:surj-dual}.
nodes.statement_short: D = min(D-hat, Delta) = Omega~(R^{3/4}).
nodes.section: 4.3 Step 3: Constructing the Final Dual Witness

nodes.name: Theorem 44 from the dual witness
nodes.statement: \Cref{thm:main-amp} follows by combining \Cref{prop:surj-dual} with the dual characterization of unbounded approximate degree given in \Cref{prop:ub-duality}.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 48 plus Proposition 13.
nodes.section: 4.3 Step 3: Constructing the Final Dual Witness

nodes.name: Theorem 43 via reductions
nodes.statement: By \Cref{cor:surj-reduction}, we conclude that $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}(\mathsf{dSURJ}_{N, R})=\tilde{\Omega}(R^{3/4})$. \Cref{thm:surj} follows by \Cref{prop:dumsurj-reduction}.
nodes.statement_short: Corollary 24 then Proposition 18.
nodes.section: 4.3 Step 3: Constructing the Final Dual Witness

nodes.name: Case k = 1
nodes.statement: If $k = 1$, then the function defined by $\omega(0) = \frac{1}{2}$ and $\omega(1) = -\frac{1}{2}$ satisfies the conditions of the proposition for $c_1 = c_2 = 1$. In what follows, we treat the complementary case where $k \ge 2$.
nodes.statement_short: Two-point omega works; assume k >= 2.

nodes.name: Normalized goals
nodes.statement: Let $E_+ := \{t \colon \omega(t) > 0, t \ge k\}$, and $E_{-} := \{t\colon \omega(t) < 0, t < k\}$. By normalizing, it suffices to construct a function $\omega : [T]_0 \to \mathbb{R}$ such that \begin{align} & \sum_{t \in E_+} |\omega(t)| \le \frac{1}{48 N} \cdot \|\omega\|_1 \\ & \sum_{t \in E_-} |\omega(t)| \le \left(\frac{1}{2} - \frac{2}{4^k}\right) \cdot \|\omega\|_1 \\ & \text{For all univariate polynomials } q \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\text{, } \nonumber \\ &\deg p < c_1\sqrt{k^{-1} \cdot T \cdot N^{-1/k}} \implies \sum_{t=0}^k \omega(t) \cdot q(t) = 0 \\ & |\omega(t)| \le \frac{(2k)^k \exp(-c_2 t / \sqrt{k \cdot T \cdot N^{1/k}})\|\omega\|_1}{t^2} \qquad \forall t = 1, 2, \dots, T. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to ratio versions of the properties.

nodes.name: Define S and omega
nodes.statement: Let $c = 2k\lceil N^{1/k}\rceil$, and let $m = \lfloor \sqrt{T/c} \rfloor$. Define the set \[S = \{1, 2, \dots, k\} \cup \{ci^2 : 0 \le i \le m\}.\] Note that $|S| = \Omega(k^{-1/2}T^{1/2}N^{-1/(2k)})$. Define the polynomial \[\omega(t) = \frac{(-1)^{t+(T-m)+1}}{T!} \binom{T}{t} \prod_{r \in [T]_0 \setminus S} (t - r).\] The signs are chosen so that $\omega(k) < 0$.
nodes.statement_short: S = {1..k} together with {ci^2}; sign chosen so omega(k) < 0.

nodes.name: Pure high degree
nodes.statement: It is immediate from \Cref{fact:combinatorial} that $\omega$ satisfies~\eqref{eqn:thr-sym-phd-ref} for $c_1 = 1/\sqrt{2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Fact 46 gives the pure high degree.

nodes.name: Decay for t <= k
nodes.statement: We now show that~\eqref{eqn:thr-sym-decay-ref} holds. For $t = 1, \dots, k$, we have \[\frac{(2k)^k \exp(-c_2 t / \sqrt{k \cdot T \cdot N^{1/k}})}{t^2} \ge \frac{(2k)^k \exp(-c_2 \sqrt{k})}{k^2} \ge 1\] as long as $c_2 \le 1/2$ and $k \ge 2$. Since $|\omega(t)| \le \|\omega\|_1$, the bound holds for $t = 1, \dots, k$.
nodes.statement_short: Trivial for t <= k.

nodes.name: Head and tail bounds
nodes.statement: For $t = cj^2$ with $j \ge 1$, we expand out the binomial coefficient in the definition of $\omega$ to obtain \[|\omega(t)| = \begin{cases} \prod\limits_{r \in S\setminus \{t\}} \frac{1}{|t - r|} & \text{ for } t \in S, \\ 0 & \text{ otherwise.} \end{cases}\] For $t \in \{0, 1, \dots, k\}$, we observe that \begin{equation} \frac{|\omega(t)|}{|\omega(k)|} = \frac{k! \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^m (c i^2 - k)}{t! \cdot (k - t)! \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^m (c i^2 - t)} \le \binom{k}{t}. \end{equation} Meanwhile, for $t = cj^2$ with $j \ge 1$, we get \begin{align*} \frac{|\omega(t)|}{|\omega(k)|} &= \frac{k! \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^m (ci^2 - k)}{\prod_{i = 1}^k(cj^2 - i) \cdot \prod_{i \in [m]_0 \setminus \{j\}} |ci^2 - cj^2|} \\ &\le \frac{k! \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^m ci^2}{(cj^2 - k)^{k} \cdot \prod_{i \in [m]_0 \setminus \{j\}} c(i+j)|i-j|} \\ &= \frac{k!}{j(cj^2 - k)^{k}} \cdot \frac{(m!)^2}{(m+j)!(m-j)!}. \end{align*} The first factor is bounded above by \[\frac{k!}{(c - k)^k j^{2k+1}}.\] As long as $c \ge 2k$ and $k \ge 2$, this expression is at most \[\frac{k^k}{(c/2)^kj^4} = \frac{(2k)^k}{c^k \cdot j^4}.\] We control the second factor by \begin{align*} \frac{(m!)^2}{(m+j)!(m-j)!} &= \frac{m}{m+j} \cdot \frac{m-1}{m+j-1} \cdot \ldots \cdot \frac{m-j+1}{m+1} \\ &\le \left(\frac{m}{m+j} \right)^j \\ &\le \left(1 - \frac{j}{2m} \right)^j \\ &\le e^{-j^2/2m}, \end{align*} where the last inequality uses the fact that $1 - x \le e^{-x}$ for all $x$. Hence, \begin{equation} \frac{|\omega(cj^2)|}{|\omega(k)|} \le \frac{(2k)^k}{c^k \cdot j^4} \cdot e^{-j^2/2m}. \end{equation} This immediately yields \[\frac{|\omega(cj^2)|}{\|\omega\|_1} \le \frac{|\omega(cj^2)|}{|\omega(k)|} \le \frac{(2k)^k}{(cj^2)^2} \cdot e^{-cj^2/(2cm)},\] which establishes~\eqref{eqn:thr-sym-decay-ref} for all $t = cj^2 > k$.
nodes.statement_short: Ratios to |omega(k)| bounded by binom(k,t) and (2k)^k/(c^k j^4) e^{-j^2/2m}.

nodes.name: False-positive mass
nodes.statement: Moreover, by \eqref{eqn:tail-bound} \begin{equation} \sum_{t > k} |\omega(t)| \le |\omega(k)| \cdot \sum_{j = 1}^m \frac{(2k)^k}{c^k \cdot j^4} \cdot e^{-j^2/2m} \le \frac{(2k)^k}{c^k} \cdot |\omega(k)| \cdot \sum_{j=1}^m \frac{1}{j^4} \le \frac{|\omega(k)|}{48 N}. \end{equation} Hence, since $\omega(k) < 0$, \[\sum_{t \in E_+} |\omega(t)| \le \sum_{t > k} |\omega(t)| \le \frac{|\omega(k)|}{48 N} \le \frac{\|\omega\|_1}{48N},\] which gives~\eqref{eqn:thr-sym-pos-corr-ref}.
nodes.statement_short: Tail mass beyond k is at most |omega(k)|/(48N).

nodes.name: False-negative mass
nodes.statement: Finally, to establish~\eqref{eqn:thr-sym-neg-corr-ref}, we combine ~\eqref{eqn:head-bound} and~\eqref{eqn:tail-sum} to obtain \begin{equation} \frac{\|\omega\|_1}{|\omega(k)|} \le \sum_{t = 0}^k \binom{k}{t} + \frac{1}{48 N} < 2^k + 1 < \frac{1}{2} \cdot 4^k. \end{equation} We calculate \begin{align*} \frac{\|\omega\|_1}{2} - \sum_{t \in E_-} |\omega(t)| &= \sum_{t : \omega(t) < 0} (-\omega(t)) - \sum_{t \in E_-} (-\omega(t)) & \text{since $\langle \omega, \mathbf{1} \rangle = 0$}\\ &= \sum_{t \colon \omega(t) < 0, t \geq k} (-\omega(t)) \\ &\ge -\omega(k). \end{align*} Rearranging and applying the bound~\eqref{eqn:mass-on-k}, \[\sum_{t \in E_{-}} |\omega(t)| \le \left(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{\omega(k)}{\|\omega\|_1}\right) \cdot \|\omega\|_1 \le \left(\frac{1}{2} - 2 \cdot 4^{-k}\right) \cdot \|\omega\|_1.\]
nodes.statement_short: Balance and mass on k bound the false negatives by (1/2 - 2/4^k).

nodes.name: Define phi
nodes.statement: Let $\varphi: \{-1, 1\}^M \rightarrow \{-1, 1\}$ be defined such that $\varphi(\mathbf{1})=1/2$, $\varphi(-\mathbf{1})=-1/2$, and $\varphi(x)=0$ for all other $x$. Notice that \begin{equation} \sum_{(x_1, \dots, x_{M}) \in \{-1, 1\}^M} \varphi(x_1, \dots, x_{M}) = 0 \end{equation} so $\Psi$ has pure high degree $1$, and that $\|\Psi\|_1 = 1$.
nodes.statement_short: phi = 1/2 at all-ones, -1/2 at all-minus-ones.

nodes.name: False positives as an expectation
nodes.statement: We now prove that (\Cref{eqn:error-amp-pos}) holds. Let $\lambda$ be the distribution on $\{-1, 1\}^{m}$ given by $\lambda(x) = |\psi(x)|$, and let $\lambda^{\otimes M}$ be the product distribution on $(\{-1, 1\}^m)^M$ given by $\lambda^{\otimes M}(x_1, \dots, x_M) = \prod_{i=1}^M |\psi(x_i)|$. Since $\psi$ is orthogonal to the constant polynomial, it has expected value 0, and hence the string $(\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots)$ is distributed uniformly in $\{-1, 1\}^{M}$ when one samples $(x_1, \dots, x_{M})$ according to $\lambda^{\otimes M}$. This allows us to write \begin{align} &\hspace{-2em}\sum_{(x_1, \dots, x_{M}) \in E^+(\varphi \star \psi, \mathsf{ OR}_M \circ f)} |(\varphi \star \psi)(x_1, \dots, x_M)| \nonumber \\ &\hspace{-2em}= 2^{M} \mathbf{E}_{\lambda^{\otimes M}} [\varphi( \dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) \cdot \mathbb{I} (\varphi( \dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) > 0 \land \mathsf{ OR}_M\left( \dots, f(x_i), \dots\right) = -1)] \nonumber\\ &\hspace{-2em}= \sum_{z : \varphi(z) > 0} \varphi(z) \cdot \Pr_{\lambda^{\otimes M}} [\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, f(x_i), \dots) = -1 | (\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) = z]. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite under the product distribution |psi|^{otimes M}.

nodes.name: Coupling with random flips
nodes.statement: Observe that for any bit $b$, \[\Pr_{x \sim \lambda} [f(x) \ne \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x)) | \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x)) = b] = 2\sum_{x \in A_b} |\psi(x)|,\] where for brevity, we have written $A_{+1} = E_+(\psi, f)$ and $A_{-1} = E_-(\psi, f)$. Therefore, as noted in \cite{sherstovhalfspaces1}, for any given $z \in \{-1, 1\}^{M}$, the following two random variables are identically distributed:
nodes.statement_short: Conditioned on signs, f-values are independent flips.

nodes.name: First random variable
nodes.statement: The string $(\dots, f(x_i), \dots)$, when one chooses $(\dots, x_i, \dots)$ from $\lambda^{\otimes M}$ conditioned on \newline $(\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) = z$
nodes.statement_short: f-values conditioned on the sign pattern.

nodes.name: Second random variable
nodes.statement: The string $(\dots, y_iz_i, \dots)$, where $y \in \{-1, 1\}^{M}$ is a random string whose $i$th bit independently takes on value $-1$ with probability $2 \sum_{x \in A_{z_i}} |\psi(x)|$.
nodes.statement_short: Independent flips of z.

nodes.name: Only z = 1 contributes
nodes.statement: Thus, Expression~\eqref{eqn:error-amp-middle} equals \begin{equation}\sum_{z : \varphi(z) > 0} \varphi(z) \cdot \Pr_y[\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, y_iz_i, \dots) = -1], \end{equation} where $y \in \{-1, 1\}^{M}$ is a random string whose $i$th bit independently takes on value $-1$ with probability $2 \sum_{x \in A_{z_i}} |\psi(x)|$. The only term in this sum corresponds to $z=\mathbf{1}$, which we now argue is at most $M \delta^+$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the z = 1 term.

nodes.name: Union bound
nodes.statement: By \eqref{eqn:error-base-pos}, each $y_i = -1$ with probability $2 \sum_{x \in A_{1}} |\psi(x)| = 2\sum_{x \in E^+(\psi, f)} |\psi(x)| \le 2\delta^+$. Hence, for $z = \mathbf{1}$, we have \[\Pr_y[\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, y_i, \dots) = -1] \le 2 M \delta^+\] by a union bound. Thus Expression~\eqref{eqn:error-amp-middle2} is at most $M \delta^+$, proving \eqref{eqn:error-amp-pos}.
nodes.statement_short: False-positive mass at most M delta^+.

nodes.name: False negatives
nodes.statement: It now remains to prove the bound~\eqref{eqn:error-amp-neg}. By an identical argument as above, we have \begin{equation}\sum_{(x_1, \dots, x_{M}) \in E^-(\varphi \star \psi, \mathsf{ OR}_M \circ f)} |(\varphi \star \psi)(x_1, \dots, x_M)| = \sum_{z : \varphi(z) < 0} \varphi(z) \cdot \Pr_y[\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, y_iz_i, \dots) = 1]. \end{equation} The only term in the sum corresponds to $z=-\mathbf{1}$, which we argue takes value $\frac{1}{2} \cdot (2\delta^-)^{M}$. Here, each $y_i=-1$ independently with probability $\sum_{x \in A_{-1}} |\psi(x)| = 2\sum_{x \in E^-(\psi, f)} |\psi(x)| \le 2\delta^-$, and $\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, -y_i, \dots)=1$ only if $y_i = -1$ for every $i$. Hence, we conclude that \[\Pr_y[\mathsf{ OR}_{M}\left(\dots, -y_i, \dots\right) = 1] \le (2\delta^-)^M. \]
nodes.statement_short: All M flips needed: probability <= (2 delta^-)^M.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: It follows that Expression~\eqref{eqn:error-amp-end} is at most $\frac{1}{2} \cdot (2\delta^-)^M$, establishing~\eqref{eqn:error-amp-pos}. This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: False-negative mass at most (2 delta^-)^M / 2.

nodes.name: Dual witness rho for OR_M
nodes.statement: \Cref{andornor} shows that the function $\mathsf{ OR}_M$ has $(9/10)$-approximate degree $\Omega(\sqrt{M})$. Hence, \Cref{prop:duality} guarantees the existence of a function $\rho : \{-1,1\}^M \to \mathbb{R}$ with $\|\rho\|_1 = 1$ and pure high degree $\Omega(\sqrt{M})$ such that \begin{equation} \langle \rho, \mathsf{ OR}_M \rangle \ge \frac{9}{10}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 14 and Proposition 11 give rho.

nodes.name: Correlation as expectation
nodes.statement:
What remains is to establish the correlation bound~\eqref{eqn:deg-amp-corr}. Letting $\lambda$ denote the distribution $\lambda(x) = |\psi(x)|$ as in the proof of \Cref{prop:error-amp}, we may write  egin{align} & \sum_{(x_1, \dots, x_{M}) \in (\{-1,1\}^m)^M} (\varphi \star \psi) (x_1, \dots, x_M) \cdot \mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, f(x_i), \dots) 
onumber \ &\qquad= 2^{M} \mathbf{E}_{\lambda^{\otimes M}} [\varphi( \dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) \cdot \mathsf{ OR}_M\left( \dots, f(x_i), \dotsight)] 
onumber\ &\qquad= \sum_{z \in \{-1,1\}^M} \varphi(z) \cdot \mathbf{E}_{\lambda^{\otimes M}} [\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, f(x_i), \dots) | (\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) = z] 
onumber\ &\qquad = \sum_{z \in \{-1,1\}^M} \varphi(z) \cdot \mathbf{E}_{y} [\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, y_i z_i, \dots)], \end{align} where $y \in \{-1,1\}^M$ is a random string whose $i$th bit independently takes the value $-1$ with probability $2 \sum_{x \in A_{z_i}} |\psi(x)|$. (Here, we are using the abbreviated notation $A_{+1} = E_+(\psi, f)$ and $A_{-1} = E_-(\psi, f)$.)
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite via sign patterns and random flips.

nodes.name: Term z = 1
nodes.statement: We first consider the contribution of the term corresponding to $z = \mathbf{1}$ to the sum. Here, by a union bound, \begin{align*} \mathbf{E}_{y} [\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, y_i z_i, \dots)] &= 1 - 2 \Pr_y[\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, y_i, \dots) = -1] \\ &\ge 1 - 2 M \cdot \left(2 \sum_{x \in A_{+1}} |\psi(x)|\right) \\ &\ge 1 - 4 M\delta^+. \end{align*} Hence, the term $z = \mathbf{1}$ contributes $\varphi(\mathbf{1}) \cdot (1 - 4 M \delta^+)$ to the sum.
nodes.statement_short: Union bound: at least 1 - 4M delta^+.

nodes.name: Terms z != 1
nodes.statement: Now we consider the contribution of any term corresponding to $z \ne \mathbf{1}$. Given such a $z$, let $i^*$ be an index such that $z_{i^*} = -1$. Then we have \begin{align*} -\mathbf{E}_{y} [\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, y_i z_i, \dots)] &= 1 - 2 \Pr_y[\mathsf{ OR}_M(\dots, y_i z_i, \dots) = 1] \\ &\ge 1 - 2 \cdot \Pr_{y_{i^*}}[y_{i^*} = -1] \\ &= 1 - 2 \cdot \left(2 \sum_{x \in A_{-1}} |\psi(x)|\right) \\ &\ge 1 - 4 \delta^-. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: One -1 coordinate: at least 1 - 4 delta^-.

nodes.name: Combine
nodes.statement: We can now lower bound~\eqref{eqn:deg-amp-middle} by \begin{align*}\hspace{-1.1em} \varphi(\mathbf{1}) \cdot (1 - 4 M \delta^+) - \sum_{z \ne \mathbf{1}} \varphi(z) (1 - 4\delta^-) &\ge \sum_{z \in \{-1,1\}^M} \varphi(z) \mathsf{ OR}_M(z) - 4M\delta^+ |\varphi(\mathbf{1})| - 4\delta^- \sum_{z \ne 1} |\varphi(z)| \\ &\ge \frac{9}{10} - 4M\delta^+ - 4\delta^-.\qedhere \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Correlation >= 9/10 - 4M delta^+ - 4 delta^-.

nodes.name: Error amplification
nodes.statement: Using the construction of \Cref{prop:error-amp} with $m = N$, $M = 4^k$, and $f = \mathsf{THR}_N^k$, we first obtain a function $\varphi : \{-1,1\}^{4^k} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $\|\varphi\|_1 = 1$ and pure high degree $1$ such that \begin{align*} &\sum_{x \in E_+(\varphi \star \psi, \mathsf{ OR}_{4^k} \circ \mathsf{THR}^k_N)} |(\varphi \star \psi)(x)| \le \frac{4^k}{48 N} \\ &\sum_{x \in E_-(\varphi \star \psi, \mathsf{ OR}_{4^k} \circ \mathsf{THR}^k_N)} |(\varphi \star \psi)(x)| \le \frac{1}{2} \cdot \left(1 - 4 \cdot 4^{-k} \right)^{4^k} \le \frac{e^{-4}}{2}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: M = 4^k reduces false negatives to e^{-4}/2.
nodes.section: 5.2.2 Constructing a Dual Witness for $\mathsf{ OR}_R \circ \mathsf{THR}^k_N$

nodes.name: Degree amplification
nodes.statement: Now by the construction of \Cref{prop:degree-amp} with $m = 4^k \cdot N$, $M = R/4^{k}$ and $f = \mathsf{ OR}_{4^k} \circ \mathsf{THR}_N^k$, there exists a function $\rho : \{-1,1\}^{R / 4^k} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $\|\rho\|_1 = 1$ and pure high degree $\Omega(2^{-k}\sqrt{R})$ such that \[ \langle \rho \star (\varphi \star \psi), \mathsf{ OR}_{R/4^k} \circ (\mathsf{ OR}_{4^k} \circ \mathsf{THR}^k_N) \rangle \ge \frac{9}{10} - \frac{4R}{48 N} - 2e^{-4} \ge \frac{2}{3}.\]
nodes.statement_short: M = R/4^k gives pure high degree Omega(2^{-k} sqrt R) and correlation >= 2/3.
nodes.section: 5.2.2 Constructing a Dual Witness for $\mathsf{ OR}_R \circ \mathsf{THR}^k_N$

nodes.name: Phi = rho * phi
nodes.statement: Let $\Phi : \{-1,1\}^R \to \mathbb{R}$ be the dual block composition $\rho \star \varphi$. Since the dual block composition preserves $\ell_1$-norms (\Cref{prop:ls}, Condition~\eqref{eqn:ls-norm}) and multiplies pure high degrees (\Cref{prop:ls}, Condition~\eqref{eqn:ls-phd}), the function $\Phi$ itself has $\ell_1$-norm $1$ and pure high degree $\Omega(2^{-k} \sqrt{R})$.
nodes.statement_short: Norm and degree from Proposition 28.
nodes.section: 5.2.2 Constructing a Dual Witness for $\mathsf{ OR}_R \circ \mathsf{THR}^k_N$

nodes.name: Associativity
nodes.statement: The claim now follows from the associativity of dual block composition (\Cref{prop:ls}, Condition~\eqref{eqn:ls-assoc}) and the fact that $\mathsf{ OR}_R = \mathsf{ OR}_{R/4^k} \circ \mathsf{ OR}_{4^k}$.
nodes.statement_short: OR_R = OR_{R/4^k} o OR_{4^k}.
nodes.section: 5.2.2 Constructing a Dual Witness for $\mathsf{ OR}_R \circ \mathsf{THR}^k_N$

nodes.name: Parameter choices
nodes.statement: We start by fixing choices of several key parameters:
nodes.statement_short: Fix the parameters.

nodes.name: d, T, alpha, N
nodes.statement: $d= \Theta(2^{-k}\sqrt{R})$ is the pure high degree of the dual witness $\Phi$ for $\mathsf{ OR}_R$ in \Cref{prop:dist-prelim}, \item $T = \lfloor (8k)^{k/2} \sqrt{R}\rfloor$, \item $\alpha = (2k)^k$, \item $N = \lceil 20 \sqrt{\alpha} \rceil R = \Theta((2k)^{k/2} R)$,
nodes.statement_short: Degree of the OR dual and sizes.

nodes.name: D-hat
nodes.statement: $\hat{D} = c_1 \sqrt{k^{-1} \cdot T \cdot N^{-1/k}} \cdot d =\Theta(2^{-k/4} k^{(k-3)/4} \cdot R^{3/4 - 1/(2k)})$, where $c_1$ is the constant from \Cref{prop:thr-sym-dual},
nodes.statement_short: Target degree.

nodes.name: beta
nodes.statement: $\beta = c_2 / \sqrt{k \cdot T \cdot N^{1/k}} = \Theta(2^{-3k/4} k^{(-k-3)/4} \cdot R^{-1/4 - 1/(2k)})$, where $c_2$ is the constant from \Cref{prop:thr-sym-dual}.
nodes.statement_short: Decay rate.

nodes.name: Compose the duals
nodes.statement: Let $\psi : \{-1,1\}^N \to \{-1,1\}$ be the function constructed in \Cref{prop:thr-dual}. Let $\Phi : \{-1,1\}^R \to \{-1,1\}$ be the function constructed in \Cref{prop:dist-prelim}, and define $\xi = \Phi \star \psi$. Then by \Cref{prop:ls}, $\xi$ satisfies the following properties: \begin{align}& \langle \xi, \mathsf{ OR}_R \circ \mathsf{THR}_N^k \rangle > 2/3, \\ & \| \xi \|_1 = 1, \\ & \text{ For every polynomial } p \text{ of degree less than } \hat{D}, \text{ we have }\langle \xi, p \rangle = 0. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: xi = Phi * psi with Proposition 28.

nodes.name: Zero out high-weight mass
nodes.statement: Recall that $\psi$ was obtained by symmetrizing the function $\omega$ constructed in \Cref{prop:thr-sym-dual}. \Cref{prop:btzeroing} guarantees that for some $\Delta \ge \beta \sqrt{\alpha} R / 4\ln^2 R = \tilde{\Omega}(2^{-k/4} k^{(k-3)/4} \cdot R^{3/4 - 1/(2k)})$, the function $\xi$ can be modified to produce a function $\zeta : (\{-1,1\}^N)^R \to \mathbb{R}$ such that \begin{align*} &\zeta(x) = 0 \text{ for all } x \not\in H_{\le N}^{N \cdot R}, \\ &\langle \zeta, \mathsf{ OR}_R \circ \mathsf{THR}_N^k \rangle \ge \langle \xi, \mathsf{ OR}_R \circ \mathsf{THR}_N^k \rangle - \|\zeta - \xi\|_1 \ge 2/3 - 2/9 > 1/3, \\ &\|\zeta\|_1 = 1, \\ & \text{ For every polynomial } p \text{ of degree less than } \min\{\hat{D}, \Delta\}, \text{ we have }\langle \zeta, p \rangle = 0. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Proposition (prop:btzeroing) yields zeta.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Observing that \[D = \min\{\hat{D}, \Delta\} = \tilde{\Omega}(2^{-k/4} k^{(k-3)/ 4} \cdot R^{3/4-1/(2k)})\] shows that the function $\zeta$ satisfies the conditions necessary to prove \Cref{prop:dist-dual}.
nodes.statement_short: D = min(D-hat, Delta).

nodes.name: Theorem 50 from the dual witness
nodes.statement: \Cref{thm:dist-promise} now follows by combining \Cref{prop:dist-dual} with the dual characterization of unbounded approximate degree \Cref{prop:ub-duality}.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 54 plus Proposition 13.

nodes.name: Theorem 49 via reductions and Beals et al.
nodes.statement:
The approximate degree lower bound in \Cref{thm:dist} is then a consequence of \Cref{prop:dumdist-reduction} and \Cref{cor:dist-reduction}. The quantum query lower bound follows via the standard fact
that the $\varepsilon$-error quantum query complexity of $f$ is lower bounded by $1/2 \cdot \widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_{2\varepsilon}(f)$ \cite{beals}.
nodes.statement_short: Prop. 21, Cor. 26, and the polynomial method.

nodes.name: Strategy and parameters
nodes.statement: We construct a dual polynomial to witness the lower bound in \Cref{sethm}. Define the parameters \begin{itemize} \item $\delta = \gamma/4$, \item $\alpha = 170/\delta$, \item $T=N=\lceil 20 \sqrt{\alpha} \rceil R \leq 310 \cdot \gamma^{-1/2} \cdot R$,
nodes.statement_short: Build a dual witness; set delta = gamma/4, alpha = 170/delta, T = N.

nodes.name: beta
nodes.statement: $\beta = c_2 \cdot \sqrt{\delta} / \sqrt{T}$, where $c_2$ is the constant from \Cref{prop:or-sym-dual}.
nodes.statement_short: Decay rate.

nodes.name: Define psi and Phi
nodes.statement: Let $\psi$ be the dual witness for $\mathsf{ OR}_N$ from \Cref{prop:or-dual} with $T=N$. Define $\Phi \colon \{-1,1\}^R \to \mathbb{R}$ as follows: $$\Phi(x) = \begin{cases} -1/2 & \text{ if } x=(-1, -1, \dots, -1)\\ 1/2 & \text{ if } x = (1, 1, \dots, 1)\\ 0 & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases}$$
nodes.statement_short: OR dual and two-point AND dual.

nodes.name: Relation to prior work
nodes.statement: The dual block composition $\Phi \star \psi$ is the same dual witness for $\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N$ which Bun and Thaler \cite{bt14} used to show that $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_{\varepsilon}(\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N) = \Omega(N^{1/2})$ for $\varepsilon = 1-2^{-R}$. This dual witness was also used in subsequent works \cite{sherstov14, bchtv}. Curiously, we are interested in this dual witness for a completely different reason than these prior works. These prior works were interested in $\Phi \star \psi$ because its correlation with the target function $\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N$ is exponentially closer to 1 than is the correlation of $\psi$ with $\mathsf{ OR}_N$. For our purposes, it will not be essential to exploit such a strong correlation guarantee---rather, we are interested in $\Phi \star \psi$ because most its ``$\ell_1$-mass'' lies on inputs either with full image or tiny image (i.e., most of its mass lies in the domain of $\mathsf{GapAND}_{R}^{\gamma} \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N$).
nodes.statement_short: Phi*psi is Bun-Thaler's witness; here its mass lies in the GapAND domain.

nodes.name: Properties of Phi*psi
nodes.statement: As in \Cref{cor:se-reduction}, let $G$ denote the set of all inputs on which $\mathsf{GapAND}_{R}^{\gamma} \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N$ is defined, i.e., $$G=\{x_1, \dots, x_R \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R} \colon (\mathsf{ OR}_N(x_1), \dots, \mathsf{ OR}_N(x_R)) \in H_{\leq \gamma \cdot R}^R \cup \{\mathbf{-1}\}\}.$$ The analysis in these prior works \cite{bt14,bchtv} implies that $\Phi \star \psi$ satisfies the following three properties. \begin{align} &\|\Phi \star \psi \|_1=1, \\ &\sum_{x \in G} ( \Phi \star \psi)(x) \cdot \left(\mathsf{GapAND}_{R}^{\gamma} \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N\right)(x) - \sum_{x \in\{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R} \setminus G} |(\Phi \star \psi)(x)| \geq 9/10, \\ &\text{For any polynomial } p \colon \{-1,1\}^{N\cdot R} \to \mathbb{R}\text{, } \deg p < c_1\sqrt{\delta T} \implies \langle \Phi \star \psi, p \rangle = 0, \end{align} where $c_1$ is the constant from \Cref{prop:or-dual}. Indeed, Properties~\eqref{ughnorm} and~\eqref{ughphd} are immediate from \Cref{prop:ls} on the properties of dual block composition. For completeness, we prove that Property~\eqref{ughcor} holds in \Cref{sec:gap-and-corr} below, making use of the fact that $\delta = \gamma/4$ and taking $R$ to be sufficiently large.
nodes.statement_short: Norm, correlation >= 9/10 (Lemma 62), pure high degree.

nodes.name: Zero out high weight
nodes.statement: \Cref{prop:btzeroing} (with $\alpha$ and $\beta$ set as above) guarantees that for some $\Delta \ge \beta \sqrt{\alpha} R / 4\ln^2 R = \tilde{\Omega}(R^{1/2})$, the function $\Phi \star \psi$ can be modified to produce a function $\zeta : (\{-1,1\}^N)^R \to \mathbb{R}$ such that \begin{align*} &\zeta(x) = 0 \text{ for all } x \not\in H_{\le N}^{N \cdot R}, \\ &\langle \zeta, \mathsf{GapAND}_{R}^{\gamma} \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N \rangle \ge \langle \Phi \star \psi, \mathsf{GapAND}_{R}^{\gamma} \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N \rangle - \|\zeta - \Phi \star \psi\|_1 \ge 9/10 - 2/9 > 1/3, \\ &\|\zeta\|_1 = 1, \\ & \text{ For every polynomial } p \text{ of degree less than } D:=\min\{\hat{D}, \Delta\}, \text{ we have }\langle \zeta, p \rangle = 0. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Proposition (prop:btzeroing) gives zeta.

nodes.name: Conclude via duality
nodes.statement: Observing that \[D = \min\{c_1\sqrt{\delta T}, \Delta\} = \tilde{\Omega}(R^{1/2})\] shows that the function $\zeta$ satisfies the conditions necessary to prove \Cref{sethm} via \Cref{prop:dualitydiedie}.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 59 gives dpdeg = Omega~(R^{1/2}).

nodes.name: Decompose
nodes.statement: We begin by observing that the quantity of interest can be written as \begin{align} &\sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R}} ( \Phi \star \psi)(x) \cdot \left(\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N\right)(x) - \nonumber \\ &\qquad\qquad \left( \sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R} \setminus G} ( \Phi \star \psi)(x) \cdot \left(\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N\right)(x) + \sum_{x \in\{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R} \setminus G} |(\Phi \star \psi)(x)| \right) \nonumber \\ \ge &\sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R}} ( \Phi \star \psi)(x) \cdot \left(\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N\right)(x) - 2 \sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R} \setminus G} |(\Phi \star \psi)(x)|. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Correlation with AND o OR minus twice the mass outside G.

nodes.name: First term
nodes.statement: We estimate each term of Expression~\eqref{eqn:buttz} separately, beginning with the first term. Just as in the proofs of \Cref{prop:error-amp} and \Cref{prop:degree-amp}, we have \begin{align*} \sum_{x \in \{-1,1\}^{N \cdot R}} (\Phi \star \psi)(x) \cdot (\mathsf{AND}_R \circ \mathsf{ OR}_N)(x) &= \sum_{z \in \{-1,1\}^R} \Phi(z) \cdot \mathbb{E}_y[\mathsf{AND}_R(\dots, y_i z_i, \dots)] \end{align*} where $y \in \{-1,1\}^R$ is a random string whose $i$th bit independently takes the value $-1$ with probability $2 \sum_{x \in A_{z_i}} |\psi(x)|$. For $z = -\mathbf{1}$, we have by~\eqref{eqn:mybullshitequation} that $2 \sum_{x \in A_{-1}} |\psi(x)| = 0$, so the contribution of the corresponding term to the sum is $1/2$. For $z = \mathbf{1}$, we use the fact that $2 \sum_{x \in A_{+1}} |\psi(x)| \le \delta$ to compute \begin{align*} \frac{1}{2} \cdot \mathbb{E}_{y}[\mathsf{AND}_R(\dots, y_i, \dots)] &= \frac{1}{2} \cdot \left(1 - 2\Pr_y[\mathsf{AND}_R(\dots, y_i, \dots) = -1 ] \right) \\ &\ge \frac{1}{2} \cdot \left(1 - 2\delta^R\right). \end{align*} Hence, the first summand of~\eqref{eqn:buttz} is at least $1-\delta^R$.
nodes.statement_short: One-sided error makes the z = -1 term exactly 1/2; total >= 1 - delta^R.

nodes.name: Second term as conditional probabilities
nodes.statement:
We now estimate the second summand, $2 \sum_{x 
otin G} |(\Phi \star \psi)(x)|$. As in the proofs of \Cref{prop:error-amp} and \Cref{prop:degree-amp}, we let $\lambda$ denote the distribution with probability mass function $\lambda(x) = |\psi(x)|$. Then  egin{align*}\hspace{-2.2em} 2\sum_{x 
otin G} |(\Phi \star \psi)(x)| &= 2^{R+1} \mathbb{E}_{\lambda^{\otimes R}} [|\Phi(\dots, \operatorname{sgn} \psi(x_i), \dots)| \cdot \mathbb{I}(x 
otin G)] \ &= 2\sum_{z \in \{-1,1\}^R} |\Phi(z)| \cdot \Pr_{\lambda^{\otimes R}}[x 
otin G | (\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) = z] \ &= \Pr_{\lambda^{\otimes R}}[x 
otin G | (\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) = \mathbf{-1}] + \Pr_{\lambda^{\otimes R}}[x 
otin G | (\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) = \mathbf{1}]. \end{align*} We analyze each term of this sum separately.
nodes.statement_short: Split by the two support points of Phi.

nodes.name: All-minus pattern
nodes.statement: For the first term, observe that by one-sided error of $\psi$, it follows that if $x = (x_1, \dots, x_R)$ is any input $\operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)) = -1$ for all $i$ then $\mathsf{ OR}_N(x_i) = -1$ for all $i$. Thus we are guaranteed that $x \in G$, so the contribution of the first summand is zero.
nodes.statement_short: Always in G.

nodes.name: All-plus pattern
nodes.statement: To analyze the second summand, let us denote by $r_i \in \{0, 1\}$ the indicator random variable for the event $\mathsf{ OR}_N(x_i) = -1$ when $x_i$ is drawn from the conditional distribution $(\lambda | \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)) = 1)$. Then \begin{align*} \Pr[r_i = 1] &= \Pr_{x_i \sim \lambda}[\mathsf{ OR}_N(x_i) = -1 | \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)) = 1] \\ &= 2\sum_{x \in A_{+1}} |\psi(x_i)| \\ &\le \delta \end{align*} by~\eqref{eqn:mybullshitequation}. Hence, \begin{align*} \Pr_{\lambda^{\otimes R}}[x \notin G | (\dots, \operatorname{sgn}(\psi(x_i)), \dots) = \mathbf{1}] &\le \Pr\left[ \sum_{i = 1}^R r_i > \gamma R\right] \\ &\le \exp\left(-\frac{(\gamma - \delta)R}{3}\right) \end{align*} by the multiplicative Chernoff bound.\footnote{The formulation we use here is as follows. Let $r_1, \dots, r_R$ be independent $\{0, 1\}$-valued random variables, $S = \sum_{i=1}^R r_i$, and $\mu = \mathbb{E}[S]$. Then for $\eta > 1$, we have $\Pr[S > (1+\eta) \mu] \le \exp(-\eta \mu / 3)$. In this application, we are taking $\mu \le \delta R$ and $\eta = \gamma R / \mu - 1 > 1$.} Thus, we have \[2 \sum_{x \notin G} |(\Phi \star \psi)(x)| \le \exp\left(-\frac{(\gamma - \delta)R}{3}\right).\]
nodes.statement_short: Chernoff bound gives exp(-(gamma - delta)R/3).

nodes.name: Combine
nodes.statement: Putting everything together, we see that Expression~\eqref{eqn:buttz} is at least $1 - \delta^R - \exp\left(-(\gamma - \delta) R / 3\right)$ as we wanted to show.
nodes.statement_short: Total at least 1 - delta^R - exp(-(gamma - delta)R/3).

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: Fix $R >0$, let $c$ be the constant from \Cref{sethm}, $\gamma<(2/3c)^2$ be a sufficiently small constant, and $N= c \cdot \gamma^{-1/2} \cdot R$. As inputs in $\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}$ are interpreted as elements of $[R]_0^N$, we can equivalently interpret them as elements of $[R+1]^N$, i.e., as inputs to $\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R+1}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}$, for any desired $0 < \gamma_1 < \gamma_2 < 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Interpret IST inputs as SDU inputs over [R+1].

nodes.name: Choose gamma_1, gamma_2
nodes.statement: Set $\gamma_1 = 1-3\gamma/2$ and $\gamma_2=1-\gamma^{1/2}/c$. Observe that since $\gamma < (2/3c)^2$, $\gamma_1$ is strictly greater than $\gamma_2$.
nodes.statement_short: gamma_1 > gamma_2 since gamma < (2/3c)^2.

nodes.name: Claim: IST preimages embed into SDU preimages
nodes.statement: We claim that \begin{align*} &\left(\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}\right)^{-1}(-1) \subseteq \left(\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R+1}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}\right)^{-1}(-1), \text{ and} \\ &\left(\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}\right)^{-1}(+1) \subseteq \left(\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R+1}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}\right)^{-1}(+1). \end{align*} Indeed, since inputs in $\left(\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}\right)^{-1}(-1)$ define a probability distribution over $[R+1]$ with support size at least $R$, with all probabilities being integer multiples of $1/N=\gamma^{1/2}/(cR)$, the statistical distance between any such distribution and the uniform distribution is at most $1-R/N = 1-\gamma^{1/2}/c$. This follows from the following calculation. Amongst probability distributions $(p_1, \dots, p_{R+1})$ over $[R+1]$ with support size at least $R$ and all probabilities $p_i$ being integer multiples of $1/N$, it is not hard to see that one maximizes the statistical distance from the uniform distribution over $[R+1]$ by setting $p_1=1-\frac{R-1}{N}$, $p_2=p_3 = \dots = p_{R}=1/N$, and $p_{R+1}=0$. The statistical distance from uniform is: \begin{align*} \frac{1}{2} \left( \left(1-\frac{R-1}{N}-\frac{1}{R+1}\right) + \left(R-1\right)\left(\frac{1}{R+1} - \frac1N\right) + \frac{1}{R+1} \right)\\ = 1-\frac{R}{N} + \frac1N - \frac{1}{R+1} \leq 1-\frac{R}{N}, \end{align*} where we have assumed that $N \geq R+1$, which is true for sufficiently small choice of $\gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: IST^{-1}(-1) within SDU^{-1}(-1) and IST^{-1}(+1) within SDU^{-1}(+1).

nodes.name: Full image is close to uniform
nodes.statement: Indeed, since inputs in $\left(\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}\right)^{-1}(-1)$ define a probability distribution over $[R+1]$ with support size at least $R$, with all probabilities being integer multiples of $1/N=\gamma^{1/2}/(cR)$, the statistical distance between any such distribution and the uniform distribution is at most $1-R/N = 1-\gamma^{1/2}/c$.
nodes.statement_short: Distance at most 1 - R/N.

nodes.name: Extremal distribution
nodes.statement: This follows from the following calculation. Amongst probability distributions $(p_1, \dots, p_{R+1})$ over $[R+1]$ with support size at least $R$ and all probabilities $p_i$ being integer multiples of $1/N$, it is not hard to see that one maximizes the statistical distance from the uniform distribution over $[R+1]$ by setting $p_1=1-\frac{R-1}{N}$, $p_2=p_3 = \dots = p_{R}=1/N$, and $p_{R+1}=0$. The statistical distance from uniform is: \begin{align*} \frac{1}{2} \left( \left(1-\frac{R-1}{N}-\frac{1}{R+1}\right) + \left(R-1\right)\left(\frac{1}{R+1} - \frac1N\right) + \frac{1}{R+1} \right)\\ = 1-\frac{R}{N} + \frac1N - \frac{1}{R+1} \leq 1-\frac{R}{N}, \end{align*} where we have assumed that $N \geq R+1$, which is true for sufficiently small choice of $\gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute the maximal distance explicitly.

nodes.name: Small image is far from uniform
nodes.statement: Similarly, since inputs in $\left(\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}\right)^{-1}(1)$ define a probability distribution over $[R+1]$ with support size at most $\gamma \cdot R +1$, the statistical distance between any such distribution and the uniform distribution is at least $1-3\gamma/2$. To see this, let $p=(p_1, \dots, p_{R+1})$ be any distribution of support size at most $\gamma \cdot R$, and let $S = \{i \colon p_i=0\}$ and $\bar{S}$ be the complement of $S$. Then the statistical distance of $p$ from uniform is at least \begin{align*} \frac{1}{2} \left(\sum_{i \in S} \left(p_i - \frac{1}{R+1} \right) \right) + \frac{1}{2} \left(\sum_{i \in \bar{S}} \left( p_i - \frac{1}{R+1} \right) \right) = \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{|S|}{R+1} + \left(\sum_{i \in \bar{S}} p_i\right) - \frac{|\bar{S}|}{R+1}\right)\\ = \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{|S|}{R+1} + 1 - \frac{|\bar{S}|}{R+1}\right) \geq \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{(1-\gamma) R}{R+1} + 1 - \frac{\gamma R + 1}{R+1}\right) = \frac{1}{2} \left(1 + \frac{R-2\gamma R - 1}{R+1}\right)\\ = 1 - \frac{\gamma R + 1}{R+1} = 1 - \gamma - \frac{\gamma + 1}{R+1} \geq 1-3\gamma/2. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Distance at least 1 - 3gamma/2.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: It is an easy consequence of the above that any $\varepsilon$-approximating polynomial of degree $d$ for $\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R+1}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}$ implies an approximation to $\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}$ of the same degree (i.e., that $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_{\varepsilon}(\mathsf{ IST}_{N, R}^{\gamma}) \leq d$). \Cref{sduthm} then follows from \Cref{sethm}.
nodes.statement_short: An SDU approximant approximates IST; apply Theorem 56.

nodes.name: Vadhan's reduction
nodes.statement: Vadhan \cite[Claim 4.4.2 and Remark 4.4.3]{vadhan} showed that as long as $H( (1+\gamma_1)/2) < 1-\gamma_2 - \lambda$, then $\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}$ is reducible to $\mathsf{GapCmprEnt}^{\alpha, \beta}_{4N, 2R}$ for some constants $\alpha, \beta$ such that $\alpha-\beta=\lambda$. This reduction (described next for completeness) implies that $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_{\varepsilon}(\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}) \leq \widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}_{\varepsilon}(\mathsf{GapCmprEnt}^{\alpha, \beta}_{4N, 2R})$.
nodes.statement_short: Cite the SDU-to-GapCmprEnt reduction and its degree consequence.
nodes.section: 6.4 Lower Bound for Entropy Comparison and Approximation

nodes.name: The transformation
nodes.statement: For completeness, we sketch this transformation, closely following the presentation of Goldreich and Vadhan \cite{goldreichvadhansurvey}. At a high level, the reduction transforms an input in $[R]^N$ to $\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}$ (interpreted as a distribution $p$ over $[R]$) into two distributions $p_1, p_2$ over $[R] \times \{0, 1\}$ as follows. Both $p_1$ and $p_2$ start by sampling an $s \in \{0, 1\}$ at random. If $s=0$, then a random sample $r$ is chosen from $p$, and if $s=1$, then $r$ is set to a uniform random sample from $[R]$. Distribution $p_2$ outputs $(r, s)$, while $p_1$ outputs $(r, b)$ for a random $b \in \{0, 1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Build p_1, p_2 over [R] x {0,1} from p.
nodes.section: 6.4 Lower Bound for Entropy Comparison and Approximation

nodes.name: Entropy gap
nodes.statement: The entropy of $p_1$ is always $v + 1$, where $v=\frac{1}{2} H(p) + \frac{1}{2} \log_2(R)$. As for the entropy of $p_2$, if $p$ is far from the uniform distribution, then the selection bit $s$ will be essentially determined by the sample $r$. Hence, the entropy of $p_2$ will be approximately $v$, which is noticeably smaller than the entropy of $p_1$. On the other hand, if the two input distributions are close then (even conditioned on the sample selected) the selection bit $s$ will be almost random and so $H(p_2) \approx v+1$, which is approximately the same as $H(p_1)$. Quantitatively, Vadhan \cite{vadhan} shows that if the statistical distance between $p$ and the uniform distribution is $\delta$, then $1-\delta \leq H(p_1) - H(p_2) \leq H( (1+\delta)/2)$.
nodes.statement_short: H(p_1) - H(p_2) is between 1 - delta and H((1+delta)/2).
nodes.section: 6.4 Lower Bound for Entropy Comparison and Approximation

nodes.name: Vector form
nodes.statement: Since we are considering distributions specified as vectors in $[R]^N$, this transformation can be equivalently described as follows. Assume for simplicity that $R$ divides $N$. If $p$ is specified by a vector $u$ in $[R]^N$, then $p_2$ is specified by a vector $w$ in $([R]\times\{0,1\})^{4N}$ defined as follows. For all $i \in [N]$ and $j \in \{0, 1\}$, $w_{i, j}=(u_i, 0)$, and for $j \in \{2, 3\}$, $w_{i, j}=(\lceil Ri/N\rceil, 1)$. Similarly, $p_1$ is specified by a vector $v$ in $([R]\times\{0,1\})^{4N}$. For $i \in [R]$ and $j \in \{0, 1\}$, $v_{i, j}=(u_i, j)$, and for $j \in \{2, 3\}$, $v_{i, j} = (\lceil Ri/N\rceil, j-2)$. Observe that when representing $u$, $v$, and $w$ as vectors in $\{-1,1\}^{N \log_2(R)}$ or $\{-1,1\}^{4N \cdot \log_2(R)}$, each bit of $v$ and $w$ depends on at most one bit of $u$.
nodes.statement_short: Each output bit depends on at most one input bit.
nodes.section: 6.4 Lower Bound for Entropy Comparison and Approximation

nodes.name: Check Vadhan's hypothesis
nodes.statement: Recall that in the statement of \Cref{sduthm}, $\gamma_1 = 1-3\gamma/2$ and $\gamma_2=1-\gamma^{1/2}/c$, where $\gamma$ is an arbitrary constant less than $(2/3c)^2$, where $c>1$ is the constant from \Cref{sethm}. Clearly, $H( (1+\gamma_1)/2)) = H(1-3 \gamma/4) = H(3 \gamma/4)$. Using the fact that for any $p \in [0, 1/2]$, \begin{align*} H(p) &= -p \log_2(p) - (1-p) \log_2(1-p) \\ &\le -2p\log_2(p) \\ &\le 6p^{3/4}, \end{align*} it follows that for some constant $\gamma \le 1/648c^4$, we have $H(3 \gamma/4) < \gamma^{1/2}/c$.
nodes.statement_short: H(3gamma/4) < gamma^{1/2}/c for small gamma.
nodes.section: 6.4 Lower Bound for Entropy Comparison and Approximation

nodes.name: Apply the reduction
nodes.statement: Hence, Vadhan's reduction from $\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}$ to $\mathsf{GapCmprEnt}^{\alpha, \beta}_{4N, 2R}$ applies to this setting of $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$, and this shows that any degree $d$ $\varepsilon$-approximating polynomial for $\mathsf{GapCmprEnt}^{\alpha, \beta}_{4N, 2R}$ implies a degree $d$ polynomial $\varepsilon$-approximating polynomial for $\mathsf{ SDU}_{N, R}^{\gamma_1, \gamma_2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Degree-d approximants transfer.
nodes.section: 6.4 Lower Bound for Entropy Comparison and Approximation

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Combined with \Cref{sduthm}, this implies that $\widetilde{\operatorname{deg}}(\mathsf{GapCmprEnt}^{\alpha, \beta}_{4N, 2R}) = \tilde{\Omega}(R^{1/2}).$
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 67 gives the bound.
nodes.section: 6.4 Lower Bound for Entropy Comparison and Approximation
